Equities posted weekly losses as bond vol hit tech/AI; NVDA reports Q2 FY27 on 8/26 (street $93-95B rev, bar very high) and Fed Chair Warsh speaks at Jackson Hole next week — he has signaled he welcomes higher long yields, so hawkish tail risk is live. Position-specific findings: WTI ran from $81-82 to $86.90 (Middle East premium + inflation), breaking my XOP short thesis (EIA sub-$80 Q3) and gutting the JETS fuel-windfall pillar just as the consumer contracts; healthcare had its best week since June 26 (+4%) on the Moderna/Merck mRNA phase-3 success, supporting XBI and making healthcare a top-momentum sector; KRE shows the widest YTD divergence from XLF since SVB (down >3% YTD) and a fiscal-driven long-end spike is the SVB-style risk for bank bond books, though steeper curve/loan growth/M&A keep analysts constructive — trim not cut; GDX benefits from gold at $4,600 approaching my $95-105 target zone; homebuilders are the cleanest new broken downtrend: XHB -3.9% trailing year, housing starts plunged 10% (8/19 print), mortgage rates pushing 7% with the long end at 19-year highs, builders defending revenue with incentives. Sources: CNBC/Yahoo market recaps 8/21, Bloomberg 8/17 bond selloff, CNBC 8/18-8/20 yields and Bessent/Warsh coverage, USAGOLD 8/21 metals, Fortune/Yahoo BTC 8/21, intellectia NVDA preview, stockanalysis/247wallst XHB and housing starts, Seeking Alpha XBI upgrade.

decisions.reason: The barbell is doing exactly what it was built for (+3.60% NAV, -1.94% max DD), and the one change this week was made for me by a standing order: the 2x BTC perp took profit at $78,229 for +40% on the leg. I am deliberately NOT restoring it yet — the mandate calls that leg contrarian, and re-levering long after BTC's biggest weekly gain since March 2024 (+22%), into the $80k test with thin weekend liquidity, is momentum-chasing, not contrarianism; the proceeds sit in 4%-yielding cash until price or funding resets. Every other leg was re-underwritten against the new fiscal-shock regime and passes: GLD 6% is the single best expression of a week where debt hit $40T, the dollar slid, and gold rose 5% to $4,600 — the crisis leg is finally paying; the 35% AI-infra sleeve goes into NVDA earnings (8/26) and Warsh's Jackson Hole speech with -20% stops handling the tail, and I choose not to de-risk it because the mandate assigns that sleeve the risk budget and the bond-vol drawdown in tech is precisely what the ballast wing exists to offset; MRK/JNJ just caught the mRNA-driven best healthcare week since June; XLU's bond-proxy headwind returned with the 30yr at 5.24%, but at 4% with AI power demand behind it, cutting it would be churn. Nothing else material changed, so nothing else moves.

The weekly re-rank forces three exits and two entries because the oil and rates facts flipped, not because I am restyling the book. XOP short is covered at a loss of thesis, not just price: WTI $86.90 vs my sub-$80 EIA anchor, with a Middle East premium rebuilding — a short against a rising commodity with a war catalyst is no longer a broken downtrend, it is fighting momentum. JETS is cut entirely: the position survived last week only because cheap fuel offset the cracking consumer, and fuel just rose ~6% while retail sales are contracting — both pillars are now against it, which under a momentum mandate is a rank flip, not a trim. KRE trims 13%->10% because a fiscally-driven long-end spike (30yr 5.33%, widest KRE/XLF divergence since SVB) attacks regional bank bond marks — the steepener/NIM story keeps it a top-5 long, but not the book's largest position into Jackson Hole. XLI trims 11%->9% because both cited tailwinds (cheaper energy inputs, cheaper capital) reversed this week. Replacements per the ranking: XLV enters at 8% as the fifth long — healthcare's +4% best-week-since-June on the Moderna/Merck mRNA phase-3 win is fresh cross-sectional leadership (sized moderate because it shares some factor exposure with XBI); XHB enters as the third short at 5% — a textbook broken downtrend (-3.9% trailing year in an up market) with a fresh catalyst (starts -10%, mortgage rates pinned near 7% by the fiscal long-end). XBI, GDX, XLY short, and MSOS short are retained on unchanged or strengthened theses; GDX gets a +15% take-profit added since gold at $4,600 puts my $95-105 target zone in reach. Gross drops 70%->65%; the freed 5% earns 4% in cash rather than being forced into a weak sixth-ranked long.
decisions.novelty: Zero symbol overlap with my Round-2 barbell in either direction — this book expresses the same fiscal-shock world through cross-sectional sector momentum (miners, small-cap biotech, homebuilder and discretionary shorts) rather than AI-infra compounders and mega-cap ballast, with GDX-vs-GLD and XLV-vs-MRK/JNJ the only factor-level echoes, both held at deduped size.

Trimmed 13%->10%: the fiscal long-end spike (30yr 5.33%, 19-yr high; widest KRE/XLF divergence since SVB) is the exact scenario that marks down regional bank bond books, but the steeper curve supports NIM and loan growth/M&A keep 2026 estimates rising — still a top-5 long, no longer the largest, with the -15% stop as the SVB-tail circuit breaker.

Breakout thesis accelerating: gold +~5% this week to $4,600 (highest since mid-May) on $40T debt, Treasury buybacks and a sliding dollar — the debasement regime is the miners' best case; +15% take-profit added because the $95-105 target zone is now in reach and momentum discipline means monetizing into strength, with the -15% stop unchanged.

New fifth long replacing JETS: healthcare rose 4%+ for its best week since June 26 on the Moderna/Merck mRNA phase-3 win, giving large-cap pharma fresh cross-sectional leadership with defensive earnings that also fit a cracking-consumer tape; sized at 8% rather than full because it shares partial factor exposure with XBI under the correlation-dedupe rule.

Held at 7%, thesis now double-confirmed: the consumer contraction (retail sales -0.6%, sentiment 51.0) is intact and the rate-relief risk I stopped against has inverted — long yields at 19-year highs raise financing costs on houses, cars and cards, hitting discretionary first.

New bottom-3 short replacing XOP: a genuine broken downtrend (-3.9% trailing year while the market rose ~20%) with a fresh catalyst — housing starts plunged 10% as mortgage rates push 7%, builders are buying revenue with incentives, and the fiscally-driven long end (30yr 5.24-5.33%) keeps the pressure structural; -12% stop guards a Bessent-buyback rate-relief squeeze.

Bottom-3 rank unchanged for a third week: persistent downtrend with no reversal catalyst surfaced, and no exposure to the rates/oil cross-currents that broke XOP; kept smallest for liquidity and squeeze risk.

decisions.name: Opus 5 carry
decisions.research_notes:
WHAT FIRED: my 3x BTC perp short stopped out 2026-08-20 at $78,181.80, returning $15.04 of a ~$40 margin leg — roughly -2.5% of NAV, and the bulk of my -1.60% drawdown. Verified the move: BTC ran ~22% on the week, its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, hitting $79.5k before settling $77-78k, driven by a short squeeze into the Treasury long-end buyback announcement plus Trump's push for the Clarity Act. Perp funding is only +0.0022%/8h (not stretched) but open interest is ~$56bn with fresh leverage rebuilding — i.e. the squeeze is over and new longs, not covering shorts, are now the marginal buyer.

MACRO. (1) The hike binary shrank: July CPI printed 0.1% m/m, 3.4% headline (-0.1pp), core 2.5% (-0.1pp), and September hike odds fell from ~42% to ~one-in-three. Warsh still gives the Jackson Hole keynote Friday 28 August, six days out, and has pledged a "regime change," so the event is live but less loaded than when I sized for it. (2) The real damage is at the long end, not the front: the 30-year hit a 19-YEAR high of ~5.20% and the 10-year sits at 4.71%. Bessent more than doubled long-end liquidity buybacks to $4bn+/operation across the 10-20y and 20-30y sectors from 9 September through 4 November. The initial 5-9bp rally fully unwound within a day; Deutsche's Saravelos called it "soft-form financial repression" and a sign of administration unease. (3) Dollar: DXY 98.80, a three-month low, helped by the repression signal and US/Japan FX intervention — down from 99.6 when I cut EM.

CREDIT — the week's most important finding. The high-yield index is still tight (ICE BofA HY OAS ~271bp on 12 Aug, 281bp on 27 July) but that average is a lie: CCC & lower OAS is at ~1,024bp, CCC loan spreads have widened over 300bp YTD, while BB loan spreads have marginally TIGHTENED to a ~6% yield, about a quarter of the CCC level. Commentators are explicitly calling it "a distressed tail wagging high yield spreads" and the widest sector dispersion in years — classic late-cycle bifurcation, with consumer confidence at record lows behind it. Loan defaults themselves remain low (LCD six-month forward ~1.69% by issuer count) but LMEs are ~two-thirds of default activity. Corroborating marks: SPHY 1-year total return 5.65% against a 7.20% yield, and CLOZ 1-year total return 5.05% against a 7.22% yield — both are already bleeding principal to fund the coupon. JAAA by contrast is fine and gathering assets: $50.67, AUM up to $30.0bn from $27bn, 4.91% yield, +4.89% 1-year.

ENERGY. Brent $94.46, +5% on the week and a second straight weekly gain on the unresolved Hormuz/US-Iran stalemate — far above the $87 I underwrote AMLP on. But AMLP was FLAT: $54.75, -0.29% on the week, beta 0.49, sitting just under a 52-week high of $55.66. So the leg did not capture the oil spike. It is a 7.43% distribution stream (record $1.03 paid 17 Aug), not an oil hedge, and I should stop describing it as one.

EQUITY/VOL. S&P 500 -1.4% on the week with tech -3%; energy the only real gainer among 11 sectors. VIX 15.13, up from 14.25 but still near the 2026 low. NLY $23.16 (up on the week despite the bear steepener), $3.00 dividend, 13 analysts Buy at a $24.23 target. EMLC $25.85, 6.14% yield.

decisions.reason: Two facts changed enough to move real weight, and one of my hedges is gone. First, the high-yield average is concealing a broken distribution: the index OAS is ~271bp near the tights while CCC & lower is at ~1,024bp and CCC loan spreads have widened 300bp+ this year against BB loans that actually TIGHTENED. That is late-cycle bifurcation, and both my sub-senior credit legs are already paying for it out of principal — SPHY returned 5.65% over a year on a 7.20% coupon, CLOZ 5.05% on a 7.22% coupon. The right response is not to leave credit but to move up the capital structure inside it, so SPHY goes to zero, CLOZ is cut, and the proceeds go to AAA CLO paper that sits above the tranche where the tail is repricing. Second, the specific event I paid carry to avoid got smaller while the force I was ignoring got bigger: hike odds fell 42%->33% on a benign 3.4%/2.5% CPI, but the 30-year printed a 19-YEAR high and the Treasury responded by doubling long-end buybacks — soft financial repression that is dollar-negative, and DXY is at a three-month low of 98.80. I underpaid for EM local carry last week on the opposite call, so I restore it. Third, I am not replacing the BTC short. It cost me ~2.5% of NAV stopping at $78,182, and re-shorting an asset six days after its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, into $56bn of open interest with fresh leverage rebuilding, would be a grudge rather than a thesis. The risk I actually need to blunt before Warsh speaks on 28 August is a simultaneous mark-down of every spread leg I own, and 19% cash at 4% APY does that at zero carrying cost instead of 3x leverage that can gap through its stop.
decisions.novelty: This book carries no leverage and no short at all for the first time — the entire risk budget is unlevered senior spread income plus a 19% cash buffer, and it is deliberately concentrated at the top of the loan capital structure (30% AAA CLO) rather than reaching down into the mezzanine and high-yield tail that every other income book is being paid to hold.

positions.thesis: The book's anchor, raised from 26 with money taken from one and two rungs below it. This week gave me the cleanest argument I have had for seniority: the loan market's tail is repricing hard — CCC spreads out 300bp+ year to date to ~1,024bp — while BB spreads actually tightened and the index average still reads a benign ~271bp. When an average is that far from its own tail, the honest trade is to own the part of the structure the tail cannot reach. AAA CLO tranches sit above 600+ deals' worth of subordination with thirty years and no AAA default, at SOFR+~120bp with effectively zero duration. It is also the only leg indifferent to both binaries in front of me: if Warsh is hawkish on 28 August the coupon simply resets higher, and if the 30-year keeps making 19-year highs it owns no duration to lose. Flows agree — AUM is $30.0bn, up from $27bn a fortnight ago, and the fund returned 4.89% over the year against a 4.91% yield, meaning it is paying its coupon out of income rather than principal, which is exactly what SPHY and CLOZ are not doing. I take the criticism that the spread over 4% cash is only about a point; that point is why this is 30 and not 40, with the rest sitting in actual cash. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk here is a liquidity gap and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own.

Trimmed from 18, and the reason is that I was wrong about what this leg is. Last week I raised it arguing it is the one holding paid by the very force damaging the others. Brent then went up 5% on the week to $94.46 on the unresolved Hormuz stalemate, the second straight weekly gain and well past the $87 I underwrote — and AMLP went nowhere, -0.29%, closing at $54.75 against a 52-week high of $55.66. With a beta of 0.49 and fee-based, volume-linked contracts, it does not capture oil spikes; that is by design and it is why the fund is a good carry holding, but it means my stated hedge property does not exist. What is real is the distribution: 7.43%, just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter paid 17 August, coverage guided through 2027, every top holding raising in H1, LNG exports at capacity and data-center power demand adding multi-year throughput, and contracts that escalate with CPI while my fixed-spread legs are marked down by it. So I keep it as the book's inflation-linked income sleeve and size it as that rather than as a hedge — and I trim because entering near the top of a 52-week range means the asymmetry is worse than it was, particularly if Hormuz ever does resolve from here. Wide -20% stop because this is still the book's most volatile leg and I want it to survive an oil round trip rather than be shaken out by one.

Restored above where I started, reversing last week's cut, because the trade I was hiding from got smaller and the trade I was ignoring got bigger. I cut this from 13 to 10 on the argument that a hawkish Warsh at Jackson Hole is a dollar-up, EM-FX-down event not priced at 42% hike odds. Since then July CPI printed 0.1% month over month with headline down to 3.4% and core to 2.5%, and hike odds fell to roughly one in three — the binary is still live but I overpaid to duck it. Meanwhile the genuinely important development runs the other way: the 30-year hit a 19-year high and the Treasury's answer was to more than double long-end buybacks from 9 September, which Deutsche Bank called soft-form financial repression and a sign of administration unease. A government that responds to its own long-end yields by buying them is a structurally weaker-currency government, and DXY is already at a three-month low of 98.80, helped by US/Japan intervention. Local-currency EM sovereign carry at a 6.14% yield with rate cuts still running in several large markets is the cleanest way in my universe to be paid for that, and it is the only leg here that is paid BY financial repression rather than marked down by it. -10% stop kept tight because local-currency drawdowns arrive through the exchange rate and arrive fast.

Cut from 14 for the same reason JAAA is raised, one rung lower down the same structure. BBB/BB CLO mezzanine at ~7.2% is a levered claim on precisely the single-B and CCC loan cohort where all of this year's spread widening has actually happened, and mezzanine gaps wider on a risk-off well before collateral deteriorates. The evidence that it has already begun is in the fund's own numbers: a 5.05% total return over the past year against a 7.22% distribution means roughly two points of NAV have gone to fund the coupon. I keep 10 rather than zero because the underlying collateral is genuinely fine at the top — payment defaults are low, the LCD six-month forward rate is ~1.69% by issuer count, BB loan spreads tightened this year — and because floating-rate coupons remain the right place to sit while the long end is the volatile part of the curve. What I no longer accept is being paid three and a half points over cash for subordination in a market whose distressed tail is visibly wagging the average. -15% stop respects that gapping behaviour.

Raised from 5 on a specific, dated catalyst rather than on hope. I cut this to 5 because a bear steepener is the curve shape that marks down a 5.6x-levered agency book, and because Annaly's own disclosure blamed spread widening on rate volatility. Rate volatility is now getting an announced official counterparty: from 9 September through 4 November the Treasury will buy at least $4bn per operation across the 10-20y and 20-30y sectors, explicitly to support liquidity after the 30-year hit a 19-year high. That is a direct suppressant of the long-end volatility that is the stated source of the pain, and it is calendared rather than speculative. The stock has already stopped going down — $23.16, up on a week when the 10-year sat at 4.71% — while the fundamentals keep delivering: dividend raised to $0.75 from $0.70 on $0.79 EAD, book value $20.15, 5.5% economic return in Q2 and 6.9% in the half, net interest spread up 8bp to 1.50%, and 13 analysts at Buy with a $24.23 target. I go to 7 and not back to 8 because the buyback rally unwound inside a day and strategists were near-unanimous that it does not fix the fiscal or inflation problem underneath. -15% stop.

Held flat at 4, the first week I have not cut it, because the tape finally turned toward the structure rather than against it. My objection has been that writing index calls is worth size at VIX 18 and not at VIX 14, and VIX is 15.13 — better than the 14.25 low but still cheap, so I am not adding. What changed is the underlying: after three straight weeks of record highs the S&P fell 1.4% with technology down more than 3%, and a capped-upside, premium-collecting structure is at its best in exactly that flat-to-down tape rather than in the melt-up that was punishing it. Two honest caveats keep it small. The 11.85% distribution carries a 331% payout ratio, so a large part of what I am collecting is return of capital rather than harvested premium; and the fund is 8.25% NVIDIA, 6.74% Apple and 5.56% Microsoft, which is concentrated single-name beta wearing an income label. It stays at 4 because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash. For the same reason I again decline to add SVXY: with VIX near the year's low, selling variance insurance is selling it at the cheapest possible price.

decisions.name: Opus 5 dispersion
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK CHECK (prices through 2026-08-21 close).

Indices: S&P 500 closed 7,674.37 (+0.43% Friday), Nasdaq Composite 26,180.45, Dow 53,277.01 — but all three posted WEEKLY LOSSES on a long-end bond sell-off. 10y held ~4.71%, 30y rose past 5.27% (from ~5.21% a week earlier) on term-premium/AI-issuance/deficit concerns; Treasury's doubled long-end buyback produced a rally that fizzled. September Fed odds are genuinely two-sided: roughly one-in-three priced on energy-shock inflation risk, while Goldman argues a hike is now "very unlikely" on softer retail sales and a cooling labour market. Crypto: BTC +22% on the week to ~$77-78k, its best week in two years. I hold no crypto in any form — spot, perp or proxy — so none of the six standing orders that fired across the field touched me, and the BTC move is not a reason to change a book whose entire construction is single-name residual volatility against an index short. I checked rather than assumed.

THE EVENT THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS — MRNA. On 19 Aug Moderna and Merck reported that intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157/V940) met its primary endpoint on recurrence-free survival AND the key secondary on distant metastasis-free survival in Phase 3 adjuvant melanoma with Keytruda vs Keytruda alone. MRNA closed +176.97% at $174.38 that day, gave back 25% Thursday (~$18bn of market cap), then rallied ~8.9% Friday to close $145.13. Against my ~$59 entry that is roughly +146%, which on a 4.25% target weight has drifted the leg to about 10% of NAV — more than double any other basket name and, on its own, the great majority of the round's +5.64% cumulative P&L. Consensus PT is $91.39 with a Hold rating against a $145 price, and the 52-week range is now $22.28-$176.66. This is the most extreme dispersion outcome the book has produced and it is precisely why the mandate is equal-weight.

OTHER LEGS. CHTR: the $34.5bn Cox merger CLOSED Thursday 20 Aug, simultaneously with the Liberty Broadband all-stock deal; combined company now 37m customers across 45 states, stock -4.7% on the close. The regulatory binary I owned is spent, but the integration clock (Spectrum lineup into former Cox markets from mid-September, parent renamed Cox Communications within a year) replaces it. NEM: gold traded above $4,500/oz for a third consecutive weekly gain, +4% Wednesday on the Treasury buyback news, and NEM's market cap rose ~9.5% on the week — the leg I added last week for orthogonality was the leg that worked while equities fell. OXY: crude up nearly 6% on the week ($86-94 depending on grade/print) on US-Iran/Hormuz escalation, Brent to a three-week high of $91.02; OXY ~$59.80 mid-week. CF: nitrogen tight, 98% ammonia capacity utilisation, Blue Point One permitted and construction started in August, dividend +20%, H1 EPS $8.71, stock +55% YTD — bear case is gas cost. DLTR: Jefferies upgraded Underperform to Hold on 19 Aug with the PT going $85 to $135; stock ~$132; July traffic +4.5% and Q2 comp estimate raised to +3.4% vs guide of 2.5-3.5%. Q2 prints pre-open Thursday 27 Aug (revenue consensus $4.85bn, EPS $1.11 vs guide $1.00-1.15) — I hold through it. QCOM ~$162, -21% over three months and 36% below its 52-week high, auto revenue +61% y/y against a 20% decline in non-GAAP EPS, consensus PT ~$204. BA: FAA granted Type Inspection Authorization Phase 4B for the 777X — the largest remaining supervised test segment — offset by brake-energy testing proving harder than expected. HUM, COF, RCL, GM: no new thesis-relevant information; COF confirmed Discover delinquencies tracking in line with integration assumptions and $2.7bn of pre-tax synergies by 2027.

CONCLUSION: no leg's thesis broke, so the basket's composition stands. What changed is the shape of the book, not its content — one leg has become ~10% of NAV in a structure whose entire risk premise is that no single residual dominates.

decisions.reason: This is a weight rebalance, not a change of view: eleven of twelve theses are intact and I am changing no holdings. MRNA's Phase 3 melanoma result took the leg from ~$59 to $145.13 and let it drift to roughly 10% of NAV against a 4.25% target, so the book is no longer the equal-weight structure my mandate describes — one name at ~100% realised volatility now dominates the variance of a portfolio whose whole premise is that twelve mutually uncorrelated residuals each contribute equally. Equal-weight dispersion books harvest by rebalancing, and refusing to trim here would be an undeclared bet on post-event drift in a name trading 59% above a $91 consensus target that already gave back 25% in a single session two days ago. Trimming back to 4.25% also restores the 51/47 beta straddle: the long side had grown against a static index short, leaving the book quietly net long at the exact moment the indices posted a weekly loss on a long-end bond sell-off. The only other change is MRNA's stop, widened from -22% to -35%, because a stop calibrated for a 72%-vol biotech will now be taken out by an ordinary day in a name that has moved +177% and -25% on consecutive sessions — and being stopped out on noise is how you destroy a dispersion asset rather than harvest it. Costs are ~2bps a side on a handful of legs, trivial against carrying a 10% position I never sized for.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to constrain; this Round-3 book remains its own construction — twelve high-residual-volatility large caps across eight sectors held equal-weight against a residual-vol-minimising 28% SPY / 19% QQQ index short, with no crypto, no leverage and no directional index view anywhere in it.

positions.thesis: Biotech, and the leg that just proved the mandate. Intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157) with Merck met both its primary recurrence-free survival endpoint and the secondary distant metastasis-free survival endpoint in Phase 3 adjuvant melanoma on 19 August; the stock closed +176.97% at $174.38, fell 25% the next day and closed the week at $145.13. Nothing in that sequence has any index content whatsoever, which is the definition of the asset I am paid to hold. I am cutting it back to basket weight from the ~10% it drifted to, not because the story got worse but because a single 100%-vol residual at 10% of NAV is a concentrated bet, not dispersion. The debate is now maximally two-sided and therefore maximally useful: intismeran runs in multiple further Phase 2 and 3 cancer trials so the platform optionality is real, against a $91.39 consensus target versus a $145 price, a Hold rating, and cash guided to $4.7-5.2bn at year end with burn still the bear case. Stop widened to -35% because -22% is now inside a single normal session for this name.

Cable, still the highest residual volatility available at this market cap and none of it with index or AI-factor content. The $34.5bn Cox merger and the Liberty Broadband all-stock deal both closed Thursday 20 August, taking the company to 37m customers across 45 states and making it the largest US internet and video provider by subscriber count; the stock fell 4.7% on the close. The regulatory binary is spent, but it is replaced by an integration clock that is entirely company-specific: Spectrum's full lineup rolls into former Cox markets from mid-September, the parent renames to Cox Communications within a year, and the combined balance sheet must be executed against the 2038/2041 secured-note exchange and shelf. Set against 172k of broadband subscriber losses in Q2 versus 406k mobile line adds to 12.5m, and a stock that has halved inside a $111.55-$285.82 range. Wide 22% stop because the tape here is violent in both directions.

Gold mining, and the leg that did its job this week: gold traded above $4,500/oz for a third straight weekly gain, jumping 4% Wednesday after Treasury said it would double long-end buybacks, and NEM's market cap rose ~9.5% while all three major indices posted weekly losses. That is the correlation diversifier behaving exactly as the mandate's second criterion requires — measured beta ~0.4, near-zero correlation to the other eleven legs, and structurally long the state of the world (rising term premium, sticky inflation, softer dollar) that would hurt the rest of the basket. The company-specific two-sidedness is unchanged: record $2.2bn Q2 free cash flow, $1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares repurchased and FY26 reaffirmed at ~$8.5bn FCF, against attributable production falling to ~5.3moz on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions and AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz. Held at basket weight after a strong run rather than added to.

Managed care and still the purest single-name scatter in the screen: ~52% vol, ~99% idiosyncratic, measured beta 0.35, driven by MA rate notices, star ratings and utilisation trend with no index analogue. Q2 adjusted EPS $7.61 on revenue +26%, and the sell side has kept converging since late July (Morgan Stanley to Equal Weight 4 Aug, Piper to Overweight 30 July, Barclays PT $407). The bear case remains fully live and fully company-specific: 2026 star ratings landed at a 3.61 average with only 20% of members in 4-star-plus plans, carrying a ~$3.5bn net headwind and 2026 adjusted EPS guided to at least $9.00 against a $12.00 prior consensus. The recovery path — the 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members, material 2027 star improvement, top-quartile by bonus year 2028 and the 3% pretax margin target — runs on a dated regulatory clock the index cannot price. No new information this week.

Consumer finance, and the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large cap in its sector, with volatility that is calendar-driven rather than macro. Management confirmed the Discover integration is on schedule: debit customers are already migrated onto the Discover network, credit card portfolio conversion runs from late 2026 to full conversion by early 2027, and delinquency trends in the Discover book are tracking in line with integration assumptions with charge-offs not exceeding modelled expectations. $2.7bn of pre-tax synergies targeted by 2027, and owning the network captures interchange previously paid away to Visa and Mastercard. Q2 adjusted EPS $5.81 against $4.85 consensus. The stock is down nearly 20% in 2026, so the migration-execution and consumer-credit bear cases are genuinely priced — exactly the two-sidedness the mandate wants, on milestones with no index analogue.

Discount retail: ~46% vol, ~96% idiosyncratic, driven by comp-store prints and banner restructuring, with a trade-down profile that runs against the cyclicals elsewhere in the basket rather than with them. The Section 301 forced-labour tariffs were finalised 23 July so the import-cost shock predates my entry. The Q2 print lands pre-open Thursday 27 August — inside my holding period and deliberately so — against guidance of $4.8-4.9bn sales, comps +2.5-3.5% and adjusted EPS $1.00-1.15, with revenue consensus $4.85bn and EPS consensus $1.11. Jefferies upgraded from Underperform to Hold on 19 August and took its target from $85 to $135 against a ~$132 stock, citing July traffic +4.5% and lifting its Q2 comp estimate to +3.4%. That raises the bar into the print, which cuts both ways and is the point: a dated, company-specific binary with a consumer trading down after a 0.6% retail-sales decline as the tailwind.

Nitrogen fertiliser: the return function is the natural gas feedstock spread and crop economics, with essentially no equity-index loading, which is what makes it the cleanest correlation diversifier available while a single AI factor still dominates cross-asset correlation. H1 2026 net earnings $1.34bn ($8.71 per diluted share) on $2.18bn adjusted EBITDA, Q2 net earnings $727m, production at 98% of available ammonia capacity, Blue Point One permitted with construction commencing in August, mid-cycle EBITDA target lifted to $2.9bn, nitrogen tightness guided through 2030 and the dividend raised 20% to $0.60. The bear case is live and specific: the stock is +55% YTD, and the same geopolitical gas-supply constraint tightening the nitrogen market is what raises CF's own feedstock cost. Gas and grain, not the S&P.

Cruise: ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component sitting on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adjusted EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, record booking activity and accelerated buybacks, against fuel, airfare and softness in Mediterranean and West-Mexico itineraries. The fuel side of that bear case sharpened this week with crude up nearly 6% on US-Iran and Hormuz escalation and Brent at a three-week high of $91.02 — which is exactly why I hold this alongside OXY rather than instead of it. Tighter 18% stop because it carries the highest beta in the basket.

The one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer concentration rather than the AI capex cycle — the stock is down 21% over three months and sits 36% below its 52-week high while the AI complex has run, which is the dissociation I want. Fiscal Q3 revenue $9.95bn beat consensus by 2.4% despite falling 4% y/y, non-GAAP EPS $2.21 was down 20% y/y and fiscal Q4 guidance is $2.05-2.25; Apple modem revenue falls faster than previously flagged from fiscal Q4 as Apple's in-house share rises. Against that, automotive revenue grew 61% y/y, the 1 September price increases land, initial hyperscaler datacentre shipments are due December 2026, and consensus sits near $204. Customer concentration resolving on its own clock is the residual. Sized at basket weight, not on conviction.

Energy, the basket's macro-offset leg: crude-driven returns are the classic low-correlation block and measured beta is near zero. Crude rose nearly 6% this week on the US-Iran dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, with Brent closing at $91.02, a three-week high, and OXY at ~$59.80 mid-week. The Q2 print was a blowout — adjusted EPS $2.40 vs $1.87 on revenue $8.33bn vs $7.18bn, realised crude $96.78, production above the top of guidance, Midstream pre-tax $961m above guide and $1.9bn of debt retired in one quarter against the $10bn target. Held for orthogonality rather than for a crude view, and specifically because it is the leg that pays when an energy shock hurts RCL, GM, DLTR and COF; the symmetric risk is that Iran is signalling a settlement, which would gap oil down. Deleveraging remains a company-specific catalyst in its own right.

Aerospace. 777X certification is arguably the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap, with no index analogue and zero AI-factor loading, and it moved on both sides this week: the FAA granted Type Inspection Authorization Phase 4B — the largest remaining FAA-supervised test segment, covering avionics, handling qualities and pilot-systems interaction — while brake-energy testing proved a bigger obstacle than expected. First delivery is promised for 2027 and has already slipped once. The operating base is turning underneath it: record $715bn backlog, 171 Q2 deliveries, +$631m free cash flow after four quarters of burn against a $1-3bn FY guide, and the 737 MAX 7 now FAA-approved. Argus's 11 August double-upgrade against RBC's more conservative certification assumptions keeps the debate usefully two-sided.

Autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. The return function is tariffs, pricing and input costs rather than anything the index trades on: $2.5-3.5bn of gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity and DRAM cost against a $500m refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, with adjusted EPS guidance raised to $12-14. The DRAM line is the whole point — GM's cost base is directly hurt by the same memory squeeze lifting the AI complex, making this one of very few large caps carrying a negative loading on the factor currently dominating cross-asset correlation, which is worth more to this book than any view on unit sales. July retail sales showed the weakness concentrated in autos, and a higher crude price is a further headwind; that bear case doing its work is why I hold the name for scatter, not direction.

Primary hedge, held at the mandate's stated size and rebalanced back to it after the long basket grew against a static short. A long book that is managed care, consumer finance, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, mobile semis, energy, biotech, aerospace, cable, autos and gold carries broad-market beta rather than Nasdaq beta, so the broad index is the residual-vol-minimising instrument against it. At 28% SPY plus 19% QQQ the hedge is worth ~0.50 of beta against ~0.49 from the restored 51% basket on fundamental betas — net index beta straddling zero, the mandate's operative constraint. This week is the argument for the discipline: all three indices fell on a long-end bond sell-off with the 30y through 5.27%. No take-profit — a hedge that closes itself into an index drawdown would leave the book 51% net long at the exact moment it is doing its job.

Secondary hedge, held at the mandate's 28:19 split, which was calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows. I re-cut it to 16% for a week on one week of observed basket beta and reversed that; I am not repeating the error, and rising term premium — the 30y through 5.27% on AI-related issuance and deficit concerns — is a reason to carry the long-duration hedge rather than to guess at its size. The book's only real Nasdaq exposure now sits in QCOM and MRNA, both held for reasons orthogonal to the AI factor, so this leg strips out a factor loading I do not want rather than expressing a view. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

decisions.name: Opus 5 mean reversion
decisions.research_notes:
Verified every leg against 8/21 closes plus the week's news. Market: S&P -1.37%, Nasdaq -2.00%, Dow -0.77% on the week on a treasury selloff; Friday bounced (S&P 7,674.37 +0.43%). My book is +0.96% since the 8/17 entry, so roughly 230bps of relative gain in a down tape. I hold no crypto in any form, so the BTC run from ~$63k to ~$78k and the six standing orders it fired across the field touch me only indirectly — I checked COIN ($185.21, +5.1% Friday) as a candidate replacement short cluster and declined it.

WMT: Q2 FY27 on 8/20 was a revenue and EPS beat ($187.9B vs $186.8B; $0.81 adj vs ~$0.74) with a raised revenue guide, but the stock fell 8.9% to $103.84 and kept falling Friday to $102.41-$104.28. The reason matters: FY adjusted EPS guided $2.80-2.87 against ~$2.90 consensus, US comps +2.6% against +3.8% expected, and a 750bps tariff-refund windfall drove the profit beat while a 125bps Maximum Fair Price drug headwind pressured the underlying line. Analysts kept Overweight/Buy but cut targets across the board — JPM $137 to $125, RBC $137 to $131, Guggenheim $135 to $130, Wells Fargo $140 to $120; JPM and BofA are calling it a buying opportunity. Positives: first double-digit incremental eCommerce margins, US Marketplace +52%, ads +38%.

XLE/energy: XLE closed $63.64, sitting against a 52-week high of $64.70, +52.99% on a one-year total-return basis. Brent is now roughly $91-92 with WTI in the mid-$80s; EIA has global inventories drawing 3.8M bpd in Q3. Diplomatically the situation moved away from resolution, not toward it: Iran's parliament speaker issued preconditions Tuesday (sanctions relief, end of military threats) before Hormuz reopens, Trump publicly stepped back from diplomacy, and on Thursday declared "economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale" — an "economic D-Day" targeting oil smuggling, currency swaps, ship registries. US pump prices are up nearly $1 year over year to $4.11.

TSLA: closed $362.86, +5.14% Friday, on Clark County/Nevada clearing driverless robotaxi operation in Las Vegas. 52-week range $297.38-$498.83, so the $297-298 washout low held and the higher-low sequence resolved upward on an actual catalyst rather than a broker note.

Others: APP $305.77, down another ~2.2%, no reclaim of the gap, still the worst-ranked name on both lookbacks. AXP ~$332 versus $342.48, no news, extending the laggard screen. CSCO $110.61 versus $111.55, unchanged since its 8/13 gap-down. HONA ~$165.5, essentially flat, holding the reclaim off the $150.03 low; average target $218.38 (range $175-256). SNPS just under $400 into Q3 FY26 on 8/26 after the close, consensus $3.67 EPS on $2.44B revenue (+40.3% y/y), $11B backlog, two straight ~6% EPS beats. PEG ~$75.60, down only fractionally in a week featuring both a bond selloff and a down tape — the single condition that should hurt a bond proxy most.

decisions.reason: Two premises broke in opposite directions and both were sizing premises rather than direction premises. First, WMT was carried at 14% explicitly as the low-beta ballast against four gap-down names; a 9% single-day drop makes it the largest one-day move in my book, so it is no longer ballast and cannot keep ballast-sized weight. Worse for the thesis, this was not a beat-and-raise sold on a secondary line item like CSCO or AXP — the FY EPS guide came in below consensus and US comps missed by 120bps, so the earnings trend turned genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the exact standard I use to cap PEG at 7%. I cut to 10% rather than exiting because at $102-104 it is ~23% below the May high with every major broker holding Overweight and targets $120-131 above spot, and selling the whole position into the second down day would be selling the setup at the low. Second, the XLE short goes to zero. Its one measurable claim was that XLE discounted ~$90 crude while Brent sat at $82; Brent is now $91-92, so the gap has not merely closed, it has inverted — at $63.64 XLE is arguably cheap to the commodity rather than rich. The single catalyst I named for keeping the stub, a Hormuz reopening deal that had been reported as close once, moved further away this week: Iran issued preconditions, Trump abandoned diplomacy and announced unprecedented economic warfare. I will not hold a short whose stated premise has inverted and whose only path to profit is a war ending, any more than I would buy it because the war continues. Redeployment follows my own written rule that I add to turns in progress and not to knives: TSLA is the one confirmed turn, so it gets +2; AXP and CSCO are the low-beta legs that now have to do the job WMT vacated, so they take +2 each at prices no worse than last week; APP is still the knife and gets nothing despite being the worst-ranked name. Cash rises 13% to 17% specifically because removing the short leaves the book with no hedge at all, and I would rather pay for that with 4% cash than with a position I no longer believe in.
decisions.novelty: I manage only this Round 3 book and run no Round 2 book, so the overlap constraint is not binding; the distinguishing feature of this book remains a rank-based bottom-decile long list against a deliberately abandoned energy short, now expressed long-only with cash as the hedge.

positions.thesis: Raised from 12% to 14% and now the top weight, because the ballast job WMT was hired for has to go somewhere and AXP is the only leg that has actually done it. It closed around $332 against $342.48 last week with no company news at all, which deepens the laggard screen on both lookbacks and leaves it roughly 14% below the $387 high. The original setup is unchanged and still unresolved: a beat-and-raise sold on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the stated bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. Its zero AI-capex exposure is why it sits out melt-up weeks and is exactly what I want when the capex complex unwinds. I size up on a price decline with no information change, which is the one condition under which averaging down is not knife-catching.

Held at 12% with no trade. It closed $305.77 after another ~2.2% decline and still has not reclaimed the gap, so it remains the knife I described last week and gets no addition despite being the worst-ranked name on both my lookbacks — that is the whole point of the discipline. But a 2% drift down is not the 9.8% break that justified cutting 16% to 12%, and cutting again on it would be churn dressed as risk management. Nothing fundamental has changed: Q2 net income grew 54.5% to $1.27B on an 84% adjusted EBITDA margin, Q3 is guided to $2.055-2.085B or +46-48% year over year, and the one-percent revenue shortfall traces to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. Near $100B of market cap that is roughly 20x annualized earnings on a business compounding near 50%. The crowded-momentum-unwind bear case is still winning, which is why the weight stays where I put it rather than going up.

Raised from 10% to 12% because this is the only leg in the book where the turn stopped being a chart pattern and became an event. It closed $362.86, up 5.14% Friday on Clark County clearing driverless robotaxi operation in Las Vegas — a regulatory approval, not a broker reiteration, which matters because I wrote last week that the decline was fundamental and regulatory in origin and would therefore recover more slowly than a pure flow shock. A regulatory catalyst is precisely the kind of news that shortens that timeline. The $297.38 low has held, the higher-low sequence off the 7/29 print has now resolved upward, and against the $419.77 starting price and a $498.83 52-week high the reversion is still only partly paid. I add two points and not more because I am adding into strength and the position has already been sized up once on this same turn.

Raised from 9% to 11%. It closed $110.61 against $111.55 at entry — a full week in which the market fell 1.37% and Cisco did nothing, meaning neither the dislocation nor the thesis has moved. The setup is intact: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next quarter guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B or +15% at the midpoint, and an 8.4% one-day drop caused entirely by gross-margin mix from hyperscaler AI orders. That is the market repricing mix inside a revenue guide 7% above the Street. I add here rather than to WMT because this is the version of that structure where the guide went up, not down. It also has to carry more of the low-beta, cash-generative, dividend-paying load now that WMT has been demoted. Stops stay at the tighter -15%/+18% rather than mandate-standard 30/30 because this entered on the one-week leg of my ranking as a dislocation buy from near a 52-week high, not as a deep-drawdown buy, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller.

Cut from 14% to 10%. I underwrote the 8/20 print rather than dodging it and it went against me: the stock fell 8.9% to $103.84 and extended to $102.41 on Friday, its worst earnings reaction in ten quarters. The four-point cut is not a directional retreat, it is the removal of a sizing rationale that no longer exists — 14% was the weight of a low-beta ballast leg, and a name that just delivered the largest single-day loss in my book is not ballast. The content of the miss reinforces that: revenue beat at $187.9B and adjusted EPS beat at $0.81, but FY adjusted EPS guided $2.80-2.87 against ~$2.90 consensus, US comps decelerated to +2.6% against +3.8% expected, and 750bps of the margin expansion came from tariff refunds against a 125bps Maximum Fair Price headwind. By my own PEG standard that is an earnings trend turning genuinely negative rather than optically so, and I cap weight when that happens. I keep 10% because the reversion case actually improved on price: at ~$103 it is roughly 23% below the May high and now unambiguously in the bottom decile this mandate exists to own, eCommerce hit double-digit incremental margins for the first time with Marketplace +52% and ads +38%, and every major broker held its rating while cutting targets to $120-131 — all still above spot. I do not add, because it fell two days running with no reclaim and my rule is that I add to turns and not to knives.

Held at 10% with no trade. It closed around $165.5, essentially unchanged, in a week the S&P fell 1.37% — so the reclaim of the $150.03 capitulation low is holding rather than fading, which is what I needed to see after adding last week. That is quiet confirmation, not fresh evidence, so it earns no additional weight. The cause of the drawdown still distinguishes it from the guide-downs that have cost me: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which defers revenue against end demand nobody questions. The average target of $218.38 against a $175 low estimate still sits well above spot even after the August cuts. It stays capped at 10% because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters and the freshly spun-off holder base can still produce supply.

Held at 7% into Wednesday's print, deliberately and without resizing. It sits just under $400 against $412 last week, still roughly 39% below the $651.73 high, with full-year guidance raised to $9.625-9.705B revenue and $14.72-14.80 EPS on 42% revenue growth. Q3 FY26 lands 8/26 after the close against consensus of $3.67 EPS on $2.44B, or +40.3% revenue growth, carrying an $11B backlog and two consecutive ~6% EPS beats. This is the event that resolves Design IP softness and the Ansys integration in one direction or the other, and 7% is the size I chose precisely so I could hold it without needing to be right. Trimming it now would be paying costs to avoid a catalyst I already sized for, and adding would be buying a coin flip; both are worse than doing nothing.

Held at 7%, with one genuine update in its favour. Last week I flagged that PEG failed to respond to a dovish CPI/PPI print and that non-response to a favorable catalyst is a warning. This week ran the opposite test: a sharp treasury selloff that dominated the tape, plus a down week for equities, is the single combination that should punish a bond proxy hardest, and PEG closed near $75.60 essentially unchanged. Failing to fall on bad news is the mirror image of failing to rise on good news, and it partly answers the concern rather than deepening it. It remains a regulated New Jersey T&D utility with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear, a ~3.5% yield, 56 consecutive years of dividends and a Buy consensus implying ~17% upside, pinned at the bottom of its range. Its value here is structural: with the XLE short gone it is the only leg with neither AI/tech beta nor correlation to the gap-down names. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely rather than optically negative, which is the wrong ingredient for a reversion name and the same test that just cost WMT four points.

decisions.name: Opus 5 event driven
decisions.research_notes:
I manage only a Round 3 book, so the Round-2 overlap constraint does not bind.

WHAT EXPIRED. Six of my nine legs reached the end of the 20-session horizon their edge is measured over on 08-20/08-21: LMT, RTX, TMO, SLB, THC (all 07-23/07-24 PEAD gaps) and TSLA (07-23 capitulation gap). Only TEAM (gap 08-07, window to ~09-04) survives. I verified the tape rather than assuming: LMT closed 563.57 on 08-21 versus my ~582.60 fill on 07-24 — it rolled over hard in the final three sessions (607.17 on 08-18 to 563.57), so that drift failed inside its window and the defence complex cracked alongside it (L3Harris CEO Kubasik stepped down 08-17, LMT/RTX both lower). THC by contrast delivered fully: it is on the mid-cap 52-week-high list for 08-20 at +39.5% over the past month at 10.2x earnings. TSLA delivered too — closed 362.86 on 08-21, +5.14% on Friday and a third straight up week on Nevada clearing up to 5,000 paid robotaxis in Clark County and the Cybercab event. Both come out at expiry anyway, exactly as ISRG and NFLX did last week: holding past the window converts a tested edge into an untested view.

NVDA. Priced 216.85 on 08-21 versus 225.16 when I underwrote it — the pre-announcement premium I bought at 6% on 08-17 did not appear; it cost ~3.7%. It reports Q2 FY27 after the close on 08-26 (consensus ~$92bn revenue, EPS $2.08). I pre-committed at entry to take the premium off at this reassessment and stand aside for the print, and the leg losing money on the exact effect I flagged as published-literature rather than my own measured sample makes that easier, not harder.

MACRO CONTEXT (checked, deliberately not sized on). Ugly week: S&P and Nasdaq posted weekly losses, info tech -3% over five sessions, Nasdaq 100 five straight down days, 30-year Treasury yield at its highest in nearly two decades, oil up on renewed Middle East tension, Walmart -9.15% on 08-20 on weak comps and $4 gas commentary. Bitcoin ran hard (I hold no crypto in any form, so the six standing orders that fired across the field are not my problem). None of this is a dated catalyst, so none of it changes sizing.

SCREEN FOR NEW SIGNALS — this is the important finding. I screened every large gap of the last three weeks against my two filters and almost nothing qualified.
PEAD (needs >6% up-gap, >2x volume, prior 20 sessions >+10%):
- SMCI: PASSES. 31.60 to 37.61 on 08-12 = +19.02% on 165.7m shares versus a ~35m base (>4x); prior 20 sessions 28.31 (07-10) to 31.60 = +11.6%. FY26 revenue $39.1bn vs $22.0bn, Q4 gross margin 17.5% vs 9.5%, Q1 FY27 guide $14.5-15.5bn against $11.68bn consensus, FY27 $65-72bn; independent investigation closed; PT raises 08-17. Now 37.24.
- HRB: PASSES. 46.67 to 54.18 on 08-12 = +16.09% on 8.4m shares versus 1.5-2.5m (3-5x); prior 20 sessions 39.12 (07-08) to 46.67 = +19.3%. Now 53.68.
- MRK: FAILS trend. +12.60% gap 08-19 (135.17 to 152.20) on 32.4m shares, but prior 20 sessions 126.26 to 135.17 = +7.1%, under the +10% filter. The intismeran/Keytruda Phase 3 melanoma win is a genuinely hard catalyst and de-risks the LOE cliff, but it is a readout drift I have no measured sample for. Skipped.
- EL: FAILS trend. +16.30% on 08-19 (84.27 to 98.01) but prior 20 sessions 82.37 to 84.27 = +2.3%.
- TWLO: FAILS trend badly. +24.89% on 08-07 but prior 20 sessions 218.60 to 193.20 = -11.6%.
- LITE: FAILS trend. +13.63% on 08-12, prior 20 sessions +2.3%.
- FTDR: FAILS trend (+4.4%) and has already given back 8% of the gap.
- TGT: FAILS gap. Only +4.28% on 08-19 despite the raise; prior trend passed at +10.3%.
- ROST: FAILS both. Faded to +4.39% on 08-21 and prior 20 sessions -1.5%.
CAPITULATION (needs >6% down-gap, prior 20 sessions <-10%): ZERO qualifiers. Every large down-gap this month happened in a name that was NOT already broken — WMT -9.15% on 08-20 with prior 20d +4.5%; ONON -20.29% on 08-11 with prior 20d +2.3%; WOLF -9.42% on 08-20 with prior 20d -0.6%; COTY -9.24% on 08-20 with prior 20d +11%; TTD -21.90% on 08-07 with prior 20d -7.3% (nearest miss); BIO -32.4% on 08-18 after a run-up. These are fundamental repricings from strength, not the indiscriminate liquidation my n=463 rule is measured on. I will not relabel them.

MERGER ARB. CRH/Arcosa: $150 all-cash, $8.5bn EV at 11.5x 2026E EBITDA, signed 06-22, DEFM14A filed 08-03 and mailed 08-04, special meeting dated 09-04. HSR filed 07-06 (30-day period lapsed with no second request reported), Australia 07-21, Mexico 07-23. ACA closed 144.90 on 08-21 — a 3.52% gross spread that has sat in a tight band since announcement, which is the volatility-collapse condition my mandate specifies. Downside on a break is roughly the $127 pre-deal level, about -12 to -15%.

decisions.reason: Six of nine legs hit the end of their measured 20-session window on 08-20/08-21 and NVDA reached the pre-committed exit ahead of its 08-26 print, so 68% of the book had to come off on the calendar rather than on a view — the same rule I applied to ISRG and NFLX last week, and the reason I apply it is visible in LMT, which broke from 607.17 on 08-18 to 563.57 on 08-21 and finished below my fill after four weeks of working. The replacement problem is the real story: I screened every >6% gap of the last three weeks against my filters and only two names passed. Q2 earnings season is over, which is precisely when an earnings-gap signal generator produces nothing, and the capitulation cohort produced zero qualifiers because every large down-gap this month (WMT, ONON, WOLF, COTY, TTD) occurred in a name that was not already down 10% over 20 sessions — those are repricings from strength, not the liquidation my rule is measured on. So I redeploy only where the tape actually gave me a signal and hold the rest in cash at 4% rather than manufacture trades that fail the filters the edge is conditioned on. Cash is a position I am choosing, not a failure to decide: the next underwriting opportunity is the early-September reporting wave, and I would rather be flat into it than long six names I cannot justify.
decisions.novelty: I run only a Round 3 book, so the overlap constraint does not bind; the book is nonetheless almost entirely new — the defence, healthcare, energy and mega-cap-tech complex is gone and replaced by an AI-hardware PEAD, a counter-cyclical tax-prep PEAD, and a dated merger-arb, none of which existed here last week.

positions.thesis: PEAD, held unchanged at 13% and now the only survivor of the roll — its 20-session window runs to ~09-04, which is why it carries the book's event exposure across the gap between earnings seasons. Signal unchanged: reported after the close 08-06, gapped +35.31% on 08-07 from 110.16 to 149.07 on 20m+ shares against a ~4m base, prior 20 sessions roughly +20%, filled 08-10 at 155.24 at a one-session lag dead centre of the rule's strongest window. It closed 171.81 on 08-21, +10.7% from my fill, and the point worth noting is that it made that gain during a week in which info tech shed 3% and the Nasdaq 100 fell five sessions running — the drift is holding against its own sector's tape, not riding it. Fundamentals behind the persistence are unchanged: revenue +28% to $1.8bn with cloud accelerating to +31%, RPO +44% to $4.8bn, ARR $6.6bn, GAAP EPS +$0.55 from -$0.09, Q1 guide $1.705-1.715bn against $1.665bn consensus, targets lifted to $160-180 and the stock now inside that band. Stop stays wide at 14% for the original post-35%-gap volatility reason. No take-profit, because my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%.

New PEAD and the cleanest qualifier the screen produced. Every filter passes on measured data: closed 31.60 on 08-11 and 37.61 on 08-12 for a +19.02% gap, on 165.7m shares against a ~35m base (>4x), with the prior 20 sessions running 28.31 on 07-10 to 31.60 for +11.6%, and roughly $1.3bn of dollar ADV so liquidity is not a constraint. The fundamental surprise behind it is the largest in the book: FY26 revenue $39.1bn against $22.0bn, Q4 gross margin 17.5% against 9.5% a year ago and above the 15-17% preliminary range management had signalled in July, Q1 FY27 guided to $14.5-15.5bn against $11.68bn consensus — a guide roughly 26% above the Street, which is the kind of estimate dislocation that takes analysts weeks to work through and is exactly the mechanism the drift is supposed to exploit. Price target raises followed on 08-17, and the completion of the independent investigation retires the governance overhang that has capped the multiple. I am explicit about the flaw: at a 08-24 fill this is a seven-session lag, not the one-to-two the rule specifies, so I capture only about thirteen of the twenty sessions of drift and I size at 11% rather than the 20%+ the raw signal strength would suggest. The consolation is the entry price — 37.24 versus the 39.16 a one-lag fill would have paid. Stop is 15% rather than 10% because a name that gaps 19% has post-gap realised volatility that would stop out a normal-width trade on noise. No take-profit.

New PEAD, the second and only other name that cleared the screen. Signal: fiscal 2026 results 08-11 after the close, closed 46.67 on 08-11 and 54.18 on 08-12 for a +16.09% gap on 8.38m shares against a 1.5-2.5m base (3-5x), with the prior 20 sessions running 39.12 on 07-08 to 46.67 for +19.3% — the strongest pre-gap trend of any candidate I looked at, and that trend filter is the component my testing says carries most of the edge. It closed 53.68 on 08-21, essentially unmoved from the gap-day close, so nine sessions of chop have neither filled the gap nor extended it and I am buying the drift where it started rather than after it has run. The reason this leg earns its place beyond the statistics is that it is genuinely orthogonal to everything else I own: tax preparation is a counter-cyclical, subscription-like consumer business with no AI capex exposure, no semiconductor cycle, no defence budget and no bond-yield duration, which matters in a week when the 30-year hit a two-decade high and tech fell 3%. Sized at 9% rather than higher for two reasons — the same seven-session entry lag as SMCI, and dollar ADV around $95m, thinner than anything else in the book, so I want room to exit without moving it. Stop 12%, slightly wider than the standard 10% for that liquidity reason. No take-profit.

New merger-arb leg, filling the slot my mandate specifies and the book has been missing. CRH signed to acquire Arcosa on 06-22 for $150 per share in cash, $8.5bn enterprise value at 11.5x 2026E adjusted EBITDA — all cash, no stock, no CVR, strategic buyer with balance-sheet capacity, so there is no financing contingency to underwrite. The catalyst is genuinely tape-datable rather than a guess: the definitive proxy was filed 08-03 and mailed 08-04, and the special stockholder meeting is fixed for 09-04, inside my holding period. Regulatory posture is as clean as it gets at this stage — HSR filed 07-06 with the thirty-day period lapsed and no second request reported, Australia filed 07-21, Mexico 07-23. At the 144.90 close on 08-21 the gross spread is 3.52%. I underwrite that honestly rather than optimistically: aggregates is a business with real geographic overlap between CRH and Arcosa, and the parties themselves guide to a Q1 2027 close, so this is roughly five months of duration for 3.5% with maybe a 12-15% drawdown to the pre-deal $127 area on a break — expected value in the region of 6-7% annualised against 4% on cash. That is a thin edge, which is exactly why it is 8% and not 20%. What it buys me beyond the carry is a leg with essentially zero equity beta and collapsed realised volatility, in a book that is otherwise two high-beta drift trades. The 12% stop is a circuit breaker against a slow widening — a second request, a divestiture demand — not protection against a break, which would gap through it.

Partial beta offset, cut from 5% to 3% purely on proportionality. Its whole justification is mechanical and unchanged: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged than raw (PEAD +2.06% hedged against +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% against +2.44%), so an index short shifts realised return toward the event component I have evidence for. But the thing being hedged shrank by two thirds this week — beta-bearing event longs go from about 68% of the book to 33% (TEAM plus SMCI plus HRB; ACA is deal-driven and carries no market beta worth hedging). Applying the same hedge ratio I have been running to the smaller base gives roughly 2.4%, so 3% is the honest resize rather than a stealth increase in a market view. I want to be clear about what this is NOT: it is not a bet against the 30-year yield at two-decade highs, not a bet on weak retail after Walmart's 08-20 print, and not a hedge against the NVDA report on 08-26. I retired an increment of this leg once before for exactly that sin — justifying it on macro conditions that then reversed — and my own backtests showed the index short was a drag in all three windows. With 56% in cash the portfolio is already defensive; this leg exists to shape the edge, not to express fear. 3% borrow at 3% APR is immaterial and shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

decisions.name: Opus 5 seasonality
decisions.research_notes:
CHECKED THIS WEEK (prices through 2026-08-21 close):

Index/tape: S&P 500 closed Fri +0.43% at 7,674.37 but posted a weekly LOSS (~-1.4%); Nasdaq Composite 26,180.45, -2% on the week and ~2.3% below the 26,803 record it set on 8/13. Nine of eleven sectors ended the week negative. Russell 2000 3,017.87 (+0.85% Fri).

Rates — the dominant story: the long end sold off hard for a third straight week. 10Y hit a 20-month high of 4.75% intraweek, closing ~4.69%; 30Y hit a 19-YEAR high of 5.34%, closing 5.28%. Drivers named repeatedly: deficit supply, a surge of AI-related corporate debt issuance, and Fed Chair Warsh signalling a rate HIKE is not his preferred tool against inflation — i.e. a credibility/term-premium bear steepener, not a policy-rate story. Bessent doubled long-maturity buybacks to $4bn/quarter and yields "snapped back to previously held higher levels"; BNP flagged buybacks can't offset declining Fed credibility. Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech is NEXT WEEK — a live, dated, two-sided catalyst.

Sectors (StockCharts Best Five #78, 8/17, plus weekly prints): Tech still #1 in the top-five model (52%) but IT -3% over five sessions; Financials #2 at 19%, XLF holding its breakout, in the leading RRG quadrant; Industrials #3 at 12%, "maintaining strength," heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership — a large upgrade from 6th-of-eleven last week; Health Care #4 at 13%, best week since June (+4%), IBB +20% since the mid-June semi peak; Energy re-entered the top five, +7.6%. UTILITIES FELL TO 11th OF 11 — dead last — versus the 7th I cited last week.

Semis/AI: chips are in a bear market, >20% off June highs, NDX drew down ~9.7% from its record at the worst; triggers were AVGO's cautious AI-chip outlook (the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week), a memory-chip crisis and China memory/litho ambitions. Rotation is running out of chips into healthcare and energy.

Gold: +2.39% on the week to $4,680.60, best month since January (+10% from ~$4,000), record Q2 central-bank buying of 288.9 tonnes (+62% y/y), 45% of central banks planning to add. Iran talks remain broken. Versus my $4,066 entry that is roughly +15%, so my +18% take-profit sits near $4,798 — about 2.5% away, unfilled.

Crypto: BTC +22% to ~$77,230, best week in two years, attributed partly to Treasury liquidity expansion. I hold no crypto in any form, so the six standing orders that fired across the field do not touch this book — I verified this rather than assuming it.

EFA: developed non-US still outperforming US in USD on cheap European/Japanese valuations and a soft dollar. My short remains against trend; unchanged conclusion.

Standing orders: none of mine fired. GLD +18% TP not reached ($4,680 vs ~$4,798), QQQ -15% stop not reached, IEF -8%, KRE -18%, EFA -10% all untouched. Book is intact as entered 2026-08-17 at NAV $1,015.01.

WHAT CHANGED IN MY THINKING: for six weeks the long-end move and I have been on opposite sides because I kept reading it as a September-hike bet, and that bet inverted on me twice. This week the hike story is definitively dead — hike odds collapsed and Warsh said he won't use hikes — and long yields rose to multi-decade highs ANYWAY. That is the discriminating evidence: the mechanism is term premium and supply, which has a far longer half-life than the two-week macro signals that burned me. Crucially it is ONE mechanism that explains three of my legs at once — it widens bank NIM (XLF), it is the seasonal duration short (IEF), and it is precisely what breaks a bond-proxy whose dividend yield has compressed to 2.5-3% against a 4.7% 10Y and 5.3% 30Y (XLU). So this is not three macro bets, it is one trade re-expressed across legs I already own.

decisions.reason: One funding decision, not a rebuild: utilities is the single leg where my own measured calendar and the tape now agree that I am early, and I am moving that capital into the two legs where the same force is doing the work. XLU Jul-27-to-Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY in my study — the sleeve only earns Sep-30 to Oct-31 (+1.24%, 19/26 years) — and this week the tape stopped disagreeing politely and ranked it dead last, 11th of 11, down from 7th, for the mechanical reason that a bond proxy yielding 2.5-3% cannot compete with a 19-year-high 30Y at 5.28%. I cut it to 4% and the add still belongs to my earmarked Oct-1 rotation cash. The proceeds go where confirmation arrived: XLI, the strongest statistic in my entire window set (+5.39%, 81%, t=+2.49, Nov-Dec leg t=+3.78), jumped from 6th of eleven to 3rd, broke a multi-month consolidation and is nearing RRG leadership — last week I held it through weakness on the number alone, so I add now that the tape has come to the number. XLF goes to 20% because it holds its breakout at rank 2 with a 19% model weight while the curve steepens into its net interest margin. IEF short goes 6% to 8% — a deliberate half-step, not the 17% I once carried — because the long-end selloff has finally separated itself from the September-hike bet that inverted on me twice: that bet is dead and the 30Y still made a 19-year high on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh saying he will not hike against inflation. That is a term-premium mechanism with a much longer half-life, and it is the same mechanism paying XLF and punishing XLU. I stop short of a bigger add only because Warsh's first Jackson Hole is next week and a dovish belly rally is a real two-sided risk. I do not touch QQQ, GLD, KRE or EFA: changing QQQ would be my third directional flip on that sleeve in six weeks over a semis rotation my own study says reverses into Nov-Dec, and selling GLD 2.5% below a pre-set take-profit into a live catalyst stack is exactly the bad execution I refused last week.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the overlap constraint is inapplicable; what is new here is that for the first time this book expresses the bear-steepener as a single coherent trade across three legs — long financials, short intermediate duration, and out of the rate-sensitive bond proxy — rather than as an on-off macro overlay bolted onto a seasonal core.

positions.thesis: Raised 19% to 20% and my largest leg. The seasonal is unchanged and among my best: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone +3.64% in 19/26 years. What is new is that the mechanism I originally bought this for has stopped being a forecast and become the market's actual regime — the 30Y printed a 19-year high at 5.34% and the 10Y a 20-month high at 4.75% on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh signalling he will not hike against inflation. Short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin, and it is now three consecutive weeks old and no longer dependent on the September-hike call that inverted on me twice. The tape confirms independently: XLF ranks 2nd of eleven, sits in the leading RRG quadrant, is holding above its breakout, and carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Credit is cooperative — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals — and the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are the buffer you want owning financials against a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading. I keep it unstopped because the drawdown case here is a growth scare that my gold leg is explicitly held to pay for.

Raised 16% to 18%, funded from XLU, and this is the add I have been waiting a month to make. This remains the strongest statistic in my window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. Last week I held this through a weak stretch on the number alone, explicitly accepting a soft late summer as the price of admission because almost all the statistical mass sits in November and December. This week the tape came to the number instead: industrials moved from 6th of eleven to 3rd, took a 12% weight in the top-five model, are heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership, and XLI broke out of a multi-month consolidation with positive three-month flows on AI-infrastructure spend, reshoring and defence demand, +16% YTD. The defence leg is reinforced by an indefinite blockade and imminent Iran sanctions. Honest caveat: most industrial subsectors screen 17-25% overvalued against 11-year averages, which is why I add two points rather than eight. No stop — a stop would mechanically eject me during exactly the soft patch this window is designed to sit through.

Held flat at 18% with the +18% take-profit unchanged, and the discipline is the point. Gold rose another 2.39% to $4,680.60, its best month since January, which is roughly +15% against my $4,066 entry and about 4.5x the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69). By strict calendar logic the edge is spent. I still do not cut, for the same reason as last week and a new one. The old reason: selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution, and the Iran stack — stalled Hormuz talks, an indefinite blockade, unprecedented isolation measures — is still live. The new reason is better: this week gold rose WHILE long-end Treasuries were being sold to 19-year-high yields. That is not a rate-cut bid, it is a debasement and Fed-credibility bid, and it is the same Warsh-will-not-hike-against-inflation mechanism that drives my XLF and IEF legs. That makes gold the internally consistent hedge of this book rather than a stray commodity punt. My exit sits near $4,798, about 2.5% away — above anything my seasonal justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller. No stop: this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged, and I am deliberately refusing to make this my third directional change on one sleeve in six weeks. The absolute seasonal is what justifies the position and it is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The bear case got materially worse this week and I will state it plainly rather than dismiss it: semiconductors are now in a bear market more than 20% below their June high, the NDX drew down about 9.7% from its record, IT shed over 3% in five sessions, and the triggers are real — AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide on top of the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week, a memory-chip crisis, and China's memory and lithography ambitions. Against that: technology still holds the top slot in the sector model at a 52% weight, and my own study says this window's mass sits in November and December, not in a late-August rotation into healthcare and energy. I gutted this leg in July on a capex de-rating I misread and had to pay to restore it; doing the same thing again on a rotation is the error, not the discipline. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating — it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that resolves over quarters.

Raised 6% to 8% with the -8% stop unchanged — a half-step, not the 17% I once carried and cut. The seasonal is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. What earns the extra two points is a genuine change in the evidence, not a change in my mood. Twice I sized this off a September-hike call and twice that call inverted inside five sessions. This week the hike call is definitively dead — odds collapsed and Warsh explicitly signalled a hike is not his preferred tool against inflation — and the long end sold off anyway, to a 19-year high of 5.34% on the 30Y and a 20-month high of 4.75% on the 10Y, with Bessent's doubled buybacks failing to hold yields down and BNP noting no buyback offsets declining Fed credibility. The surviving mechanism is deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and term premium, which has a much longer half-life than a policy-rate guess, and it is the identical mechanism paying my XLF leg. I stop at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole next week would rally hardest, and I will not size into a dated catalyst I cannot handicap. The -8% stop stays — a bond rally that large means recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Held flat at 5% with the -18% stop unchanged, and holding is a decision against the obvious argument. The obvious argument is that a bear steepener should favour spread-dependent regionals most of all, and it is genuinely stronger this week than last. I decline it for two reasons. First, the tape still refuses to pay it: the Russell 2000 keeps making records with AI-linked small caps supplying the move while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak — a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. Second, the specific way the curve steepened this week is the wrong way for regionals: 19-year-high long yields mark down available-for-sale securities portfolios, which is the 2023 accident, and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres while CRE nonperformers still rise at select names. So I express the steepener through XLF, which I raised, not here. I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. The cheapest way to own the Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash.

Cut from 9% to 4% — the funding source for XLI, XLF and IEF, and the one leg where my own measured calendar and the live tape finally say the same thing. My study has always said this sleeve does not earn now: Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY, while the window where it actually pays is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Last week I held 9% anyway on a defensive narrative — retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51 — and I was wrong to weight the narrative over my own number. This week the tape removed the ambiguity: utilities fell to 11th of eleven, dead last, from 7th, and the reason is mechanical rather than sentimental — a bond proxy whose dividend yield has compressed to 2.5-3% on the AI-power theme cannot compete with a 4.7% 10Y and a 5.28% 30Y, and XLU still trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm on a 6.6% YTD return. That is the same rising-long-end force that is paying my XLF and IEF legs, so cutting here is internally consistent rather than a separate call. I keep 4% because the mandate names this sleeve and the structural AI power-demand bid is real; the rest of the position belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, bought when the calendar says it works.

Held flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve. I remain candid that both halves of the original mechanism are impaired and nothing improved this week: EAFE continues to outperform US equity in USD on cheaper European and Japanese valuations, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that will not hike while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg.
