That is exactly why this is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is modest carry, with the -10% stop capping the tail if European outperformance accelerates. Adding to a losing thesis because the calendar likes it would be the mirror of the error I just corrected in XLU.

decisions.name: Opus 5 pairs
decisions.research_notes:
Verified every leg at the 2026-08-21 close and both earnings events that landed inside my book this week.

MARKS (entry 08-17 vs 08-21 close): WFC $87.5 -> $83.84 (-4.2%); BAC $65.20 -> $61.69 (-5.4%); TSM $430.49 -> $418.95 (-2.7%); KLAC $203.72 -> $183.99 (-9.7%); LOW $218.47 -> $216.09 (-1.1%); HD $338.86 -> $335.61 (-1.0%). Reconstructing P&L from those gives roughly +0.63% gross, which ties to the packet's +0.48% after costs, so my price set is good. Crypto: I hold none, so the BTC $63k->$78k run and the six standing orders it fired across the field touch me only as a risk-on tell.

MACRO: the week's driver was the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its highest since 2007 before easing Friday when Treasury doubled long-end buybacks to at least $4bn per operation. S&P was -1.4% week-to-date into Friday, then +0.43% to 7,674.37. A semiconductor gauge fell 5% on the week. That is a rate shock plus a semis de-rating, both of which hit my legs as common factors rather than as spread information.

LOW/HD (both printed): HD 08-18 - sales $47.9bn +5.7% vs $47.24bn consensus, comps +1.7%, adj EPS $4.92 vs $4.73 expected, full-year guidance reaffirmed. LOW 08-19 - adj EPS $4.40 vs $4.22, but revenue $25.96bn missed $26.16bn, comps only +0.2%, and FY guidance cut to the bottom end ($92bn total sales, comps flat, vs $92-94bn and flat-to-+2% before). The execution difference I said I was betting on arrived and it favoured HD, the leg I am short. Prices barely moved on it. The target-implied gap I underwrote has halved: LOW $254.36 target = +17.7% upside vs HD $377.50 = +12.4%, a 5.3-point gap against 9.1 at entry. LOW now 18.3x vs HD 23.5x.

TSM/KLAC: KLAC's fall was sector, not company - it was down with LRCX, AMAT, ASML, MU and AMD on a broad chip-supply-chain de-risking, and Reuters has KLAC guiding fiscal Q1 revenue and profit ABOVE Wall Street estimates on AI infrastructure demand. So the multiple compressed (55.7x -> 50.3x) while the fundamentals improved. The TSM/KLAC price ratio moved 2.113 -> 2.277, about +7.8% in a week against a screen that offered roughly 19% of convergence with a 34-day half-life: ~40% of the modelled move captured in one fifth of the half-life. Target gap narrowed from 13.2 points (TSM 27% vs KLAC 13.8%) to 6.3 (TSM +32.3% vs KLAC +26.0%).

WFC/BAC: the pair converged about 1.2 points on beta-matched sizing, and the metric I underwrote got MORE stretched, not less - WFC upside 19.6% ($100.24 target) vs BAC 11.5% ($68.77), an 8.1-point gap against 7.2 a week ago. Year-to-date the divergence is stark: BAC +15%, WFC -8%, a 23-point split in a pair with 0.80 daily-return correlation and near-zero two-year drift. New and specific to the short leg: Berkshire cut its BAC stake by a further $1.6bn. WFC reaffirmed 2026 guidance, dividend to $0.50 payable Sept 1. Neither bank reports again until mid-October.

PAIRS I CHECKED AND REJECTED. XLU/D: disqualified outright. Dominion is now the target of NextEra's $66.8bn acquisition, with the Virginia governor saying she will intervene in the regulatory review. D's spread against XLU is now a function of deal probability, not mean reversion, which is precisely the regime break my stationarity gate exists to exclude. XLU itself sits at $42.77 near its 52-week low of $41.15 on the yield spike, but I will not pair it against a takeover target, and shorting the acquirer NEE instead would be merger arb wearing a pair's clothes. QUAL+IWF vs MTUM: does not clear my entry gate this week. The stretch is real on a trailing year (MTUM +26.6% vs QUAL +20.4% and IWF +11.6%, a ~10-point gap to a 50/50 blend) but the reversion has already run - MTUM at $305.17 is 11.7% below its $345.59 high while IWF is only 5.2% off its own high and QUAL rose Friday. MTUM is 16% Micron/AMD/AVGO, so the semis crack I would be shorting has already been paid. My gate is a stretched z-score, not a trending one, and shorting into a move that is a fifth of the way done is chasing. I would rather hold cash at 4% APY than manufacture a sixth pair without the evidence my mandate requires.

decisions.reason: Two of my three pairs delivered the thing I said I was waiting for, and my own stated exit rule says convergence gets taken rather than admired. TSM/KLAC moved about 40% of the modelled 19% convergence in a single week - one fifth of its 34-day half-life - and it did so while the fundamental case for the short eroded: KLAC guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit above consensus, so the entire 10% fall was multiple compression from 55.7x to 50.3x. My short thesis was explicitly that 'the multiple is the binding constraint'; the multiple has now partly paid out, which makes the leg less attractive at exactly the moment it made money. I cut it by about 38% rather than closing because 6.3 points of target gap remain. LOW/HD is a different problem: the reason I carried it at full size was a specific pre-print asymmetry, and the print is over. Worse, the execution difference I claimed to be buying arrived and pointed the wrong way - HD comped +1.7% and reaffirmed, LOW comped +0.2%, missed revenue and cut FY guidance to the bottom end - so my long leg's de-rating now has a cause rather than being noise. The gap that got me in halved from 9.1 to 5.3 points. I keep half the pair because 5.2 turns of multiple and 5.3 points of target gap still favour LOW, the hedge quality is the second-best I own, and both names are now a clear quarter away from any catalyst. The freed capital goes partly into WFC/BAC and mostly into cash. I add to the bank pair for the same reason I added last week and for no other: the measure I actually underwrote got more stretched, from a 7.2-point target gap to 8.1, and the year-to-date split is now BAC +15% against WFC -8% in a spread with 0.80 correlation and near-zero two-year drift. The Berkshire sale of another $1.6bn of BAC is new evidence on the short leg. I add moderately rather than to the hilt because this pair is now about two-thirds of gross; I accept that ratio only because gross itself is down to 66% and every leg is beta-cancelled, so the absolute risk of the concentration is small. I leave 33.6% in cash at 4% rather than force a sixth pair: XLU/D is disqualified by NextEra's $66.8bn bid for Dominion, which replaces mean reversion with deal probability, and the QUAL+IWF vs MTUM factor spread has already reverted 12% before I would have entered. Carrying no stops remains deliberate - stopping one side of a beta-matched pair leaves the other side naked directional, which is the failure mode this mandate exists to avoid.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to constrain; this Round-3 book is my only book and stands entirely on its own screen.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 21.0 to 23.0 because the spread stretched further on the one measure I underwrote. WFC at $83.84 carries a $100.24 consensus target implying 19.6% upside against BAC's 11.5%, an 8.1-point convergence gap versus 7.2 a week ago, and it is still 14% below its $97.76 52-week high while BAC only just came off a fresh high. The year-to-date divergence is the cleanest statement of the case: BAC +15%, WFC -8%, a 23-point split in a pair whose two-year drift is near zero. Fundamentals do not support that split - WFC reaffirmed 2026 guidance with broad-based segment growth, improved efficiency and robust credit, and the dividend went to $0.50 payable Sept 1. At 12.2x trailing against BAC's 14.3x, the multiple is what carries the reversion. This remains the best stationarity evidence in my universe: 17 mean-crossings in a year, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77. Neither bank reports again until mid-October, so nothing on the calendar sits inside my horizon. The risk I own is that this pair is now roughly two-thirds of gross; I accept it because gross is only 66% and the legs cancel.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 22.7 against 23.0 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.01% of NAV. Nothing is wrong with BAC and that is still the entire point - Q2 EPS $1.21 beat by 8%, Global Markets revenue +34%, IB fees +50%, EPS $4.33 up 27.7% year over year. I am short the price of an excellent franchise after a 15% year-to-date run has compressed sell-side headroom to 11.5% on a $68.77 target, not the franchise. New this week and specific to this leg: Berkshire cut its BAC stake by a further $1.6bn under Abel, which removes a marginal buyer that has underpinned the stock for years. BAC fell 5.4% into the yield spike versus WFC's 4.2% - the rate shock is common to both legs and cancels, so what is left is the valuation gap I am actually trading. The risk remains that an accelerating capital-markets cycle re-rates BAC past the sell side, which is exactly why this is beta-cancelled rather than an outright short.

Long leg vs KLAC, cut from 8.0 as I take convergence rather than admire it. TSM closed $418.95 and the TSM/KLAC ratio moved from 2.113 to 2.277 in one week, capturing roughly 40% of the ~19% convergence my screen offered against a 34-day half-life - four times the pace the model assumed, which is when a mean-reversion mandate books profit. What keeps the residual on is that TSM at 28.2x still trades at a large discount to the equipment names it feeds, with a $554.45 average target implying 32.3% upside and a Strong Buy consensus, and Tepper and Druckenmiller both added over the quarter. The 15 mean-crossings and -12% two-year drift are unchanged, so last year's relative fall still reads as oscillation, not decay. I cut the long and the short in the same proportion so the trim does not quietly convert a spread into a directional semis bet.

Short leg vs TSM, cut from 6.4 to 4.0 against a 5.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta still exceeds TSM's 2.15 - beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC closed $183.99 after falling 9.7% on the week, but I trim rather than press because the reason for the fall argues against me: this was a sector-wide de-risking that hit LRCX, AMAT, ASML, MU and AMD alike, and KLAC itself guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit ABOVE consensus on AI infrastructure demand. Every dollar of the decline was multiple compression, 55.7x to 50.3x, on improving fundamentals. My thesis was that the multiple was the binding constraint; it has now partly given way, so the cheap part of the short has been paid. What holds the residual is that 50x trailing is still an extraordinary price for a cyclical and the target gap versus TSM has not closed to zero, at 6.3 points. This stays my smallest and most violent spread on purpose - a name with a 52-week range of $83 to $307 is the leg most likely to be wrong fastest, which is why it is now the smallest leg in the book.

Long leg vs HD, cut from 11.0 to 6.0 because the specific reason for full size has been consumed and the evidence partly went against me. LOW printed 08-19: adj EPS $4.40 beat $4.22, but revenue of $25.96bn missed $26.16bn, comps rose only +0.2% against HD's +1.7%, and FY guidance was cut to the bottom end - $92bn sales and flat comps versus $92-94bn and flat-to-+2%. That is my long leg guiding down while the leg I am short reaffirmed, which is a fundamental point against the pair, and the pre-print asymmetry I was paid to carry no longer exists. I keep half rather than none because the valuation and target evidence still points my way: LOW at $216.09 sits just above its $199.40 52-week low at 18.3x with a $254.36 target implying 17.7% upside against HD's 12.4%, a 5.3-point gap and a 5.2-turn multiple discount, and total sales still grew 8.3% against HD's 5.7% with online up 15.7%. Hedge quality is second only to WFC/BAC - 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings, -6% two-year drift - and with both prints behind us there is no catalyst inside a full quarter.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 5.7 against 6.0 so the 0.68 and 0.65 betas cancel to within 0.03% of NAV. I state the evidence against this leg plainly: HD cleared the harder bar on 08-18 with sales of $47.9bn up 5.7% versus $47.24bn expected, comps +1.7%, adj EPS $4.92 against $4.73, and full-year guidance held despite the housing slump - all delivered with CEO Ted Decker still on medical leave and the CFO covering, which answers the governance question I raised last week in HD's favour rather than mine. That is why the leg is halved rather than held. What keeps it on is price: at $335.61 HD trades at 23.5x with only 12.4% upside to a $377.50 target, while the demand mix management described is small projects and Pro rather than big discretionary renovation, which is the same soft-DIY backdrop that is being used to mark LOW down five turns cheaper. I carry no stop here, as before: stopping out one side of a beta-matched pair would leave me naked long LOW, and with both companies now a full quarter from their next print, the common housing shock is the only thing left to move them together.

decisions.name: Opus 5 unrestricted
decisions.research_notes:
VERIFIED THIS WEEK (prices through 2026-08-21 close):

OIL / HORMUZ — the thesis strengthened, hard. Brent $93.86 on 8/21 (+5%+ on the week, second consecutive weekly gain), vs $88.52 last week and $61-ish XLE. XLE $63.58 on 8/19 vs $61.06 a week ago. No de-escalation: Trump declared an "economic D-Day," saying ANY country trading with Iran will be sanctioned — the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country" — and Bessent holds a press conference MONDAY 8/24 with details, having already committed to the Hormuz blockade plus "the toughest sanctions in history." The war is near its six-month mark with no diplomatic or military off-ramp; the strait remains significantly choked. Secondary sanctions on Iran's buyers is a supply-REMOVAL policy, not a de-escalation, and it lands into an IEA Q3 deficit estimate of 1.8 mb/d.

REFINING — the new information that actually changed my book. US 3-2-1 crack spread hit a record ~$64/bbl; the DIESEL crack hit a record $99.125/bbl, +264% year over year. Marathon Petroleum's refining & marketing margin went from $17.58 to $36.33/bbl; Valero's realized margin roughly doubled y/y; industry refining margins have nearly tripled since the start of 2026. The driver is structural — a global refining capacity shortage, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and reduced fuel exports — which is why product prices stayed elevated even on crude pullbacks earlier this year. MPC closed $358.23 on 8/20 against an all-time-high close of $365.21 set 8/18.

MACRO — Powell at Jackson Hole opened the door to a September cut ("the baseline outlook and the shifting balance of risks may warrant adjusting our policy stance"), explicitly citing downside employment risk after the July jobs report. Fed funds futures now price ~91% odds of a 25bp September cut. He kept inflation risks "tilted to the upside" with tariff pass-through "clearly visible" — i.e. cutting into sticky inflation, which is the textbook gold regime.

PRECIOUS METALS — gold $4,600.91-$4,607 spot on 8/21, +2.03% on the day, three-month-plus high and record territory, vs ~$4,371 last week (+5.4% on the week). Silver $69.87, +3% on the day, +8.8% on the week, vs $64.21 last week. Gold/silver ratio now ~65.9 vs 67.22 last week — the catch-up I was waiting on finally started moving. US federal debt topped $40 trillion; dollar weak.

CRYPTO — I verified the market note. BTC $78,335 Friday close, +7.26% on the day and +22% on the week, its strongest weekly run since 2024, highest since May, driven by Treasury long-end buybacks pulling yields down, a weaker dollar, and the largest spot-ETF daily inflow since May (BlackRock took 83% of Thursday's $606m). My DOGE 3x short was stopped out 8/20 at $0.0907 for ~$3.89 back to cash — beta ran it over exactly as I said the risk was. Analysts flag overbought signals into thin weekend liquidity.

AIRLINES — the global airline industry has nearly HALVED its 2026 profit forecast, citing Middle East conflict fuel costs; US carriers' fuel bill was ~$6.7bn in May, +85% y/y; carriers are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft. JETS 12-month range $23.48-$34.06. With the jet/distillate crack at a record, the cost side of my short is now worse for airlines than at any point since I put the trade on.

HEALTHCARE — XLV reached "Confirmed Leader" status on 8/7, +1.60% as of 8/18 and the second-strongest sector behind energy, ~18x forward, beta 0.65-0.75, Q2 beats and GLP-1 franchise growth intact.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: every leg I own is working and the two catalysts ahead (Bessent Monday, September FOMC) both cut my way. The one thing I did NOT do is chase crypto after a 22% week — I already own the debasement trade in a laggard form (silver is still well below its February mid-$80s high while BTC just went vertical), and re-shorting DOGE days after being stopped out in a liquidity-driven melt-up would be revenge trading, not edge.

decisions.reason: Because I found a way to increase energy exposure while REDUCING my worst tail. My single largest risk has always been one headline wide: a Hormuz deal lands, crude gaps down, and a 2x fund halves the move twice over. Refining margins are the one energy exposure that does not share that failure mode — the diesel crack hit a record $99.125/bbl (+264% y/y) and the 3-2-1 hit a record ~$64 on a structural refining-capacity shortage plus Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and product prices stayed elevated through earlier crude pullbacks precisely because the bottleneck is refining, not crude. So I cut ERX from 24 to 22 and put 12 into MPC: total energy exposure rises from 48% effective to 56%, but the crude-beta share of it falls, and if the deal I fear actually lands, cheaper feedstock into a still-short product market is a partial offset rather than a second loss. Everything else is a modest lean into what verified: Brent $93.86 with Bessent announcing secondary sanctions on every country that trades with Iran on Monday, Powell opening the door to a September cut at 91% market-implied odds, gold at a record and silver finally compressing the ratio. I raised silver 7 to 10 and funded it plus MPC out of an XLV trim and cash. I deliberately did NOT re-add crypto after BTC's biggest week since 2024, and I did not re-short DOGE after being stopped out on 8/20 — both would be chasing.
decisions.novelty: This book is not a Round-2 derivative — I run no Round-2 account — and the substantive novelty this week is that my energy risk is no longer a single levered crude-beta expression: adding MPC splits it into a crude-price leg and a refining-margin leg whose payoffs diverge in exactly the scenario that would otherwise blow the book up, while the crypto sleeve is now deliberately empty rather than short.

positions.thesis: Trimmed 24 to 22 — not because the thesis weakened but because I am now expressing part of the same view through MPC, which does not die on the same headline. The crude case got materially better this week: Brent $93.86, a second straight weekly gain, against $88.52 last week, while Trump declared an 'economic D-Day' promising to sanction ANY country that trades with Iran and Bessent details it Monday. That is supply removal, not de-escalation — secondary sanctions strand Iranian barrels that are currently reaching buyers, layered on top of a blockade, a strait still significantly choked six months into the war with no off-ramp, and an IEA Q3 deficit of 1.8 mb/d. XLE at $63.58 has not caught up to what a $94 Brent plus that policy implies, and ERX is 2x that gap. This is still my largest directional risk and the bear case is unchanged and honest: a deal lands, crude gaps down, and the stop gaps through it. Size is the real protection, which is why 22 and not 30. New take-profit at +40%, roughly a 20% XLE move — around $115-120 Brent, the level where demand destruction, SPR politics and pressure on Tehran to settle invert the risk/reward and I would rather be paid than greedy. Stop held at -22%, capping the leg at ~4.8% of NAV.

Trimmed 25 to 20 to fund MPC and silver, not because it stopped working — it hit 'Confirmed Leader' status on 8/7 and is the second-strongest sector behind energy, at ~18x forward with a 0.65-0.75 beta, carried by real Q2 earnings beats and the GLP-1 franchise rather than by defensive flows. It remains the ballast that makes a 2x energy fund carryable, and 20% is still enough of it to do that job. The honest reason for the trim is that a Fed cutting in September into a weak dollar is a regime where low-beta quality compounds steadily but does not lead, and I found two places this week where the same capital has a sharper edge. No stop, unchanged reasoning: this is the position I want to still own if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I want to be holding it.

Held flat at 20 because this week is what I bought it for and adding after a 5.4% weekly run is chasing. Gold printed ~$4,607 on 8/21, up 2% on the day to a three-month-plus high in record territory, on Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds — while he simultaneously kept inflation risks 'tilted to the upside' with tariff pass-through 'clearly visible.' Cutting into sticky inflation with federal debt through $40 trillion and a soft dollar is the exact monetary setup gold is built for, and it is stacked on a Hormuz premium and central-bank buying, so the bid is layered rather than single-source. It also remains the only asset here that wins in both tails of my own book: stalemate keeps the geopolitical bid alongside ERX, and a sudden settlement that kills ERX lands on a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs and a Fed already cutting. Still bullion rather than GDX — mining operating leverage on top of a 2x energy fund would concentrate variance in the one thing I am trying to reduce. Stop tightened -13% to -12%, capping the leg at 2.4% of NAV: still far outside any headline shakeout, but a 12% break from a record would mean the rate-cut repricing died, and at that point this has stopped hedging.

New 12% position, and the most important change I made. Refining margins are not a crude-price bet, they are a product-scarcity bet, and the scarcity just went to records: the US 3-2-1 crack spread hit ~$64/bbl and the diesel crack hit $99.125/bbl, up 264% year over year, on a structural global refining-capacity shortage compounded by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and reduced fuel exports. MPC's own refining and marketing margin went from $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel and industry margins have nearly tripled since the start of 2026 — that is realized cash, not a forecast. The reason this earns a place next to ERX rather than duplicating it is the divergence in the tail I actually fear: if a Hormuz deal lands and crude collapses, ERX halves the move twice, but a refiner buying cheaper feedstock into a market that is still physically short distillate keeps or widens its crack — earlier this year products stayed elevated through exactly that kind of crude pullback. Unlevered equity at 2bps, no leveraged-ETF decay, and it pays a dividend while I wait. Entering near an all-time-high close ($365.21 on 8/18, $358.23 on 8/20) is the cost of the setup; the risk is that record cracks mean-revert as capacity or demand adjusts, which is why this is 12 and not 20. Stop -18% caps the leg at ~2.2% of NAV.

Held at 10% — both drivers strengthened again and this is the natural pair to a record distillate crack. The cost side is now brutal and confirmed by the industry itself: the global airline sector has nearly HALVED its 2026 profit forecast citing Middle East fuel costs, US carriers' fuel bill ran ~$6.7bn in May at +85% y/y, jet fuel sits in the record-crack complex I just went long via MPC, and carriers are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft — that is management telling you the margin math no longer works. Brent went from $88.52 to $93.86 this week, so the pressure is still increasing, not peaking. The demand side is independent and intact: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically soft reads directly on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure flinches first as fares rise to cover fuel. Portfolio-wise this is my only equity hedge with the index at records. I am naming the concentrated failure mode rather than hiding it: a Hormuz deal costs me on ERX and this leg simultaneously, though MPC now blunts that. Squeeze risk stays specific — the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is ~30bps a year. Stop -18% caps it at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25%.

Raised 7 to 10 because the catch-up I was sized small for waiting on finally started. Silver ran to $69.87, up ~3% Friday and ~8.8% on the week against gold's 5.4%, pulling the gold/silver ratio to ~65.9 from 67.22 — the compression is now accelerating rather than grinding. Same dovish engine as GLD with more beta: a September cut at 91% implied odds, a weak dollar, and record-territory precious metals. Two things make me want more of it here specifically rather than more gold: silver is still meaningfully below its February mid-$80s high while gold is at a record and BTC just posted its best week since 2024, so this is the laggard expression of the debasement trade rather than the chased one; and a Fed easing into 'clearly visible' tariff inflation supports the industrial half of silver demand that a weakening labor market had been cutting against. It stays 10 and not 20 because that industrial component genuinely cuts both ways and because this metal's own history is violent — mid-$80s to $64 to $70 inside a year. Stop stays wide at -18%, capping the leg at 1.8% of NAV; anything tighter is noise on a chart like this.

decisions.name: Opus 5 trend following
decisions.research_notes:
Verified every leg against Friday 2026-08-21 closes rather than trusting the packet or the prompt's summary.

CRYPTO (the leg that matters): BTC ~$77,000 at the Friday close after touching $79,500 intraday, +22% on the week — its best five-day run since March 2024 — and it reclaimed the 200-day moving average for the first time in ~270 sessions (since Nov 2025). Drivers: Treasury doubling long-end buyback operations from $2bn to $4bn per op (effective Sept 9), a White House crypto summit / CLARITY Act push, ~$800m of spot ETF inflows over two days, and a short squeeze. 1-month +17.5%, 1-year -31.8%. Against my entry of $62,875 my short is ~23% offside; my -30% stop (~$81.7k) did NOT fire, so this is my decision, not the engine's.

MACRO: the week's real story is the long end. A bond selloff took the 30-year to its highest yield since 2007 on fiscal deterioration plus US-Iran escalation; Bessent's buyback expansion pulled 30y back 9bp to 5.196% and 10y to 4.647%, but strategists were explicit that this treats the symptom, not the cause. S&P 500 closed 7,674.37, -1.4% on the week despite Friday's +0.43%. Long-end stress, hard assets bid, equities soft is one coherent debasement/geopolitical impulse, and it is what is simultaneously driving oil, copper, ags and now BTC.

ENERGY: Brent closed $94.39 (from $88.38), +5%+ on the week, WTI $87.06. US moving to full economic isolation of Iran, Trump's "economic D-day" detail due Monday; ~8 mb/d still lost through Hormuz vs ~20 mb/d pre-war. XLE $63.64 against a 52wk range of $42.35-$64.70 and up from $61.06 a week ago; +53% 1yr total return. Strongest and most re-accelerating trend I own.

EQUITY SLEEVES: XLV $174.62, up from $168.01, just under a 52wk high of $176.60 with +29.2% 1yr — it OUTPERFORMED a down tape by ~5 points. (An early search hit claiming XLV fell 4.2% and is down 29% y/y was simply wrong; the primary quote page contradicts it, and acting on it unchecked would have cut my best relative trend.) XLF $57.48 vs 52wk high $58.41 — flat, trend intact, no new information. CPER $39.99 vs $40.12 last week — stalled just under the $40.97 high; I re-checked Section 232 and refined cathode is STILL exempt with no decision made, phase-in only contemplated for 2027 at 15%, so the binary jump risk I trimmed for last week is entirely unresolved. DBA $28.32 vs $27.59 — +2.6% and pushing the top of its $25.40-$28.84 range, so the sideways leg has resumed trending.

decisions.reason: My BTC short's signal inverted, and a systematic trend book that will not close a falsified short has no claim to being systematic. I shorted on price below the 20/50/100/200-day EMAs with decisively negative 3m momentum; BTC has now closed above its 200-day for the first time in roughly 270 sessions, sits far above a 50-day anchored in the abandoned $60-64k range, and 3m momentum has flipped positive (~$73.5k end-May to ~$77k). All three filters point the other way, so the position goes regardless of the ~23% mark-to-market loss — my stop did not fire, so this is judgment applied to my own rules rather than the engine bailing me out. I flip rather than sit flat because my rules are symmetric, and because the same impulse driving BTC is driving the rest of the book: a 30-year yield at its highest since 2007 on fiscal and war risk, with the Treasury forced into doubled buybacks, is a debasement tape, and Brent at $94, copper near its high and ags breaking their range are the same trade in other wrappers. But every BTC filter is marginal — a one-day-old 200dma reclaim, +4.8% 3m momentum, after a 22% squeeze week — so I take the signal at the smallest inverse-vol size I can justify, 4% at 1x with no liquidation-relevant leverage, and let a stop back inside the old range settle whether the breakout was real. Elsewhere I rotate rather than expand: gross goes 87 to 88, essentially unchanged, taking two points from SPY (the only equity leg whose slope actually decelerated) and one from a stalled CPER carrying unresolved tariff jump risk, into the three trends that measurably accelerated — energy, healthcare and ags.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to constrain; the only structural change here is that my crypto sleeve has inverted from short to a small long, flipping the sign of my sole non-equity, non-commodity exposure.

positions.thesis: Trimmed from 22 to 20 — the first cut I have made to it — because this is the one equity leg whose slope rolled over. The index closed 7,674.37, down 1.4% on the week after a record 7,800 the prior Thursday, so the trend filter still passes comfortably against both moving averages and 3m momentum is still strongly positive, but momentum stopped being added to while three other legs added to theirs. At ~13% realised vol it remains my lowest-volatility trend and therefore still my largest single weight under inverse-vol sizing; I am funding better trends from it, not doubting it. The pressure is identifiable and not yet in price: a 30-year at its highest yield since 2007 with a buyers' strike in the long end since June, which the Treasury's doubled buyback tempers without curing. Wide -15% catastrophe stop — an index drawdown that size is a regime change, and weekly reassessment is my real exit.

Raised from 17 to 19 because the physical driver intensified rather than merely persisted. Brent closed $94.39 against the $88.38 I sized on a week ago and the ~$82 I wrongly cut on two weeks ago, WTI $87.06, with roughly 8 mb/d of the pre-war 20 mb/d Hormuz flow still lost and the US now moving to cut Iran off from banking, shipping registries and settlement entirely — the 'economic D-day', detail due Monday. XLE at $63.64 versus $61.06 last week against a 52wk range of $42.35-$64.70, +53% on the year: new highs into an escalating supply story is the cleanest configuration in my universe. It stays below SPY's weight only because its ~24% realised vol is the highest in the book and inverse-vol sizing refuses to let a strong signal buy unlimited size. Stop stays wide at -25% precisely because a headline de-escalation gap is the known failure mode and a tight stop guarantees being taken out on the first one.

Raised from 15 to 17 for exactly the reason I own it: it rose 3.9% to $174.62, within a percent of its $176.60 52wk high, in a week the S&P fell 1.4%. That is about five points of relative strength earned at a 0.56 beta, and it is the only leg that both extended its own trend and diversified the tape. Above both moving averages with the golden cross intact, the strongest 3m time-series momentum among my low-volatility sleeves, +29.2% on the year, ~18% realised vol. I re-verified this against a stale source claiming healthcare fell 4% on the week and is down 29% year-on-year; the tape says the opposite, and trusting that number would have cut my best relative trend. With the long end stressed and gross tilted into two cyclical commodity legs, a low-beta trend that works when the index does not is worth more weight now than last week.

Raised from 10 to 11 because the flat leg started trending again. $28.32 against $27.59 a week ago, +2.6%, now pressing the top of its $25.40-$28.84 twelve-month range rather than sitting mid-range as it has for a month, and above both moving averages. I explicitly declined to trade it last week on a 0.1% move and I add now only because this move is real and directional. Its ~0.12 beta makes it the least equity-correlated thing I own and its ~13% realised vol the cheapest risk unit available under inverse-vol sizing, which is what the book needs while I carry energy and copper into an unstable long end. Agriculture is also a natural beneficiary of the same fiscal-debasement impulse that lifted oil, copper and bitcoin this week, without carrying any of their headline binaries.

Held flat at 9 with no change and no new information. $57.48 against roughly $57.00-$57.60 a week ago and a $58.41 52wk high — the trend filter passes, price has not broken, and 3m momentum is still not being added to, which is precisely the state I sized for when I cut it from 11 last week. The rate picture cuts both ways and therefore cuts neither: a 30-year at its highest yield since 2007 steepens the curve in banks' favour, while a buyers' strike in the long end and a Treasury forced into doubled buybacks is systemic stress that lands on financials first. With last week's consumer prints — the worst retail sales in over a year and UMich at 51 — still the live downside, this earns its inverse-vol baseline and nothing more. Re-trading a flat week would be pure cost.

Trimmed from 9 to 8, again for risk rather than signal. The trend is intact but has stalled: $39.99 versus $40.12 last week, still near the high end of a $27.37-$40.97 range with +44.6% on the year on electrification, grid buildout and AI datacentre demand. What has not moved is the binary I trimmed for a week ago — I re-checked Section 232 and refined cathode remains exempt with no determination made, the phase-in at 15% still only contemplated for 2027, and CPER holds exactly the COMEX futures that carry the US tariff premium. A stalled price and an unresolved gap risk in the same leg is worse than either alone, because vol-based sizing prices neither. With the trend no longer paying me to sit through the decision window, I keep taking size off by hand a point at a time while the -25% stop stays wide enough not to be hit by ordinary copper volatility.

Replaces last week's 5% short, which my own filters have falsified. I shorted at $62,875 with price under the 20/50/100/200-day EMAs and 3m momentum decisively negative; BTC closed the week near $77,000 after tagging $79,500, +22% — its best five sessions since March 2024 — and reclaimed the 200-day moving average for the first time in about 270 days. Price is now above a 50-day anchored in the abandoned $60-64k range and above the 200-day, and 3m momentum has turned positive from ~$73.5k at end-May. My rules are symmetric, so the same evidence that forces me out of the short puts me into a long. It is also not an isolated crypto event: the catalyst was the Treasury doubling long-end buybacks into a 2007-high 30-year yield, plus a White House crypto push and ~$800m of two-day ETF inflows — the identical fiscal-stress impulse lifting Brent to $94 and copper toward its high. I size at the bottom of the inverse-vol range and run 1x with no liquidation-relevant leverage because every filter is marginal, a one-day-old 200dma reclaim on +4.8% 3m momentum, and a 22% squeeze week is the worst possible entry price. Funding is 10% APR on longs, roughly 0.008% of NAV a week at this size, which is not a reason to avoid the wrapper. The -20% stop sits near $61.5k, back inside the seven-week range, which would falsify the breakout outright rather than merely bruise it.

Regional-bank weakness is NIM/CRE/private-credit grind, not a fresh event.

R3 UNIVERSE SCREEN (same three metrics): SNOW 97.9/+36.2/+19.4, PANW 85.0/+77.6/+6.6, FTNT 84.1/+94.9/-1.6, TWLO 80.3/+83.3/+8.5, NET 77.9/+36.1/+9.4, MU 77.5/+756.6/+0.2, XYZ 93.0/+3.2/+4.7 versus SMH 71.7/+102.5/-4.9, CRWD 75.7/+77.2/-0.6, DDOG 71.7/+89.2/-5.5, AVGO 41.9/+36.5/-5.1, VRT 55.1/+140.5/-10.9, KLAC 46.0/+151.8/-16.3, AMAT 59.4/+253.7/-12.1, WDC 57.3/+649.8/-16.2, STX 74.1/+495.7/-4.6. Essentially the whole semi-cap-equipment and memory-storage complex is below its 50-day; the cause is reported as rising long yields compressing the most extended multiples in the sector plus Samsung/SK Hynix supply additions and AI-capex-peak fears, not company news. MU fell only 0.50% while WDC -9.7%, STX -12.7%, KLAC -9.6% - genuine relative strength, though Netlist has filed new ITC and federal actions over DDR5 RDIMM/MRDIMM seeking exclusion orders, a fresh negative I did not have last week.

CRWD SPECIFICS: five consecutive down days, -16%, ~$36B of market cap gone; CTO Elia Zaitsev departing to launch an AI/security fund with no named successor; earnings confirmed 2026-08-26, inside my holding window, with options pricing roughly a 10% move.

EARNINGS DATES CHECKED: CRWD 08-26 (in window), MRVL 08-27 (in window - ruled out as an add despite 12-1 of +194.6% and being the only semi up on the week), MDB/ZM/OKTA/VEEV all late August (ruled out), PANW 09-01 confirmed after close (outside), SNOW 09-02 (outside), TWLO reported 08-06 and FTNT 07-29 (both clear), XYZ and UPST reported early August (clear), ORCL ~09-10 (outside).

LAGGARD SCREEN for the second short slot: the deep-negative 12-1 cohort is squeezing hard - NOW 12-1 -47.6% but +39.7% on the month, ADBE -40.0%/+29.8%, WDAY -43.8%/+56.4%, TEAM -51.3%/+114.4%, ZS -48.3%/+30.1%, SOFI -28.6%/+13.6%. That junk-rally is the direct cause of my drawdown and I will not stand in front of it. UPST is the exception: 12.3% of its 52-week range (lowest in my universe), 12-1 of -56.6% (worst), below its 50- and 200-day, and flat at -0.43% in the exact week HOOD did +13.2% and COIN did +25.6%. ORCL is the other: 15.0% of range, 12-1 -47.9%, and it fell 2.69% while its own laggard cohort bounced.

decisions.reason: Leadership rotated inside breadth and my weights are pointed at the half that lost it. Industrials and regional banks closed at 100% of their 52-week ranges eight sessions ago and are now 84.3% and 85.3% of range and both below their 50-day, on a rates grind (30-yr 5.27% after touching 5.33%) plus private-credit and CRE pressure on NIM - so I take XLI 11->7 and KRE 10->6 rather than defending sizes set on readings that no longer exist. The money goes where the breadth signal actually is: XBI back to 12, undoing a cut I made a week ago on the argument that the 30-year had risen, after which XBI returned +5.29% with the 30-year rising. That rate argument has now failed twice in a row on the same asset, so I am retiring it rather than re-running it - XBI is my best-ranked leg in this book on every price measure I use (95.3% of range, 12-1 of +70.1%, +8.1% over its 50-day) and it is literally the small-cap equal-weight construction my mandate names. New XLB at 5 because materials closed at a literal 52-week high with positive 12-1 and 17 vol, replacing the cyclical exposure I just trimmed with the cyclical that is working and without double-counting energy. ETH gets rebalanced back to its 3% target, which banks the excess of a +31.5% week, and its stop comes from -30% to -25% because that stop was set when the asset had 11% realized vol and it now has 101% - the old stop is no longer a stop.

positions.thesis: Untraded at 19 for a fourth week and still the anchor. Closed at 97.4% of its 52-week range and outperformed QQQ by 1.9 points this week and by 8.7 points over three months, so the anti-concentration view continues to be carried by the long leg rather than the short. Not pressed at a near-record close because that is how a breadth basket quietly becomes a momentum basket, and not trimmed because nothing in the reading changed.

Untraded at 19. Down 1.68% on the week but still 93.7% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +30.6% and above its 50-day, and small-cap value (IWN) sits at 95.9% of range - so the small-cap complex is consolidating a record, not breaking one. I have twice now traded this book off the 30-year yield and been wrong both times; I am holding this on its own price reading and letting the rate question resolve itself.

Held at 13, the size I rebuilt to last week, and it is working: +2.79% on the week, +10.68% over two, crude from $82.40 to $87.06, 99.5% of its 52-week range with 12-1 of +41.8% and XOP at a flat 100% of range. Deliberately not pressed despite being my best cyclical - it is 10.8% above its 50-day and I have already been whipsawed on this sector twice, so the discipline is to let a correctly-sized position work rather than to reward myself for finally getting it right. Stop stays -18%, capping the leg at 2.3% of NAV.

Restored 8->12, back to the size I cut a week ago. The cut's premise was that the 30-year had risen to 5.26%; the 30-year then touched 5.33% and XBI returned +5.29%, so the premise has now been tested and rejected twice on this exact asset and I am discarding it rather than re-running it. On the measures this mandate is built from XBI is my strongest leg: 95.3% of its 52-week range, 12-1 momentum of +70.1%, +8.1% over its 50-day, +24.9% over three months, with breadth underneath it (average constituent up about 7% on the week, IBB +7.72%, XLV at 97.5% of range) driven by $106B of 2026 sector M&A and a heavy FDA calendar. It is also the equal-weight small-cap construction my mandate explicitly names. Sizing is now set on its own price reading and I am committing not to trade it on a macro rate argument again - only the -22% stop, about two monthly sigma at 38 vol, takes it out.

Cut 11->7. Last week I sized this on industrials closing at 100% of their 52-week range; it is now 84.3% of range and below its 50-day after -3.36%, and the infrastructure read-through (PAVE -3.75%, also below its 50-day) confirms it is the sector rather than the wrapper. Trimmed rather than exited because 12-1 momentum of +22.3% is still solidly positive and 84% of range is a consolidation, not a breakdown - I am removing the size that was justified by a record close that no longer exists, not abandoning domestic cyclical breadth.

Cut 10->6. Last week's best non-energy leg is this week's worst at -3.94%, and it now sits at 85.3% of range below its 50-day. The reason matters: with the 30-year at 5.27% the pressure is deposit costs and net interest margin, and the standing credit worry - payrolls at -23,000 with negative revisions, CRE and private-credit non-performing loans - lands on banks first. I said last week that a labour-market crack shows up here first and capped it at 10 for that reason; the sector is now the weakest cyclical I own, so I act on my own stated logic and take the size down rather than restate the worry a third time.

Untraded at 6. Down 5.21% on the week against IWM's -1.68%, which is precisely the 3x daily compounding drag I have said all along is the reason this stays small - a chopping small-cap tape costs decay whether or not the direction eventually resolves my way. Not cut, because 12-1 of +83.8% and 90% of range mean the underlying trend is intact and one down week is what this instrument does; not pressed, for the same reason. Stop stays -25%, capping the leg at 1.5% of NAV.

New at 5. Materials closed at a flat 100.0% of their 52-week range, +1.90% on the week and +3.8% over its 50-day with positive 12-1 momentum - one of only three sectors I track making a genuine high this week alongside energy and biotech. It replaces the cyclical exposure I just trimmed out of industrials and banks with a cyclical that is actually leading, and unlike XOP it does not double-count the energy weight I already carry. Sized small at 5 because 12-1 of +13.3% is a middling reading and only 17 vol, so it earns a slot on breadth and confirmation rather than on conviction.

Rebalanced back to the 3% target after +31.5% since 08-17, which banks the excess of the move. Last week I called this dead weight with 11% realized vol; it now has 101% realized vol on the CLARITY Act push and Treasury buyback liquidity, with BTC's best five days since March 2024. I am not adding on that: ETH is still only 29.1% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of -60%, so this is a violent bounce off a deep hole, not an asset that qualifies as a leader, and chasing it at 35bps a side after a 34% week is the definition of paying up for someone else's catalyst. The stop comes -30% -> -25% purely as arithmetic - a -30% stop set against 11% vol is not a stop against 101% vol - which caps this leg at 0.75% of NAV while leaving the convexity the mandate wants intact.

Untraded at 6 and paying for a second straight week: QQQ -2.41% against RSP -0.49%, and over three months QQQ is -0.04% against RSP's +8.70% with QQQ at 83.0% of its range while RSP sits at 97.4%. The concentration spread is doing exactly what this leg exists to capture. Explicitly not upsized into that success - pressing this leg after it works is the mistake I made three weeks ago and paid for, and the mandate asks for a small anti-concentration short, which 6% against 90% of longs is.

decisions.reason: Three separate things broke and each one has its own answer. First, the COIN short: my entire stated thesis was that a name at 3% of its 52-week range failing to participate in a melt-up is a laggard confirming itself. It then participated violently - +25.6% in five sessions on BTC's best week in two years, the CLARITY Act push and $800M/day of ETF inflows, taking it to 18.4% of range and above its 10- and 50-day. The non-participation signal is gone, so the position has no thesis left; I cover at roughly -24% rather than let it random-walk the last point into my own -25% stop and have the decision taken from me. Second, CRWD: I bought it one week ago on 93.8% of range and closes above all three moving averages, and it is now 75.7% of range and below its 50-day after five straight down days and -16%, its CTO has left with no named successor, and it prints on 08-26 - inside my holding window with options pricing a ~10% swing. Two of the three legs I bought it on are gone and there is a binary event in the window; a momentum mandate does not hold a broken screen through a print. I replace it with FTNT, which is a strict upgrade on my own metrics - 12-1 of +94.9% against CRWD's +77.2%, 84.1% of range against 75.7%, 38 vol against 52, and no earnings in the window. Third, SMH: I cut it 24->15 last week because the diversified wrapper was netting my thesis away, and this week it did -4.66% against MU's -0.50%, leaving it at 71.7% of range and 4.9% below its 50-day for a third consecutive week of failing my screen. I stop paying for a vehicle that keeps ranking badly and hold the semiconductor exposure in the one name that passes. I am not forcing the proceeds back in: the whole semi-cap-equipment and memory-storage cohort is below its 50-day, and when few names clear a cross-sectional screen the correct book is a smaller one, so gross goes 85->82 with cash at 18 earning 4%.
decisions.novelty: Round 2 is broad-market ETFs - equal-weight, small-cap, energy, materials, industrials, banks, biotech, a 3x small-cap amplifier and an ETH tail - while Round 3 is single-name software, semis and fintech with two dedicated short legs; the two books share no symbol at all and no same-direction gross weight, and this week they point opposite ways on rate-sensitivity, with Round 2 buying the rotation into biotech and materials while Round 3 cuts the long-duration software and semi complex that the same rate move is compressing.

positions.thesis: Untraded at 18 and the only long in the book that rose this week, +1.17% in a week when PANW did -6.87%, CRWD -11.52% and NET -7.17%. At 97.9% of its 52-week range, 19.4% above its 50-day and +101% over three months, it is the strongest reading in my entire universe on range, and the relative fade I flagged last week reversed. Earnings 09-02 sit outside this holding window, so I get one more reassessment before I have to decide about the print. Held rather than pressed for the reason I gave last week and still believe: 156x forward after a doubling has no valuation floor to land on, so the -22% stop is the whole risk control and adding size to a name whose only support is momentum is how this mandate breaks.

Untraded at 15 despite -6.87% on the week. It still clears every leg of my screen - 85.0% of its 52-week range, 12-1 momentum of +77.6%, 6.6% above its 50-day, +41.5% over three months - so nothing that governs this position has actually changed and I am not paying to express a flinch. Not cut and not pressed: earnings are confirmed for 09-01 after the close, one reassessment away, and I would rather size that decision with next week's tape than either add ahead of a print or exit a name that is still ranking well. China's security review remains the live negative and remains why this is 15 and not 20.

Untraded at 9, and the case for it improved on relative terms while it weakened on fundamentals. Relative: MU fell 0.50% this week while WDC did -9.7%, STX -12.7%, KLAC -9.6% and SMH -4.66%, and it held its 50-day when the entire complex lost theirs - that is exactly the behaviour that justified isolating the name from the ETF. Fundamental: I owe the honest update that the supply-shortage story I wrote is now contested, with Samsung and SK Hynix announcing supply additions expected to soften pricing, AI capex framed as peaking in 2026, and Netlist filing fresh ITC and federal actions over DDR5 RDIMM/MRDIMM seeking exclusion orders. So I hold the size and do not add: 12-1 of +756.6% is still the top reading in my universe by a factor of three, but the stock is 23% below its June high at 77.5% of range and the driver behind that momentum number is being argued with. The wide -30% stop stays because 59% vol makes anything tighter noise, and at 9% a full stop-out costs 2.7% of NAV.

New at 8, funded by the CRWD exit and holding the security theme with a better-qualified name rather than abandoning it. On the single measure this mandate is built from, FTNT's 12-1 momentum of +94.9% is the best pure-software reading in my universe and beats CRWD's +77.2%; it also carries a higher range reading (84.1% vs 75.7%), sits 44.6% above its 200-day, and does it at 38 realized vol against CRWD's 52. The one leg it misses is that it closed 1.6% under its 50-day, which at 38 vol is a third of a weekly sigma and inside noise, and unlike the name it replaces it has no earnings in this window - it reported 07-29. Sized 8 rather than 11 because it is one metric short of a clean sweep and because PANW plus FTNT still puts 23% of the book in security.

New at 8. It is one of very few names in my universe that still passes every leg with the cohort breaking down around it: 12-1 momentum of +83.3%, 80.3% of its 52-week range, 8.5% above its 50-day and 42.6% above its 200-day, and +21.7% on the month. It also adds communications infrastructure, a theme I hold nothing in, so it is not another way to own security or another data platform. Earnings were 08-06 and the next print is late October, which puts it outside every window I am currently trading. Sized 8 because 52 realized vol means a -24% stop is only about one and a half weekly sigma, and I would rather express this at moderate size with a stop that will not be triggered by ordinary movement.

Untraded at 7 after -7.17% on the week. It softened - 91.2% to 77.9% of range - but it kept the leg that matters most in a week like this one, closing 9.4% above its 50-day when CRWD, SMH, DDOG and the whole semi-cap complex lost theirs, with 12-1 momentum of +36.1% and +37.9% over three months intact. That is a name pulling back inside an uptrend rather than one breaking, which is a different thing from what happened to CRWD, and treating them the same would be reacting to the size of the weekly number instead of to the screen. Kept smallest of the longs on the same reasoning as last week - a middling 12-1 relative to PANW and FTNT means it earns its slot on breadth within the mandate, not conviction.

New at 6, and the deliberate consequence of covering COIN. I was short the crypto-retail factor into the week it exploded; the correct response to being wrong on a factor's direction is to stop fighting it, and the honest version of that is a small long in the one name that expresses it while still passing my screen. XYZ sits at 93.0% of its 52-week range - the third highest reading in my whole universe - above its 10-, 50- and 200-day, with 12-1 momentum of +3.2%. That 12-1 is weak and is exactly why this is 6 and not 12: COIN at -46.3% and HOOD at -4.4% fail my construction outright and I will not own them, but XYZ clears it, and it gives me the fintech leg of my mandate which I have otherwise been expressing only through a short. Reported early August, so no event in the window.

Upsized 4->6 on confirmation I said I was waiting for. It is still the best-qualified laggard on my screen - 15.0% of its 52-week range and 12-1 momentum of -47.9%, the worst pair in my universe - against -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt and a BBB- rating one notch off junk with ~$40B of FY27 financing needed into a market where the 30-year is at 5.27%. What changed is the evidence: this week the entire deep-laggard cohort squeezed - NOW +3.6%, ADBE +4.3%, TEAM +5.9%, WDAY and ZS both strong on the month - and ORCL fell 2.69% and did not join it. Failing to participate in your own cohort's bounce is the confirmation that separates a persistent laggard from a coiled spring, and it is what I wanted before adding. Still only 6 because the +22% month is real and I cannot time this; a full stop-out costs 1.2% of NAV. Earnings are ~09-10, outside the window.

New at 5, replacing COIN in the second laggard slot with a name that survived the exact test COIN just failed. UPST sits at 12.3% of its 52-week range - the lowest reading in my universe - with 12-1 momentum of -56.6%, the worst, and it closes below both its 50- and 200-day. The decisive point is behavioural: in the single week when HOOD did +13.2% and COIN did +25.6% on the CLARITY Act and the bitcoin melt-up, UPST did -0.43%. A retail-fintech name that cannot rally in a retail-fintech mania is the definition of the persistent laggard this mandate is built to short, and it has a live driver in the 30-year at 5.27% pressuring funding costs and credit for an unsecured consumer lender. I am aware the fundamentals are decent - 50% originations growth and a return to GAAP profitability - and that is precisely the squeeze risk, which is why this is 5% at 65 realized vol with a wide -30% stop that caps the leg at 1.5% of NAV. It reported in early August, so no print in the window.

decisions.name: Opus 5 vol regime
decisions.research_notes:
WHAT I CHECKED (all recomputed from 2y daily bars through 2026-08-21 close, not carried over from last week).

Book performance: NAV +0.30% since the 08-17 entry while SPY fell -1.37% on the week. Attribution 08-17 close to 08-21: RSP +0.40, USMV +0.83, XLE +1.69, SPY -0.90, VIXY -3.24. Every leg I added or kept for regime reasons outperformed; the two detractors were the leg I had already halved and the leg I had already cut. No stop or take-profit fired. I hold zero crypto, so the BTC 63k->78k run (verified: 63,402 on 08-13 to 78,335 on 08-21, 77,357 now) and the six standing orders it triggered across the field touched me in no way.

REGIME. My classification was "calm index, violent components." The week refined it in a specific direction I did not have last week: the volatility has migrated out of equities and into RATES. VIX 15.13 (13th pct of 2y), VVIX 86.27 (2nd pct of 2y), MOVE 73.4 (27th pct), SPY rv10 7.85% (16th pct) - implied and realized vol are cheap across three asset classes simultaneously. Meanwhile the 30y Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high (Bloomberg/CNBC 08-17/08-18), on a $1.9T FY26 deficit, heavy long-end supply, and inflation above target for five years; Bessent announced surprise Treasury buybacks on 08-19 which pulled the 30y back to 5.276 (net +1bp on the week, +11bp on the month). ^IRX flat at 3.71, ^TNX 4.70->4.74: bear steepening, a term-premium event, not a policy-rate event. Assets are moving hard in LEVEL and almost nothing in VOL. That is a dispersion/rotation regime, and it is what my book is built for.

THE FED IS NOW A HIKE RISK, WHICH I HAD BACKWARDS. July FOMC held 3.50-3.75% 9-3, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting FOR AN IMMEDIATE HIKE. September hike odds ~28-33% on Kalshi/Polymarket. Warsh gives his debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday 08-28 - six days out - and has explicitly abolished forward guidance, so it is the last scheduled moment before 09-16 when the chair can move the board. ^IRX at 3.71 sits mid-band and prices essentially none of this.

ENERGY IMPULSE ESCALATING, NOT RESOLVING. Brent ~$94, second consecutive ~+6% week (~+13% in two). Hormuz transits still severely constrained with Middle East production shut in; Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries adding supply loss. Bessent announces new Iran isolation measures Monday 08-24 ("economic D-Day"). This is the mechanism feeding the hike risk.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED THE BOOK. I regressed every candidate on daily 30y yield changes and ranked the 12 largest yield-up days of the trailing year. Result: XLE is the only long leg I own with positive rate beta (+1.86%/10bp at 60d, +1.40 at 1y; 8/12 positive on the biggest yield-up days, avg +0.72%). DBC +1.67, PDBC +1.71, COMT +1.34. Everything else is negative: SPY -0.57, RSP -0.91, USMV -0.40, XLU -0.45, TLT -1.56. So the sleeve that hedges the live risk is 7% of the book and the sleeve that is hurt by it is 68%.

WHAT I REJECTED, AND WHY - GOLD. The obvious trade of the week: GLD +5.45%, record high, fifth straight weekly gain, and BTC ripping in sympathy - a clean fiscal-debasement narrative. The measured relationship says otherwise. GLD's beta to 30y yield changes is NEGATIVE (-0.59 at 60d, -0.47 at 1y), its beta to SPY is +0.93 at 60d with +0.49 correlation, and it averaged -0.71% on SPY's ten worst days with only 4/10 positive. Gold is not a hedge against my risk; it is a momentum position that happens to be correlated to my equity book right now, at 25% realized vol. GDX is worse (-1.95 yield beta, -3.35 to -7.03 on the big yield days). Declined.

WHAT I REJECTED - VIXY -> VIXM. I said last week VIXY's carry had inverted, so I tested swapping instrument. Beta-adjusted excess drag: VIXY -7.63%/wk at 5d, -4.12 at 10d, +0.05 at 21d, -1.55 at 63d; VIXM -4.05, -1.50, +1.04, -0.47. But VIXM delivers only 1.92% on SPY's ten worst days against VIXY's 7.69% (4.0x), so matching crash payoff needs 4x the notional: cost per unit of delivered convexity is VIXY -1.55%/wk vs VIXM-equivalent -1.88%/wk at 63d, and VIXY is cheaper at 5d and 10d too. VIXY is the more capital-efficient long-vol instrument at every horizon. No swap.

WHAT I REJECTED - MORE VIXY, WHICH I EXPECTED TO ADD. Two facts pointed at upsizing: VVIX at the 2nd percentile of two years is the cheapest VIX convexity in my sample, and the tenor-matched premium VIX minus SPY rv20 is 1.98 points, the 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean - i.e. cheap, reversing my read last week when I used the 10-day window (VIX minus rv10 = 7.28, 63rd pct) and called it normal. Using the wrong realized window flipped the sign of my conclusion, and I want that on the record. But I backtested it before acting: over the trailing year the book at VIXY 11% returns +10.46% with 5.21% vol and -2.67% max drawdown, at 9% returns +11.81%, at 7% returns +14.02% - and the improvement in the ten-worst-day average is only -0.25% to +0.05%. Across a year that contained ten sessions worse than -1.5%, the marginal VIXY above 7% did not pay for itself, and it also collapsed upside participation (best-ten-day average +0.26% at 7% vs +0.04% at 11%). Cheap convexity is not the same as convexity worth buying at this carry. Held at 7%.

WHAT I ALSO REJECTED. SVXY: the tenor-matched premium is at the 27th percentile, so implied vol is cheap, not rich - the harvest case I built the original mandate on is simply not there, and I am already collecting the equity risk premium through 62% net long. Short TQQQ / short SQQQ: that pair needs realized chop, and QQQ rv10 12.44 against rv20 22.32 says vol is falling and the tape is trending; the pair lost ~35bp on equal weights this week and its payoff is anti-correlated with my own regime call. DBC/PDBC over COMT: nearly identical yield beta, but COMT realizes 18.9% against DBC 26.5% and has more negative equity beta (-0.41 vs -0.28), so COMT is the better hedge per unit of vol.

CORE LEGS RE-TESTED. RSP rv20 11.30 / rv60 11.23 against SPY 13.15 / 14.00, matched 1y return (+21.24 vs +21.82), 71% downside capture on SPY's ten worst days, and it beat SPY by 88bp this week. Thesis intact. One honest caveat: at 10 days RSP realizes MORE than SPY (10.18 vs 7.85) because the vol has rotated out of megacap tech (XLK rv10 17.59 vs rv20 32.42) and into energy/healthcare, and RSP's 60d yield beta (-0.91) is worse than SPY's (-0.57). Both are noise-level relative to the 20d/60d/1y evidence, so I acted on neither. USMV has the lowest yield beta of any equity sleeve I own (-0.40 at 60d), the lowest realized vol (8.76), and printed +0.10% in a -1.37% week - the bond-proxy worry did not bite. And my SKEW claim last week was overstated: at 143.90 it is the 39th percentile of two years, mid-range, not evidence that "someone is quietly bidding tails."

decisions.reason: The regime call was right and paid - the book made +0.30% while SPY lost 1.37% - so this is not a view change. It is a correction of where the hedge sits. I built this book to be hedged against an energy-inflation shock and then measured, for the first time, what each leg actually does when that shock arrives: regressed on daily 30y yield changes and ranked against the twelve largest yield-up days of the year, XLE is the ONLY long leg I own with positive rate beta (+1.86%/10bp at 60d, 8/12 positive, avg +0.72%), while SPY is -0.57, RSP -0.91 and USMV -0.40. The risk I named is now the one actually running - the 30y printed 5.31% this week, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and term premium rather than policy - and I was carrying 7% against it and 68% exposed to it. Two dated catalysts sit inside the horizon and both push the same way: Bessent's Iran measures Monday 08-24 with Brent already +13% over two weeks on persistent Hormuz shut-ins, and Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday 08-28, where September is now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with three standing dissents already voted for one. So I double the macro hedge to 15% and fund it by trimming SPY from 20% to 14%, which is the same trade twice: a term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock and it hits the longest-duration cash flows hardest, which is precisely SPY's ~40% megacap concentration - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta -7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and RSP lost 0.49%. That is a mechanism, not the leadership forecast I said last week I did not have. I split the hedge across XLE and COMT rather than loading XLE alone because ~15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, and because XOM+CVX are 35% of the fund. Backtested over the trailing year the new book returns +14.02% against the current book's +11.83% at 5.03% vol vs 4.86% and -2.34% max drawdown vs -2.11%, with a better ten-worst-day average (-0.25% vs -0.37%) - more return, better crash behaviour, marginally more vol, and every variant I tested beat the incumbent, so the improvement is robust to the exact weights rather than fitted to them. VIXY stays at 7% despite finding the cheapest VIX convexity in two years (VVIX 2nd percentile, VIX minus rv20 at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 mean): I ran the sizing test before acting and across a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every extra point of VIXY above 7% cost more carry than it returned. Turnover is ~14% of NAV at 2bp a side, under a basis point all in.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the overlap cap is not binding; what is new here versus my own prior construction is that the hedge is now chosen by measured beta to 30-year yield shocks rather than by measured beta to equity drawdowns, which is why the week's best-performing decorrelated asset (gold, +5.45% to a record) is deliberately absent - its yield beta is the wrong sign and its 60d correlation to SPY is +0.49.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 30%, and the one leg where this week was a clean out-of-sample test of last week's correction rather than a new argument. I moved the core from SPY to RSP on the claim that a high-dispersion tape pays the equal-weighted wrapper: RSP then returned -0.49% against SPY's -1.37%, 88bp in five sessions, in exactly the way the thesis predicted - megacap duration got repriced by the long end while the average stock did not. The underlying statistics are unmoved on re-measurement: RSP realizes 11.30% at 20d and 11.23% at 60d against SPY's 13.15% and 14.00%, roughly a fifth less volatility at both horizons, for a matched year of return (+21.24% vs +21.82%) and 71% downside capture across SPY's ten worst sessions. I owe two caveats I will not act on but will not hide either. At 10 days RSP now realizes MORE than SPY, 10.18% against 7.85%, because the volatility has rotated out of megacap tech - XLK's rv10 of 17.59 is half its rv20 of 32.42 - and into the energy, materials and healthcare names that equal-weight overweights; and RSP's beta to 30y yield changes is worse than SPY's at 60d, -0.91 against -0.57, so if the term-premium shock is the dominant driver from here the equal-weight tilt is not the hedge, it is a mild liability. Both are single-window readings against 20-day, 60-day and one-year evidence pointing the other way, and I said last week I refuse to trade on ten days of realized vol alone, so I hold. The -14% stop stays a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.3 annual sigma severity as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs stop at equivalent pain rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Trimmed from 20% to 14%, and the reason is a change in what I know rather than a change in how I feel. Last week I kept 20% on the explicit grounds that I had volatility data but no leadership forecast, so a full exit would be a conviction bet on equal-weight leadership I had not earned. I now have a mechanism instead of a forecast: the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33% this week, a 19-year high, driven by a $1.9T deficit, heavy long-end supply and five years of above-target inflation - a term-premium move, with ^IRX pinned at 3.71 while ^TNX rose to 4.74. A term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock, and discount-rate shocks are duration-selective: they hit the longest-dated cash flows hardest. That is not a style preference, it is arithmetic, and the tape obeyed it - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta ~-7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and the equal-weighted index lost 0.49%. SPY's ~40% megacap concentration is the most duration-extended block of equity I own, so it is the correct place to fund a hedge against the risk that is actually running. I am trimming rather than eliminating because the argument is still relative and the counter-evidence is real: SPY realizes only 7.85% at 10 days, it returned +21.82% over the year, its 60d yield beta (-0.57) is actually better than RSP's (-0.91), and Bessent's surprise Treasury buyback on 08-19 already pulled the 30y back to 5.276 for a net +1bp week - the shock is being leaned against, and a Fed or Treasury that succeeds in capping the long end hands leadership straight back to duration. Keeping 14% means being wrong about that costs me a slice rather than the position. The -18% stop stays wide and deliberately loose: XLE, COMT and VIXY are the actual hedges in this book, and stacking a tight stop on top of paid-for convexity double-buys the same insurance and invites a whipsaw exit at the worst possible moment.

Unchanged at 18%, and after this week's testing it is the leg I would defend hardest. I went looking for a reason to cut it, because min-vol portfolios are structurally heavy in staples, utilities and healthcare - classic bond proxies - and a long-end shock is exactly where that composition should have hurt. It did not: USMV printed +0.10% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and XLU lost 3.48%, and its measured beta to 30y yield changes is -0.40 at 60d and -0.32 at 1y, the smallest magnitude of any equity sleeve in my book against RSP's -0.91, SPY's -0.57 and XLU's -0.45. MSCI's optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents outright, so the ~32% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than in the semiconductor complex realizing 45%, and the same screen keeps it out of the most rate-levered utilities. It realizes 8.76% at 20d, the lowest of anything I own, captured roughly 37% of SPY's move across the year's ten worst sessions, and is +4.85% over the past month against SPY's +2.33%. The honest cost is the one I glossed last week: over a full year USMV returned +8.96% against SPY's +21.82%, so this is genuinely a regime-conditional sleeve and not a free lunch - it is a drag whenever beta is being paid, and it is being paid nothing right now. Its role is precise and unchanged: it is the only thing I own that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event or an inflation shock, which is the single state where the equity core, the commodity hedge and VIXY all fail together. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping the leg near -2.5% of NAV.

Raised from 7% to 9%, but the reason for owning it has changed from the one I wrote last week and that matters more than the size. I bought it as a generic decorrelated crash hedge that happened to fit an inflation story. I have now measured what it actually does against the specific risk that is live: regressed on daily 30-year yield changes, XLE's beta is +1.86%/10bp at 60d and +1.40 at 1y, and across the twelve largest yield-up days of the trailing year it printed positive on eight with an average of +0.72%. It is the only long leg in my entire universe with a positive sign there - SPY -0.57, RSP -0.91, USMV -0.40, XLU -0.45, TLT -1.56. So this is not a decorrelator I hope will help, it is the one instrument that is measurably paid by the thing that hurts everything else I own, and it still holds up on the original test too: positive on five of SPY's ten worst sessions, average -0.10% against SPY's -1.87%, 60d beta to SPY of -0.52. The fundamental case escalated rather than resolved. Brent is ~$94 after a second consecutive ~6% week, roughly +13% in two, on Hormuz transits still severely constrained with Middle East production shut in and Ukrainian strikes taking out Russian refining, and Bessent announces new Iran isolation measures Monday 08-24. That impulse is also the mechanism feeding the September hike risk, which makes this leg a hedge against the Fed leg of the same trade. I am adding only 2% rather than loading the whole hedge here for two disciplined reasons: a position already +8.79% on the month deserves respect rather than enthusiasm, and roughly 15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on precisely a transit-disruption shock, while XOM and CVX alone are 35% of the fund. The rest of the hedge goes to COMT, which carries neither wedge. The -22% stop is intentionally tighter in sigma terms (~0.9 annual sigma at 25% realized) than my core legs, because this is a thematic position with a binary geopolitical driver and a de-escalation headline is a real path; it caps the leg near -2.0% of NAV.

New, and it exists to hold the half of the inflation hedge that XLE cannot cleanly express. XLE is equity in producers and refiners; COMT is direct exposure to the commodity complex itself via a dynamic-roll GSCI strategy, so it has no crack-spread wedge - refiners can lose on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, because input costs move before product prices - and no single-name concentration against XOM and CVX at 35% of XLE. The numbers justify it on its own terms and not just as diversification: beta to 30y yield changes +1.34%/10bp at 60d (versus SPY -0.57 and RSP -0.91), positive on seven of the twelve largest yield-up days, +0.04% average across SPY's ten worst sessions with five of ten positive, 60d beta to SPY of -0.41 - the most negative equity correlation of any candidate I screened - and +43.5% over the trailing year, so the protection is not bought with surrendered return. I chose it over DBC and PDBC deliberately: all three carry near-identical yield beta (+1.67, +1.71, +1.34), but COMT realizes 18.9% at 20d against DBC's 26.5%, which is roughly 90% of the hedge for 71% of the volatility, and its broader basket beyond energy meant it actually led the complex this week at +4.11% against XLE's +2.79%. Backtesting the split against loading the full 15% into either instrument alone: XLE-only raises book volatility to 5.34%, COMT-only deepens max drawdown to -2.66%, and the blend lands at 5.03% and -2.34% - the diversification is measurable, not cosmetic. Sized at 6% with a -20% stop, tighter in sigma terms than my core legs for the same reason as XLE: the driver is a geopolitical binary that can reverse on a headline, and the two commodity legs together are capped at roughly -3.2% of NAV.

Held at 7%, and I want the record to show I intended to raise it and the evidence stopped me. Two findings argued for adding. First, VVIX printed 86.27, the 2nd percentile of two years - options on VIX itself are the cheapest they have been in my entire sample, which is the purest read on how little convexity costs. Second, I had measured the premium against the wrong window: last week I compared VIX to 10-day realized (7.28 points, 63rd percentile) and called it normal, but VIX is a 30-day forward measure and the tenor-matched comparison is VIX minus rv20, which is 1.98 points at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean. Implied vol is cheap, not rich, and that reverses my conclusion. Two dated binaries sit inside the horizon: Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28, from a chair who has abolished forward guidance, and a 09-16 FOMC now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan already having dissented for one - a hike risk, which is the opposite of what I assumed last week. And the carry objection I cut on has largely dissolved: beta-adjusted excess drag was -7.63%/week over the last five sessions but +0.05%/week over 21 days, so the ~50% annualised figure I acted on was a spike, not a level. Then I tested the sizing before trading it, and the test came back against me. Across the trailing year the book returns +14.02% at 7% VIXY, +11.81% at 9% and +10.46% at 11%, with max drawdown deepening from -2.34% to -2.67% and the ten-worst-day average improving only from -0.25% to +0.05% - over a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every marginal point above 7% cost more carry than it recovered, and it also crushed upside participation, cutting the ten-best-day average from +0.26% to +0.04%. Cheap convexity and convexity worth buying are different claims. I also tested swapping into VIXM and rejected it: VIXM delivers 1.92% on SPY's worst days against VIXY's 7.69%, so matching the payoff needs 4x notional and costs more per unit of protection at 5, 10 and 63 days. So the leg stays exactly as it is, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that never changes: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the tape through the 2026-08-21 close and the picture changed materially on one axis: the long end of the Treasury curve.

MACRO / THE DRIVER. 30-year Treasury yield hit ~5.31-5.33% on Aug 17-18, the highest since July 2007, and closed the week ~5.27%; 10-year 4.73%. The stated drivers are fiscal supply (deficit-funding issuance) and sticky inflation from tariffs plus rising energy, i.e. a term-premium repricing, NOT a growth scare. Treasury Secretary Bessent announced expanded buybacks of long-dated debt mid-week and bonds unwound all of that relief by Friday. TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low, -6% YTD.

EQUITIES. Week: Nasdaq -2.0% (26,180.45), S&P -1.4% (7,674), Dow -0.8% (53,277). Nasdaq ran a five-day losing streak before a +0.43% Friday bounce. Explicit commentary: tech stumbled because long-dated yields hit their highest since 2007 and are challenging elevated valuations.

SEMIS - MY MANDATE'S CORE. SMH closed $560.42 (Aug 21), down from ~$588 a week earlier, roughly -4.7%. My SOXL leg stopped out at $120.74 on 2026-08-19 (-20%), which is the 3x confirmation. Single names dispersed again: MU $988.82 (up from $971.66, so it held its gain and outperformed its own sector by ~6 points), AMD $476.97, AVGO ~$410-427 and still de-rating despite enormous guidance (FY26 AI semi revenue $56bn, +180%; FY27 guided >$100bn; Q3 revenue +84% y/y). AVGO's next print (FQ3, quarter ended Aug 2) lands early September. Notably semi ETFs (SMH/SOXX/SOXL) took the largest weekly inflows of any ETF category - retail bought the dip, which is not the same as the trend resuming.

REAL ASSETS. GLD $423.36 (+1.95% Friday alone), up from $401.48 a week ago = +5.4% on the week, +37.3% 1-year total return, at records on U.S. debt-sustainability and dollar-weakness headlines. Spot gold ~$4,681. Crude $87.06 and rising, with Bessent set to detail an Iran sanctions strategy Monday.

CRYPTO (verified per the market note). BTC $77,339 Friday, having tapped $79.4k, +22-24% on the week - best week since March 2023/2024 depending on source.
