Drivers were (1) the Treasury buyback announcement read as liquidity support, (2) a short squeeze - ~$1.42bn of BTC liquidations on Aug 19 alone plus another ~$1bn over the next 24 hours, (3) reclaiming the 200-day EMA. So one-third technical, one-third liquidity, one-third forced covering. I hold no crypto in either book.

ROTATION. Healthcare/biotech is the destination: IBB +20% since mid-June against semiconductors -20% over the same stretch. Crypto-adjacent equities ripped Friday (HOOD +13.7%, COIN +8%).

CONCLUSION I DREW. Rising long real rates are a multiple-compression mechanism pointed at the longest-duration assets on the board, and leveraged semis are precisely that. The same force is simultaneously paying gold, energy and hard assets. That single observation drives both books this week: cut levered equity duration and nominal bond duration, raise real assets and cash, and stay flat crypto rather than chase a squeeze or short a 200-day reclaim.

decisions.reason: The trend this mandate rides inverted, and the reason is macro rather than idiosyncratic, so momentum discipline says cut leveraged beta and raise cash rather than average into a break. SMH went 588 -> 560.42 (-4.7%), Nasdaq -2.0% on a five-day slump, and my own 3x leg told me first by stopping out at -20% on Aug 19. The mechanism is that the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and tariff/energy inflation - a term-premium repricing, not a growth scare. Rising long real rates compress multiples hardest on the longest-duration equities on the board, which is exactly what leveraged semis are, so this is the discount rate moving underneath my thesis rather than noise inside it. I therefore kill both remaining pure-leverage expressions (TQQQ out, no SOXL re-entry - paying daily-rebalance decay to fight a de-rating is the worst trade available), cut the semis sleeve from 51% to 34%, exit the two positions with no momentum left (MSFT's drift was already fading and this regime is the specific thing that ends it; AVGO keeps falling on excellent news, which is a de-rate I do not get paid to sit through into an early-September print), and rotate that capital into the three legs the regime actually pays: energy with crude at $87.06 and an Iran sanctions announcement due Monday, defence on the same geopolitical impulse with zero AI-capex correlation, and healthcare, which is the documented destination of this rotation at IBB +20% since mid-June against semis -20%. Cash goes 11% -> 33% because at 4% APY cash is a positively-carrying position while the trend is broken, and weekly reassessment means I can re-add leverage the week the trend resumes rather than needing to own it through the repair. I am staying flat crypto despite my mandate naming short perps: the downtrend it was written against is dead, BTC reclaimed its 200-day EMA on a +24% week, and roughly $2.4bn of shorts were liquidated Aug 19-21 - that is how shorts died across the field this week - but a move two-thirds built on forced covering and a buyback headline is equally not something I chase long at 10% APR funding. Flat is the honest position, not an omission.

positions.thesis: Cut from 17% but kept as the largest leg, because the index is still how I stay long semis without betting on which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks - the lesson I paid for on memory. Reduced rather than exited because the break is real: 588 -> 560.42 is a genuine lower high after weeks of trend, and retail buying the dip (SMH/SOXX/SOXL took the largest weekly ETF inflows on record for the sector) is a sentiment fact, not a trend-resumption signal. Stop tightened from -12% to -9% precisely because the argument for owning this at all is that the uptrend resumes quickly; if it does not, I want to be out well before a -12% loss, and a wide stop on a broken trend is just a slow exit.

Held flat at 12% and now my largest single-name conviction, because it is the only thing in the sleeve that actually went up in a down week: $971.66 -> $988.82 while SMH fell 4.7%, roughly six points of relative strength on top of the +12.9% it already gave me from entry. That is textbook momentum - the leader leads hardest when the sector breaks - and selling it to reduce risk would mean funding my de-risking out of the one position that is working. Not raised either, because raising it would rebuild the narrow 'I am right about DRAM pricing' bet that burned me two weeks ago, and the bear case (YMTC now the third-largest NAND player, Citi's four-quarter deceleration call) is dormant rather than refuted. Stop stays wide at -15% because that is about one week of this name's realised range and strangling my best performer with a tight stop is how I lose it to noise; added a +30% take-profit so that if the memory trade goes parabolic into a squeeze the exit is defined in advance rather than improvised.

Trimmed from 11% at $476.97 as part of cutting the semis sleeve, not because the rotation-into-merchant-compute thesis failed. It is still the right second leg alongside MU - owning compute and memory rather than doubling memory is what makes this a claim about where capital is moving rather than a call on one pricing curve. But it is a high-multiple name in the exact cohort a 19-year-high long yield de-rates, so it takes its share of the reduction. Stop tightened -15% to -13% to match the shorter leash the whole book is now on.

Raised from 7% to co-largest non-semis leg because it is the one position that is long the actual regime rather than hedged against it. Crude closed $87.06 and rising, and energy inflation is explicitly named as a driver of the same bond selloff that is de-rating my equity book - so this leg gets paid by the mechanism that is hurting everything else, which is the definition of a real hedge rather than a diversifier. Bessent details an Iran sanctions strategy Monday, a live supply catalyst on top of a +49% one-year trend. It also remains the only sleeve that pays if inflation rather than employment turns out to be the binding problem, and this week made that the more likely of the two.

Raised from 8% and now co-largest outside semis. It is the trending half of the defence pair (+3.5% the prior week to $608.68 against RTX flat) and it gets the same Iran-sanctions geopolitical impulse that is bidding crude, so the catalyst is shared with XLE while the P&L driver - backlog and government contracts - is completely different. Critically it carries near-zero correlation to the AI-capex debate that every semi position here depends on, which matters far more now that the AI complex is de-rating on rates rather than on fundamentals. Stop tightened to -10% since this is a low-realised-vol name and -12% was more room than it needs.

Raised from 5% to 8% - the biggest proportional add in the book - because this stopped being a defensive anchor and became a momentum position. Biotech (IBB) is +20% since mid-June against semiconductors -20% over the identical window; that is not defensive outperformance, it is the rotation destination, and a momentum mandate that ignores a 40-point relative move because the sector is nominally 'defensive' is applying a label instead of a rule. Expressed through XLV rather than IBB because I am reducing book risk this week and want the broader, lower-beta vehicle while I add to a trend I did not previously own.

Held flat at 7% as the smaller half of the defence pair. It went sideways again ($222.97 vs $223.03), so on pure momentum it does not earn an add - but the sleeve's job is zero AI-cycle correlation expressed across two names rather than concentrated in one, and that job is more valuable this week than last. The Monday Iran sanctions catalyst applies here as much as to LMT, so I am content to be paid to wait. Stop tightened to -10% in line with the rest of the book.

decisions.reason: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.
decisions.novelty: Round 3 shares exactly one name with Round 2 - XLE at 8% here against 9% there, roughly 10% same-direction gross-weight overlap - because the two books are now expressing opposite sides of the same macro fact: Round 2 is reducing exposure to the long-duration growth equities that a 19-year-high 30-year yield de-rates, while Round 3 is a zero-leverage, zero-semiconductor, zero-crypto basket of gold, min-vol equity, belly duration, credit and dividend carry whose entire purpose is to earn a return that does not depend on the AI capex cycle at all.

positions.thesis: Raised 13% -> 16% and now the top weight, which is a real change of role rather than a size tweak. Last week I added only one point and said adding hard after a 7% run is how a low-vol book imports volatility; gold then added another 5.4% to $423.36 with a +1.95% session Friday, and the reason it is running is now explicit in the headlines - U.S. debt sustainability and dollar weakness, the same fiscal fact that took the 30-year to a 19-year high. That changes the calculus: this is not a momentum chase, it is the only asset in the basket that is structurally paid by the specific shock repricing everything else I own. It also does the job my Treasury sleeve just failed at - in a fiscal/inflation shock bonds and equities fall together, so gold is now carrying the diversification load that duration used to. Capped at 16% rather than higher because inverse-vol weighting must still bind on what is now one of the highest-vol assets here, and the -12% stop stays to survive post-squeeze mean reversion after a two-week run.

Untouched at 14% and now the largest equity sleeve. Nothing about a min-vol equity book deteriorated this week in a way specific to it - the S&P fell 1.4% and min-vol is designed to take less than its share of that. It remains the vehicle I want owning the equity risk premium in a tape where the index is falling on discount-rate compression rather than on earnings, since low-vol names carry less multiple to compress. Left alone deliberately: this rebalance is along the rates axis, and touching legs the axis did not move is churn.

Cut 15% -> 12% and demoted from top weight, but deliberately not gutted the way TLT was. The distinction is the one my framework already draws and that keeps being confirmed: the fiscal supply problem sits at the back of the curve, and the belly has consistently outperformed it through this repricing. At a 4.73% ten-year the carry is genuinely attractive on an absolute basis for the first time in this cycle, and this is still the only asset in the basket that rallies outright if the labour-market crack resolves as a real growth scare rather than the inflation problem the tape is currently pricing. Trimmed rather than held because that scenario is now the less likely of the two and I should not have my largest position in the branch the market is voting against.

Raised 6% -> 8%. Crude at $87.06 with rising energy costs named directly as a driver of the inflation keeping the long end elevated, which makes this the leg most tightly coupled to the regime and the only one that does not need rates to fall in order to work. That property is worth more now than it was a week ago, because the entire rest of a carry book is implicitly short rising long rates. Held to 8% rather than pushed higher because it is the highest-volatility sleeve in the basket and inverse-vol weighting has to cap it regardless of how well the thesis is running - the discipline is the point.

Held at 7%. Selected on a pure realised-volatility screen where USMV is optimisation-based, so the two hold materially different constituents and genuinely diversify rather than duplicate a single factor. Running both is what allows the equity-premium allocation to stay above 20% in a book whose mandate is variance minimisation. Untouched for the same reason as USMV: the rates axis moved, this leg did not.

Cut 8% -> 6%, continuing the direction I have been trimming rather than reversing it. Spreads still have not widened and the ETF has been quiet, so this is not a reaction to damage - it is a judgement that the compensation has become thin relative to the alternative. Roughly 7% of yield for credit risk standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex, a contracting labour market and a government whose borrowing costs just hit a 19-year high, when cash next to it pays 4% with zero duration and zero default risk, is about 300bp for a genuinely fat left tail. Kept at 6% rather than zero because spread carry is explicitly in my mandate and tight spreads can stay tight for a long time; the -6% stop remains the thing that makes the asymmetry survivable.

Cut 9% -> 6%, the largest reduction among the equity carry sleeves, because REITs are the most rate-sensitive asset I own outside the Treasury complex - they are levered vehicles whose cost of capital is the long yield that just hit a 19-year high, so they take the hit twice, through the discount rate on the cash flows and through refinancing. I wrote last week that I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve because at least here I get paid a contractual yield while waiting; that is still true and is why this survives at 6% rather than going to zero, but if I am cutting duration as a portfolio decision it would be incoherent to cut TLT to zero and leave the levered real-estate proxy at 9%.

Held at 6%. Staples earn their place through the distinction that drives this whole rebalance: their effective duration is short and their pricing power passes inflation through to revenue, so unlike REITs or the long bond they are not simply a levered bet on rates falling. They take the defensive dividend-carry role at a similar yield to utilities without the AI-datacenter-power exposure that has turned utilities into a proxy for the same capex cycle this book exists to avoid, and they are the equity that holds up if the next payroll print gets read as recessionary.

Held at 5%. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple and a stable, growing dividend, and it shares the inflation pass-through property that is the reason I am keeping staples while cutting the pure bond proxies. Essentially no exposure to the AI capex debate and no fiscal-duration exposure, which in a week when both the equity index and the long bond fell together is precisely the profile the basket needs more of.

Trimmed 5% -> 4%. The diversification case is intact - regulated domestic cash flows, a real coupon, near-zero correlation to the AI capex cycle - but the reason it is the one dividend name I am cutting is that telecom carries heavy balance-sheet debt, so a structural repricing of borrowing costs to a 19-year high hits it through refinancing in a way it does not hit KO or the staples basket. A one-point trim rather than an exit, because that is a slow-burning headwind on a genuinely diversifying yield stream, not a thesis break.

decisions.name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED for this session, so all verification was done by direct WebFetch of quote/fundamental pages (stockanalysis.com) plus what those pages carried as news context. Marks are Aug 21, 2026 closes.

MACRO REGIME — this is the week's actual story, and it is not "risk-off":
- 30-year Treasury yield topped 5.1%, highest in nearly a year; TLT $82.05, at the bottom of its 52-week range ($81.17-$92.19) and its lowest in over two decades.
- Spot gold broke above $4,600/oz (from ~$4,450 a week ago); GLD $423.36. Cited drivers: weaker dollar, Treasury buyback announcements, and US debt-sustainability concerns.
- SPY $765.72, up on the day and within 1.8% of its high; BTC ran ~$63k to ~$78k per the desk note (I hold no crypto in either book, so no direct action, but it corroborates the read).
- XLU $42.77, -2.28% on the day and near its 52-week LOW ($41.15) — bond proxies broke while equities held.
That combination — long yields up, gold up, dollar down, utilities down, index up — is a fiscal-credibility/debasement rotation, not a growth scare. It is precisely the tape that pays my Round 3 book and taxes my Round 2 book. Round 2 lost 6.16% in the same week SPY rose, which confirms the loss is theme-specific derating, not beta.

ROUND 2 MARKS (all vs. last week's entry levels):
- AVGO $368.45, fwd PE 23.35, target $526.30, -24% from its June peak, earnings Sept 2.
- GEV $956.85 (from $1,063.25, -10.0%); fwd PE 44.68 — the richest multiple I own; profit line missed on the print even with revenue guidance raised; target $1,239.46.
- ANET $188.65 (from $198.82, -5.1%, though +2.67% Friday); fwd PE 40.61; Q2 revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, FY guide $12.6B; target $241.82.
- AMAT $492.32, fwd PE 27.91, target $641.03 — essentially unchanged on the week after last week's post-beat selloff. No new information.
- MU $966.78, roughly flat on the week; fwd PE 6.72; target $1,515.11 (+57%); customers are asking for ~50% MORE memory than Micron can commit; announced a $10B AI memory research lab in Boise. Still 23% below its $1,255 high.
- VRT $261.95, down on the week; fwd PE 33.52, target $338.15.

THE TWO FACTS THAT BROKE MY AVGO THESIS (both verified, not price-driven):
1. Google signed an expanded custom-AI-silicon agreement with MARVELL worth up to $120B through 2033, and handed Google a warrant for ~$12.2B of MRVL stock. MRVL is $237.04, 52wk $61.44-$329.88. I held AVGO at co-largest weight explicitly because its custom-silicon customers were "Apple, Google and Samsung, the strongest balance sheets on earth." Google just bought a second source at nine-figure-billions scale and took equity alignment with the competitor.
2. Broadcom is reported in talks to raise $60B+ (some accounts $70-100B) of DEBT to finance AI chip deals for compute buyers. I held AVGO explicitly because it was NOT on the debt-financed side of the AI buildout — the vendor-financing pattern the market started punishing after Nvidia trimmed its OpenAI guarantee. Broadcom is now doing exactly that.
Both legs of my stated reason are gone in one week. The stock itself is fine at 23x forward with 43% consensus upside — which is why this is a demotion, not an exit.

SHORT CANDIDATE VERIFIED: CRWV $87.85, -43% from its $153.20 high, unprofitable (-$1.93B), ~$35B of debt against $35-39B of planned 2026 capex, revenue $7.59B ttm. It is the purest debt-financed BUYER of the equipment my book SELLS. NVDA ($214.72, fwd PE 21.42) reports Aug 26 — inside the window — which is the right kind of risk for this pairing: a blowout print hurts the short and pays the longs, a weak print does the reverse.

ROUND 3 MARKS — the thesis fired:
- GDX $102.83 (from $89.97, +14.3%); PE re-rated 13.6 -> 16.23; now only 12% below its $117.18 high versus 23% when I sized it up. The exact miners-lag-bullion divergence I raised weight for closed inside one week.
- COPX $94.59 (from $85.70, +10.4%, +5.18% on Friday alone); now 5.4% below its $99.99 high versus 14% before.
- XLE $63.64 (from $61.91, +2.8%) and it printed a NEW 52-week high — the range top moved from $63.46 to $64.70. Yield 2.38%, PE 20.0.
- EWZ $35.06 (+2.7%), PE 9.68, yield 3.87% — the laggard of the commodity complex this week.
- EWJ $95.18, near its $98.79 high, yield 3.74%; Japan exports +23.2% y/y, fifth straight acceleration, driven by chip shipments.
- EZU untouched, no new information.
- UUP $27.90 (from $28.11, -0.75%). The dollar leg I nearly wrote off last week for failing a live test just passed one: gold's break above $4,600 was explicitly attributed to a weaker dollar and debt-sustainability worries, with the long end confirming at 5.1%.

decisions.reason: I am not cutting this book because it fell; I am cutting the one leg whose stated reason for existing was destroyed by verifiable news, and rotating the proceeds into the leg the same news makes safer. Two weeks ago I wrote that AVGO earned top weight because its custom-silicon customers were Apple, Google and Samsung rather than debt-financed buyers. This week Google signed Marvell for up to $120B of custom AI silicon through 2033 with a $12.2B warrant attached, and Broadcom itself was reported raising $60B+ of debt to finance customers' compute. Both halves of my sentence are now false, so AVGO cannot stay co-largest at 17 — it goes to 6, kept only because 23x forward with 43% consensus upside and the Apple/Samsung work is a real business, not because I still believe the moat argument. The money goes to MU, which is the anti-AVGO: customers are begging for 50% more supply than it can commit, so its order book is a shortage rather than a financing decision, and at 6.7x forward against a $1,515 target it is the cheapest physical bottleneck I can own. Second, the macro changed underneath the whole theme — the 30-year cleared 5.1%, TLT is at a 22-year low, and utilities broke to 52-week lows while the index rose. Long-duration capex equities derate in that tape, so I trim the two fattest multiples I own (GEV at 44.7x after a profit miss, VRT at 33.5x) rather than defend them. Third, my mandate calls for a small laggard short that I have not been carrying, and the regime finally names it: I own the sellers of AI infrastructure, so I short CoreWeave, the buyer funding $35-39B of 2026 capex on $35B of debt while losing money. If AI financing strain is real my longs survive it and CRWV does not; if NVDA blows out on Aug 26 the short pays for itself out of my longs. I am at -14.61% drawdown, the exact tolerance this mandate was written to respect, so I take net exposure from 82% to 72% long against a 6% short and hold 22% cash at 4% instead of adding the 3x-semis kicker — that kicker is capped by the drawdown limit, and the drawdown limit is where we are.

positions.thesis: Raised 11 to 18 and now the anchor. This is the only leg in the book whose demand is physically rationed rather than financed: management says customers are asking for roughly 50% more memory than Micron can commit, and it just committed $10B to an AI memory lab in Boise. That distinction is the whole argument of the week — an order that cannot be filled cannot be deferred by a tightening credit market, whereas a wafer-fab tool order or a custom-ASIC program can. At $966.78 it sits 23% below its $1,255 high on a 6.72 forward multiple against a $1,515 consensus, which is a 57% gap and by far the cheapest thing I own. Keeping the wide -22% stop: it has run enormously and memory is a genuine cyclical, so it needs room to be wrong without being a catastrophe. Earnings Sept 22, outside the window.

Trimmed 17 to 14. The physical-constraint case is intact — $176B backlog, raised revenue guidance, turbines sold to hyperscalers off their own balance sheets rather than through SPVs — but two things argue for less: the print missed on profit even as revenue guidance rose, and at 44.68x forward this is now the richest multiple in my book at the precise moment the 30-year cleared 5.1% and every long-duration infrastructure buildout gets discounted harder. The stock fell 10% to $956.85 on that combination, not on any damage to the backlog. Target $1,239 leaves ~30% of room, so this stays a core holding, just not a co-largest one. Stop tightened -20 to -18 because a name that has started missing on margins deserves less rope.

Held at 14, essentially untouched. Revenue over $3B at +37.7% y/y with the full-year guide at $12.6B is the cleanest fundamental record in the book, and it closed +2.67% on Friday while the rest of my theme was being sold. Its customers are the hyperscalers paying cash, and compute-fabric demand depends on neither turbine lead times nor wafer-fab order timing, which is why it survives the financing question that just took AVGO down a peg. The risk is honest and unchanged: 40.6x forward against a $241.82 target is a growth multiple in a rising-long-rate tape, which is why it is 14 and not 18.

Held at 12 with only an arithmetic nudge, because nothing new happened. Last week I cut it hard on the read that the market rejected a genuine beat on multiple rather than on quarter, and that wafer-fab equipment is the most financing-elastic link in the chain; this week it went sideways at $492.32 while its peers fell, which is mild confirmation rather than new information. At 27.9x forward against a $641 target the discount is real and I keep a meaningful position, but nothing about the week earns it a promotion. Stop stays -18%: if the competitive threat is structural I want to be taken out early rather than proved right slowly.

Cut 17 to 6 — the largest single change I have made, and it is about my reasoning being falsified rather than about the price. I held this at co-largest weight on one specific sentence: that Broadcom's customers were Apple, Google and Samsung rather than debt-financed buyers, so it sat on the safe side of the AI financing question. This week Google signed Marvell for up to $120B of custom AI silicon through 2033 and took a ~$12.2B warrant in the competitor, and Broadcom was reported in talks to raise $60B+ of its own debt to finance customers' compute. The second-source risk and the vendor-financing risk I said did not apply here both now apply. I keep a stub rather than exiting because the Apple multi-year work and the Samsung manufacturing collaboration are untouched, 23.35x forward against a $526 target is the cheapest growth multiple I own after MU, and the Marvell revenue is back-half loaded across seven years. Stop tightened -20 to -15 and I carry Sept 2 earnings knowingly on a size where a bad print costs me under a point of NAV.

Trimmed 9 to 8. I raised this last week arguing the market was starting to agree that revenue deferred in a capex cycle this size is not revenue lost, and it promptly fell instead — so I mark that read as not yet confirmed and take the weight back down rather than average into it. The underlying case survives: power distribution and liquid cooling are physical bottlenecks on the same side of the ledger as GEV, revenue is +26.2% with net income more than doubled, and 28 analysts hold a Strong Buy with a $338 target against $261.95. But 33.5x forward on a name that just missed and whose CEO called the problem temporary is a claim awaiting evidence, so it stays the smallest long. Stop stays -20%.

New, and the laggard short my mandate calls for but I have not been carrying. Every long in this book sells equipment into the AI buildout; CoreWeave is the customer buying it with borrowed money. It is planning $35-39B of 2026 capex against roughly $35B of existing debt while losing $1.93B, with no earnings to discount and a stock already 43% below its $153.20 high — so it is the leg that breaks first if the financing strain the market started pricing this month is real, and the week gave me two fresh datapoints in that direction with Nvidia trimming its OpenAI guarantee and Broadcom itself now borrowing tens of billions to move product. Sized at 6% because consensus is against me at a $144 target and this is a hedge, not a thesis I want to be large in. The Aug 26 NVDA print is deliberately embraced: a blowout hurts this leg while paying my six longs, a miss does the reverse, which is exactly the offset I want carrying a -14.6% drawdown. Stop at a 30% adverse move to survive a squeeze without being an accident; take profit at 35%.

decisions.reason: The book was built for exactly the tape that just arrived, so I am harvesting the two legs that paid rather than changing the thesis. Gold broke above $4,600 with the stated drivers being a weaker dollar, Treasury buybacks and debt-sustainability concerns; the 30-year cleared 5.1% and TLT hit a 22-year low; utilities broke to 52-week lows while the S&P rose. That is fiscal-credibility repricing, and it is the single cleanest confirmation this mandate has had. The specific trade I put on last week was that miners had not followed bullion — GDX flat at $89.97 while gold made new ground. That gap closed in one week: GDX is $102.83, up 14.3%, the discount to its high went from 23% to 12%, and the multiple re-rated from 13.6 to 16.2. The divergence I bought no longer exists, so I take 25 back to 21 — that is completing a trade, not doubting gold, and I still hold no take-profit on it because a monetary-credibility position should not be closed by a price target. Same logic on COPX, up 10.4% and now 5% from its high instead of 14%, trimmed a point. XLE goes 20 to 18 for a different reason: it printed a new 52-week high, and with retail sales at -0.6% and sentiment at 51.0 the demand risk I flagged is growing while the price is at the top of its range — that is the wrong direction for a leg to be at maximum size. The proceeds go where this week's move has not yet reached: EWZ up to 12 at 9.68x with a 3.87% yield, the same lag-the-complex setup GDX just resolved, with Vale and Nu levered to the identical weak-dollar commodity impulse; and EWJ up to 10 on exports accelerating 23.2% y/y for a fifth straight month plus yen upside if the dollar keeps sliding. UUP short goes 4 back to 5: last week I nearly wrote this leg off for failing a live test, and this week it passed one — the dollar actually broke, and it was named as the reason gold moved. I am adding a point, not restoring the full size, because the carry still costs roughly 6% annualized. EZU is untouched at 10 because nothing new happened to it. Net gross goes 93 to 91, so risk is essentially constant; this is rotation within a working thesis, not de-risking. Stops tightened on the three legs now sitting in real profit.

positions.thesis: Trimmed 25 to 21, still the anchor. I raised this to 25 last week on one specific observable — miners refused to follow bullion, leaving GDX flat at $89.97 while gold pressed higher. That trade paid in five sessions: $102.83, +14.3%, and the discount to the $117.18 high compressed from 23% to 12% while the multiple re-rated from 13.6 to 16.2. The reason for the extra three points is consumed, so I take them back. The core position stays large because the macro case strengthened rather than weakened: gold above $4,600 on a weaker dollar, Treasury buybacks and open debt-sustainability worries, with the 30-year at 5.1% confirming the fiscal channel and producers earning record margins at this metal price. Still no take-profit — a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target. Stop tightened -18 to -15 because the position now carries a large unrealized gain that deserves protecting, and 15% is still a full volatility band for a miner ETF.

Trimmed 20 to 18. This has been right and I am not fighting it — $63.64 is a new 52-week high, the range top moved to $64.70, refiner margins are at records and Middle East supply risk is live, all for a 2.38% yield at 20x. But two things say this is the wrong moment for it to hold its maximum weight: the price is at the very top of its range, and the consumer data underneath it is deteriorating, with retail sales -0.6% and sentiment at 51.0. Energy is the one leg in this book that is a demand cyclical as well as a hard asset, so it is the one where a new high should reduce size rather than justify it. It stays a strong second position.

Trimmed 16-equivalent to 15 after a 10.4% week to $94.59, including +5.18% on Friday alone. The industrial counterpart to GDX did exactly what it was bought to do: copper miners are levered simultaneously to the falling dollar, a long end repricing fiscal risk, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification. The reason for only a token trim rather than a real one is the distinction I keep returning to — copper demand from the AI buildout is realized in poured concrete and strung wire, not in financed equipment orders, so it is insulated from the financing strain that is currently taxing my Round 2 book. The discount to its $99.99 high has narrowed from 14% to 5%, which is why the stop tightens -22 to -18 rather than why I sell it.

Raised 10 to 12, funded by the two legs that just ran. This is the same setup GDX presented me a week ago and then resolved: the commodity complex moved violently while EWZ managed only +2.7% to $35.06, leaving the cheapest carry available to me at 9.68x with a 3.87% dividend yield and Vale plus Nu Holdings at roughly a fifth of the fund giving direct leverage to the weakening dollar the rest of this book is positioned for. Brazil's central bank is easing from 14% into moderating inflation, so it runs a domestic cycle ahead of the Fed's. It is 12 rather than 15 because the 25% US tariff and the floated sugar and ethanol penalties are a real and unresolved drag, and I want the discount to do the work rather than the weight.

Raised 9 to 10 on new information rather than housekeeping: Japanese exports accelerated 23.2% y/y for a fifth consecutive month, driven by semiconductor shipments — which gives me AI-cycle participation through a 19.5x index with a 3.74% yield instead of through the 40x US names that are currently being derated. The governance-reform and buyback cycle keeps compounding underneath that, and the leg's second job is currency: if the dollar keeps breaking the way it did this week, a firmer yen adds to dollar-based returns here. Near its $98.79 high at $95.18 and carrying part of the weak-dollar expression at a positive yield rather than the UUP short's negative carry.

Held at 10, untouched for a third week, because no new information arrived and none is required. Eurozone value near its 52-week high on broadening earnings growth at 17.6x with a 2.57% yield is a non-US, non-AI earnings stream with zero exposure to the hyperscaler capex financing argument that is currently costing my Round 2 book real money — which is precisely the diversification I want in the week that argument got worse. A leg making new highs on improving fundamentals does not need managing, and moving a weight without a reason is how good books get churned into mediocre ones.

Raised 4 to 5, a modest add on a leg that just passed the live test it failed a week ago. I cut this to a tail expression because soft retail sales, flat PPI and sentiment at 51.0 should have broken the dollar and did not. This week it did break — UUP fell to $27.90 out of the upper half of its range, and the weaker dollar was named directly as a driver of gold clearing $4,600 alongside Treasury buybacks and debt-sustainability concerns, with the 30-year at 5.1% supplying the fiscal channel the thesis always required. That is confirmation, so it earns a point back. It does not earn full restoration: the roughly 6% annualized cost of the 3.32% distribution plus 3% borrow is real, and I already own weak-dollar beta more cheaply through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ. Tight -8% stop kept.

decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol, no sector and no direction with my Round 2 AI-infrastructure book — Round 2 is long US semis, power equipment and networking against a short in a debt-financed neocloud, while Round 3 owns gold and copper miners, energy, Brazil, Japan and Europe against a short dollar — and the two are structurally opposed this week, since the same 5.1% long-end yield and fiscal-credibility repricing that is derating Round 2's long-duration capex equities is exactly what is paying Round 3's hard assets, giving same-direction gross-weight overlap of zero.

decisions.name: Opus Quality Defensive
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED before I began, so I priced everything directly off market data endpoints (Yahoo chart API, CoinGecko) rather than reading narrative. That is arguably a better discipline for a week like this one.

REGIME READ — this is a debasement/hard-asset week, not a growth week:
- Crypto: BTC $77,275 (peaked $78,318, now 1.4% off). Trajectory is textbook: 3 weeks pinned in $62.8k-$65.0k, then $64.7k -> $69.4k -> $73.1k -> $78.3k in four sessions, +20% off the base. ETH $2,427 (peaked $2,524), same shape: four weeks flat at $1,860-$1,915, then vertical, +29% on the week and ~4% off the peak. Both are long-base breakouts with a shallow pullback, not blow-offs from an extended trend.
- Gold: GLD $423.36, +12% in 21 sessions ($377.01). Critically, it is still 17% BELOW its 52-week high of $509.70. So this is a recovery trend out of a deep correction, not a chase into a top — which is precisely the setup I bought two weeks ago and it has now been confirmed by four straight higher weeks.
- Dollar: UUP $27.90 vs $28.39 a month ago, -1.7%, and it made a fresh leg down in the last two sessions.
- Rates, and this is the datapoint that changed my mind on one leg: the 10-year backed UP 19bp over the month, 4.545% -> 4.738%. The 13-week bill rose 6bp, 3.647% -> 3.710%. Long yields rising while the dollar falls and gold and crypto rip is a fiscal/debasement signature, not a disinflation signature. It also means long-duration bond-proxy defensives get no help.
- Equities: SPY 765.72, +2.5% on the month, near highs. Breadth fine but leadership is narrowing away from small caps: IWM printed 305.18 then faded to 299.96, -1.7% off its high.

POSITION-LEVEL CHECKS:
- XLV $174.62 vs $152.85 21 sessions ago, +14% on the month, 1.1% under its 52-week high of $176.60. My largest position is also the strongest large-cap sector on my board. Extraordinary, and it is why the book is up.
- SMH $594.07, up from $569.41 a month ago and up ~3.5% on the week (569-575 range -> 594). This is the second consecutive week the semis short has cost me.
- USMV $101.23 (+4.8% month, high $101.82); SCHD $35.11 (+2.4%, high $35.31); XLP $85.99 vs $85.36 a month ago (+0.7%, and 4.6% under its 52-week high of $90.14) — third straight assessment where staples do nothing.
- DBMF $31.37-31.54 near its $31.66 high; EFA $108.24 near its $108.89 high; JEPI $57.92 flat, +2% month; XLF $57.48, off the $58.41 high; PDBC $18.65, +3.9% month and near its $18.95 high (better than I gave it credit for last week); CPER $39.99, faded 2.4% from its $40.97 high but still above where it was a month ago.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: my Round 2 semis short has now failed the exact falsification test I wrote down for it, and my Round 3 crypto marker has now passed the exact confirmation test it failed a week ago. Both of those were pre-committed conditions, and both triggered. Acting on them is the discipline, not a change of mind.

decisions.reason: Two things forced my hand and I am changing nothing else. First, the semis short has failed the test I explicitly wrote down for it. Two weeks ago I halved it and said I would not call the view dead because SMH was 'still 4.6% below where it was a month ago and below its 50-day.' Both conditions have now flipped: SMH closed 594.07, up 4.3% on its month-ago level after running from the 569-575 shelf, and has reclaimed the 50-day. That is my own stated falsification condition triggering, so I close it. My valuation view is unchanged — 44x earnings and still 11.6% under the 671.83 six-month high — but I have been wrong on timing two weeks running, and paying 3% borrow to hold an opinion that keeps costing me is not discipline, it is stubbornness. I would rather re-enter on a failed rally than keep bleeding into a rate-cut bid. Second, the macro tape has resolved into a debasement signature: the dollar fell 1.7% on the month and made a fresh low, gold rose 12%, and the 10-year backed UP 19bp to 4.738% while the front end rose only 6bp. Rising long yields with a falling dollar is the one configuration that specifically punishes bond-proxy defensives and specifically rewards bullion. So gold goes from 8% to 11% — still 'small' as my mandate requires, and still a diversifier rather than a core — and staples, the leg that has now been flat for three consecutive assessments, funds part of it. The rest goes to SCHD, whose cash-flow-and-return-on-capital screen is the defensive expression that does not depend on falling long rates. XLV I deliberately do not add to despite it being the best thing I own: +14% in a month leaves it 1.1% from its 52-week high, and adding there is chasing.

positions.thesis: Unchanged in size and still the conviction position, but I want to be explicit that I am holding rather than adding, and why. It has done something remarkable: 174.62 against 152.85 twenty-one sessions ago, +14% in a month while SPY managed +2.5%. That is the single strongest large-cap sector trend on my board and it is the reason this book is up 4.45% with only a 1.34% drawdown. The case for owning it is untouched — 0.56 beta, earnings that do not depend on the payroll count, leadership broad across pharma and managed care rather than one drug. But it now sits 1.1% below its 52-week high of 176.60 after a vertical month, and adding size to something that has just gone up 14% is chasing, not conviction. A third of the book in my best idea is already an aggressive concentration for a defensive mandate. I hold.

Raised three points, and the reason is the rates picture rather than anything about the fund. SCHD screens on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage, which makes it a genuine quality-factor sleeve rather than a duration proxy — and duration is the thing that just got repriced, with the 10-year backing up 19bp to 4.738% while the dollar fell. In that configuration the defensive sleeves that suffer are the ones priced like long bonds (staples, utilities), and the ones that hold are the ones backed by near-term cash generation. It is quietly doing its job at 35.11, +2.4% on the month and within a whisker of its 35.31 high. I also prefer it to QUAL here precisely because it does not carry QUAL's roughly 30% technology weight, which matters more now that I no longer hold an offsetting semis short.

Held unchanged because it is doing exactly what min-vol ballast is supposed to do and there is nothing to fix. 101.23, +4.8% over 21 sessions and 0.6% off its 101.82 high — participating in the upside while being the lowest-volatility thing in the book. I continue to prefer it to SPLV, and this week strengthens that: SPLV's utilities concentration is a long-duration bond proxy, and long duration is the specific thing being sold as the 10-year backs up toward 4.75%. USMV's broader construction spares me that.

Raised from 8% to 11% — a real increase, but still 'small' as my mandate specifies, and I am deliberately not letting it become a core holding. Two weeks ago I bought this as a trend that was turning rather than one that was finished. That has now been confirmed rather than merely hoped for: 423.36 against 377.01 twenty-one sessions ago, +12% on the month, four consecutive higher weeks. The macro behind it got cleaner too — a 1.7% monthly fall in the dollar with a fresh leg down, alongside a 19bp RISE in the 10-year. Hard assets bid while the long end sells off is a debasement signature, and bullion is the purest defensive expression of it. What keeps this a good risk rather than a chase is that GLD is still 17% below its 52-week high of 509.70 after a deep correction, so I am adding into a recovery with room, not into a blow-off. I keep the stop at -9%, which from here sits below the recovery trend, and hold bullion rather than miners for the same reason as before: leverage to a squeeze is not the exposure I want in a defensive book.

Cut from 9% to 5% and demoted to a marker. This is now the third consecutive assessment at which staples have done nothing: 85.99 against 85.36 a month ago, +0.7%, while every other leg in this book compounded — XLV +14%, GLD +12%, USMV +4.8%. It also sits 4.6% under its 52-week high of 90.14, the only leg in the book not near its own highs. I have been patient with it on the argument that staples are the truest low-beta cash-flow ballast, and I still believe that in a genuine risk-off. But the specific regime that has arrived is the worst one for it: staples are nominally-priced, real-asset-poor and priced partly off long rates, and long rates just rose 19bp while the dollar fell. I keep 5% because the mandate names staples and I am not willing to have zero true defensive ballast, but it does not deserve a weight comparable to sleeves compounding ten times faster, and it is the correct funding source for gold.

decisions.reason: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.
decisions.novelty: The two books share no symbol at all and zero same-direction gross weight: Round 2 is a five-line domestic defensive equity book (healthcare, quality dividends, min-vol, staples) plus bullion, expressing capital preservation and hard-asset protection through low-beta cash-flow equities, while Round 3 is a nine-line cross-asset trend and carry book whose risk sits in spot crypto, managed futures, unhedged international, small-cap momentum, copper roll yield and call premium — and the two express the same debasement read in deliberately opposite instruments, with Round 2 owning bullion for its lack of volatility and Round 3 owning crypto precisely for its volatility.

positions.thesis: The structural core of the mandate, untouched for a third week, and it keeps earning the top slot. 31.37-31.54 against 30.94 a month ago and within 1% of its 31.66 high — a steady grind rather than a spike, which is what a well-behaved managed-futures sleeve should look like. Its value to me is that it re-positions itself across asset classes without my having to be early on every leg by hand, and its negative beta means it is the one line in this book that can be structurally short equities if the tape rolls over. That matters more this week, not less: I have just added 13% of volatile crypto beta, and DBMF is the offsetting exposure that makes carrying that risk reasonable.

Held at full weight, and the case got stronger rather than merely holding. 108.24 against 104.37 twenty-one sessions ago, sitting within 0.6% of its 108.89 high — a consolidation at a high, not distribution. The reason I am not trimming into that consolidation is the currency leg of the trade, which is now doing real work: UUP fell from 28.39 to 27.90 over the month and printed a fresh low in the last two sessions. Unhedged developed-international returns get that dollar move mechanically added on top of local equity returns, so this line is trend and currency carry in one instrument, which is exactly what the mandate asks for. It also never had the AI-capex air pocket the US momentum complex went through, so there is no unwind overhanging it.

Trimmed two points, and this is a judgement about the tape rather than a criticism of the fund. It is doing precisely what it is built to do — 57.92 against 56.79 a month ago, essentially flat over the last ten sessions while paying roughly 8% in distributions, so its price return badly understates what it earns. But the market is making new highs with SPY at 765.72, and in a trending-up tape a covered-call sleeve is capped by construction: I give away the upside and keep the premium. That is the right trade in a choppy market and the wrong one in a trending market, and right now the tape is trending. I keep 13% because harvested call premium is a genuine carry source the mandate names, and because if this melt-up does turn choppy this is the leg that starts outperforming immediately. I keep the 10% stop and no take-profit, since a capped-upside instrument has no upside target to take.

Held, and I will say plainly that I under-rated this leg two weeks ago. I cut it to a residual on the argument that a contracting labour market is demand-negative for oil and that one strong week did not repair a broken three-month trend. It has now put in a second strong week — 18.65 against 17.95 a month ago, +3.9%, and within 1.6% of its 18.95 six-month high — and the driver is no longer just a crude bounce. The dollar fell 1.7% on the month while the 10-year rose 19bp, and a broad commodity basket is a direct beneficiary of that specific combination in a way that a demand-driven oil call is not. I am not adding, because I do not want to reverse a considered decision on momentum alone and because the fund is still majority energy with genuine cyclical exposure. But the reasons to cut it further have gone away, and holding a broad commodity basket into a confirmed debasement regime is right.

Held unchanged. 57.48 against 56.31 a month ago, a little off its 58.41 high after four soft sessions, so the trend is intact but no longer leading. What keeps it at full weight is that the rate move this week is the good kind for banks rather than the bad kind: the 13-week bill rose only 6bp while the 10-year rose 19bp, which is a straightforward bear steepening, and a steeper curve is the textbook setup for wider net interest margin. Consumer credit deterioration remains the live risk and remains exactly why I own XLF rather than KRE — money-centre banks, insurers and exchanges are far better collateral than regional-bank loan books if card and auto delinquencies keep climbing. I keep the wider 12% stop because I expect this sector to be volatile around the rate repricing rather than because I want to be shaken out of it.

Raised from a 3% marker to a real 8% position, because the confirmation test I set last week has been met on its own terms. I kept 3% rather than zero specifically because I was 'not willing to call it a confirmed downtrend either,' and I said the deciding evidence would be participation in broad risk-on. It has now participated violently: four weeks pinned between $1,860 and $1,915, then a break to $2,524, closing $2,427 for +29% on the week. A long flat base followed by a decisive break and a shallow 4% pullback is the highest-quality entry pattern a trend follower gets, and it is the opposite of the squeezed, already-extended conditions I refused to buy in gold miners. I hold spot rather than a perp deliberately: the funding objection has flipped now that the primary trend is up, but 10x-plus leverage into something that just moved 29% in four sessions means an ordinary retrace liquidates the leg, and I would rather own the trend than gamble on its path. Stop stays at 18%, which from here sits around $1,990 — above the four-week base, so it triggers if and only if the breakout has genuinely failed. I cut the take-profit from 55% to 40% because roughly $3,400 is a realistic extension from this higher entry, whereas the old target was set from a much lower base and would have me holding for a level the move no longer needs to reach.

Cut from 10% to 6%, and unlike the rest of this book that is a response to a trend that actually broke rather than one that merely paused. Last week it printed a 52-week high; it has since faded from 305.18 to 299.96, down 1.7% and the only leg on my board that is meaningfully off its high on falling prices rather than consolidating. The rate move makes the reason clear. This leg was powered by the market pricing aggressive cuts, and this week the front end went the other way — the 13-week bill rose 6bp — while the 10-year rose 19bp. Small caps are the most rate-sensitive and most consumer-credit-sensitive thing I own at beta 1.12, and higher long rates plus elevated card and auto delinquencies hit small-cap balance sheets and small-cap earnings first and hardest. I keep 6% because the mandate requires equity momentum exposure and the six-month trend is still well intact, but I stop paying full size for the weakest trend in the book, and it is the natural funder for the strongest. Stop stays tight at 8%.

New, and added alongside ETH rather than instead of it because BTC is the leg actually leading this move. The pattern is the cleanest on my entire board: three weeks compressed between $62,802 and $65,033, then $64,664, $69,418, $73,098, $78,318 in four consecutive sessions, closing $77,227 — a 20% break out of a tight base with a pullback of only 1.4%. I want the leader as well as the higher-beta follower, because if this is a real crypto trend BTC will carry it with materially less drawdown than ETH, and if it is a false break BTC is where I lose least. Sizing it below ETH at 5% reflects that ETH already gives me the convex expression and I do not need to double it. Spot rather than a perp, for the same reason as ETH: I am not putting leverage on an asset mid-parabola where the 5%-of-margin liquidation rule turns an ordinary shakeout into a total loss on the leg. The 15% stop lands near $65,600, just above the pre-breakout base — a retrace to the base means the breakout failed and I want out rather than hoping.

Trimmed one point as a small risk adjustment, not a change of view. The carry logic that made this the cleanest setup on my board is unchanged: copper calendar spreads at their widest since 2021 means the curve is backwardated and the fund earns positive roll yield simply by holding, which is literally the commodity carry the mandate names rather than a directional bet dressed as carry. But the price has stopped making progress — 39.99 after touching 40.97, so it has given back 2.4% from its high and is only 2.4% above where it was a month ago, which is a flattening trend rather than the record-chasing one I bought. The structural demand story around datacentre power, grid buildout and supply constraints is intact and is why this stays in the book at all, so I take one point rather than acting decisively. Stop and take-profit unchanged.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet deep value
decisions.research_notes:
CRYPTO CHECK FIRST (per the market note): I hold no crypto, no perps, no crypto-adjacent equity. The BTC $63k->$78k run and the six standing orders that fired across the field touched nothing in my book. My own stops/TPs are all still listed in the packet, so none of mine fired either. Verified rather than assumed.

MARKS THROUGH 2026-08-21 CLOSE vs my 2026-08-17 book entry:
- PFE $26.79 -> $28.07 (+4.8%). Fwd PE 10.13, yield 6.13%, 28 analysts Buy, consensus $28.61 (only +1.9%).
- CVX $200.00 -> $205.27 (+2.6%). Fwd 13.26x, yield 3.47%, consensus $217.88 (+6.1%), 25 analysts Buy.
- C $139.33 -> $131.65 (-5.5%). Worst leg. Fwd 11.28x, PEG 0.46, consensus $154.50 (+17.4%), Buy, +41.3% over 52 weeks, 200dma $121.53.
- VZ $48.48 -> $49.45 (+2.0%). Fwd 9.75x, yield 5.72%, consensus $51.56 (+4.3%).
- VLO $341.67 -> $348.86 (+2.1%). 52wk high $352.70, so 1.1% off the high. Fwd 8.41x. Consensus $312.53 - now 10.4% BELOW spot.
- MO $65.70 -> $66.09 (+0.6%). Fwd 11.46x, yield 6.42%, consensus $70.00 (+5.9%), rating Hold, FY26 EPS guide narrowed to $5.61-5.72.
- SMH short: $587.82 last week -> $560.42 (-4.7% this week, +1.6% in my favour vs the $569.41 entry). Still 44.89x, NVDA 21.70%, top-10 71.46%, beta 1.74, +94.6% twelve-month total return.

MACRO I CHECKED:
1) OIL IS THE DOMINANT LIVE VARIABLE AND IT ESCALATED AGAIN. Brent $94.39, WTI $87.06, Murban $103.50 (+2.4% on the day). Brent is up from $88.52 last week - a second straight weekly gain, explicitly attributed to mounting Iran risk and Hormuz shipping disruption. Venezuelan export delays and Iraq pushing to double output against OPEC add to the dislocation; Japan's imports hit an all-time high on energy cost; USO +83% over twelve months. Crucially this is now two consecutive weeks of confirming price action plus the IEA five-year-widest deficit forecast, not a single headline - which is the distinction that matters given I was whipsawed sizing off one de-escalation headline two weeks ago.
2) LONG END STILL BROKEN. TLT $82.05 against a 52-week range of $81.17-$92.19, effectively on the low; coverage cites the lowest price in 22 years and notes bonds unwound all the Bessent buyback-plan gains. Duration remains a headwind for bond proxies and a tailwind for the curve-steepener bank case.
3) SEMIS: the de-rating mechanism I named finally showed up in the tape - SMH -4.7% on the week while the long end stayed at its lows. Sell-side is genuinely split (JPMorgan flagging a summer buying opportunity, Morgan Stanley cautious), with sustainability of AI capex the live question.
4) TELECOM: SpaceX Starlink Mobile expanding into wireless is now explicitly named as pressuring telecom shares. My stated terminal-value risk on VZ has gone from a thesis-level worry to a live news item.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: I was underweight the confirmed winner of the dominant macro variable (CVX) while carrying two positions whose theses decayed on their own terms - MO, which I already conceded is not a discount trade, and VZ, whose discount narrowed to 4.3% just as its bear case turned concrete. That is the wrong configuration, so I rotate within the same 80% gross rather than add leverage or spend cash. Method note: my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of the session, so all of the above was gathered by direct WebFetch of quote/statistics pages and commodity coverage.

decisions.reason: The single macro variable driving this book escalated for a second consecutive week and I am underweight it, while two legs decayed on their own stated terms - so I rotate weight toward the confirmed driver instead of leaving the book configured for last week's world. Brent went $88.52 -> $94.39 on mounting Iran risk and Hormuz disruption; I sized CVX at 16% explicitly on Brent being $88-90, so 16% is now stale by my own arithmetic and it goes to 22%. That add is funded by exiting MO entirely and trimming VZ, not by spending cash: gross stays 80%, cash 20%, so this is a rotation, not a risk increase. I exit MO because last week I wrote in plain words that it survives 'purely as ballast and carry' and is 'not a discount trade and I will not pretend it is one' - a Hold-rated name with 5.9% to target, flat revenue, narrowed guidance and an inverted duration argument (TLT at 22-year lows) does not belong in a concentrated deep-value book, and holding it now would be sentiment rather than analysis. I trim VZ 13% -> 11% because the discount is nearly closed at 4.3% to target while the exact risk I named as the reason to keep it small - SpaceX direct-to-cell - became a live tape-moving story with Starlink Mobile's wireless push; when my named bear case converts from hypothetical to live, weight comes down, and applying that rule only to losers would be self-serving. I raise the SMH short 5% -> 7% because last week I refused to add for one specific stated reason: the market had been handed my de-rating mechanism and rejected it. This week it accepted it - SMH fell 4.7% with the long end still at its lows - so the condition I set for adding was met, and a larger hedge is warranted anyway now that oil beta is bigger. I HOLD PFE at 20% rather than applying my past-target harvest rule, because that rule triggers on trading ABOVE consensus (VLO, 10.4% above) and PFE is 1.9% BELOW it, on targets that visibly have not caught up to the raised guidance; at 10.1x forward against a ~19x sector it remains an absolute-multiple holding, not a closed target gap, and it is the only leg with no crude beta and no AI duration, which is what keeps this from becoming a one-factor energy book. I HOLD C at 14% despite it being the only loser: the credit risk I named got genuinely worse ($94 Brent onto negative payrolls, and the tape marked it down 5.5%), but the curve-steepener tailwind I named got genuinely stronger and the discount widened to 11.3x with 17.4% to target on the cheapest large-cap US bank - those offset honestly, so I neither add nor dress up a cosmetic 1% trim as a decision. I HOLD VLO at 6% and refuse to chase it 1% off its 52-week high and 10.4% above consensus even though cracks are blowing out further, because that is exactly the mean-reverting cash flow I said it was; the honest way to buy more of this shock is CVX. I tighten CVX's stop from -18% to -15% because a 22% weight riding a geopolitical driver that one de-escalation headline can reverse is precisely the exposure that cost me the CVX round-trip, and it deserves a pre-committed exit rather than an improvised one. Turnover is roughly 15% of notional at ~2bps a side, about 0.3bp of NAV - immaterial against the repositioning.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so no overlap constraint binds; what is distinct about this Round-3 book is that it now expresses the Hormuz supply shock through the integrated producer with beta 0.49 and a covered 3.5% dividend rather than through the refiner whose crack-spread windfall already sits 10% past consensus, and pairs that with a materially larger short in the 44.9x semiconductor cohort whose discount-rate de-rating the tape has just confirmed for the first time.

positions.thesis: Raised 16% -> 22% and now the top weight, because the one number I sized this on has moved decisively in my favour for a second straight week. I wrote that 16% was justified by Brent at $88-90. Brent is $94.39, with WTI $87.06 and Murban $103.50, on mounting Iran risk and continuing Hormuz shipping disruption, against an IEA forecast of the widest global supply deficit in five years, Venezuelan export delays, and a US posture that has not softened. The distinction from the round-trip that cost me money is that I cut on a single de-escalation headline; I am adding on two consecutive weeks of confirming price action plus a supply-balance forecast, which is evidence rather than a news item. The company leg was never the question: record quarterly net income of $20.59bn up 50% year over year, production up on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement that monetises the AI buildout without paying an AI multiple for it. At $205.27 it is 13.26x forward with a 3.47% yield, beta 0.49, and a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts at Buy implying 6.1% more. This is the cheapest, lowest-beta, dividend-paying way to own the crude dislocation and it is the book's inflation hedge. I tighten the stop from -18% to -15% deliberately: a 22% weight sitting on a driver a single Hormuz de-escalation could reverse does not deserve the same wide stop it had at 16%, and the whole lesson of last month is that the exit should be pre-committed rather than improvised under a headline.

Held at 20% and deliberately NOT harvested, because my past-target rule does not apply here and I will not misapply my own discipline just to look consistent. That rule triggers when a name trades ABOVE consensus - VLO is 10.4% above, which is why it was cut. PFE at $28.07 is 1.9% BELOW its $28.61 consensus, and that consensus visibly has not been refreshed for the raised FY26 revenue guidance, the $2.5bn of incremental productivity savings through 2029, the EMA validation of the Lyme vaccine candidate, or the CEO's $1m open-market purchase after the print - the datapoint I weight most heavily anywhere. The real case is absolute, not relative-to-target: 10.13x forward against a roughly 19x industry, a 6.13% yield, 28 analysts at Buy, and it is up 4.8% since my fill. It earns the top-tier weight for a structural reason that has only become more valuable as I add oil: it is the sole holding with no AI-capex duration, no crude beta and no economic cyclicality, so it is what stops this being a one-factor energy book. The honest negative is unchanged - a 6% yield is a weaker relative proposition with the long bond at 22-year lows. That argument retired MO this week and it does not retire PFE, because PFE is a valuation-and-pipeline holding that happens to yield 6%, not a bond proxy, and the tape agrees: PFE rose while the actual bond proxies did not. Stop stays wide at -18% so a multi-year valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by one bad session.

Held flat at 14% - the book's only loser at -5.5%, and I am neither adding to it nor quietly shaving it, because the two forces genuinely offset and pretending otherwise would be theatre. Against me: the exact risk I named as the reason not to restore full weight has intensified. A $94 Brent shock landing on a labour market that printed negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward consumer-credit signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered, and the tape marked it down 5.5% in a week when the rest of my book rose - that is the market pricing exactly that. For me: the mechanism I said was the larger NIM driver is not just intact but stronger, with TLT at $82.05 against an $81.17-$92.19 range and coverage citing 22-year lows, which is real curve steepening. And the discount widened as the price fell: 11.28x forward, PEG 0.46, a $154.50 consensus from 21 analysts at Buy implying 17.4% upside, still the cheapest large-cap US bank, on 2025 revenue of $75.7bn up 6.7% with earnings up 13.6%, and management using the balance sheet offensively via Kard Financial, a $4.6bn Japan-US facility, senior hiring from BofA and Morgan Stanley, and a seat on the Anthropic IPO. There is also a book-level reason to keep it: higher crude helps CVX and VLO and hurts a consumer lender, so this leg is a partial internal hedge on the very shock I just increased. My own correction stays on the record - at roughly 1.34x tangible book there is no buyback-accretion kicker, just an ordinary cheap bank. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate keeps the group volatile in both directions and a value thesis needs room.

Trimmed 13% -> 11%, continuing last week's measured retreat rather than reversing it, because both reasons to hold it weakened one more notch. The valuation reason is nearly used up: at $49.45 the $51.56 consensus from 26 analysts leaves only 4.3% of upside, and a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4% gap. The risk reason got worse in exactly the way I flagged: I wrote that the one thing keeping this from being larger was that SpaceX direct-to-cell is a genuine long-run terminal-value question on the network moat. This week that stopped being hypothetical and became a tape-moving story, with Starlink Mobile's push into wireless named as pressure on telecom shares. When my named bear case goes live, weight comes down. What keeps a real 11% rather than an exit is that the operating leg keeps beating and the stock keeps rising while its rate proxy makes new lows, which says the market is paying for the company and not the coupon: 184,000 postpaid adds, raised full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance, a $4.5bn buyback target, the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent instead of costing it multiple, and now NetSense with Lockheed and NVIDIA. At 9.75x forward with a 5.72% yield covered by free cash flow and beta 0.24 it remains genuinely cheap low-beta carry. Stop unchanged at -15%.

Raised 5% -> 7%, and the reason is precisely the test I set for myself last week and wrote down. I refused to add then for one stated reason: the market had been handed my de-rating mechanism - a long end backing up to multi-year lows - and rejected it, with SMH rallying 3.2% against me; adding to a losing short on a thesis the tape had just refused is how a hedge becomes a bet. This week the tape accepted it. SMH fell from $587.82 to $560.42, -4.7%, while TLT sat at $82.05 near a 52-week low of $81.17 amid commentary citing 22-year lows - the discount-rate mechanism finally transmitted to the longest-duration equity cohort, and the leg is now 1.6% in my favour against the $569.41 entry. The valuation case never moved and is honestly the most stretched cohort available, which is what the mandate asks for: 44.89x with NVIDIA at 21.70% of the fund, the top ten at 71.46%, beta 1.74, after a 94.6% twelve-month total return. The narrative has also turned two-sided, with sustainability of the AI capex boom openly questioned and the sell-side split between JPMorgan calling a summer buying opportunity and Morgan Stanley warning on the sector. There is a second, portfolio-level reason: I just took oil exposure to 28% of NAV, and insurance against a broad multiple de-rating should scale with the beta it insures. It stays sized for survival rather than for a view - 7% with a -22% stop risks about 1.5% of the book, and 3% borrow on 7% is roughly 21bp a year, negligible carry. The +30% take-profit is unchanged; this is insurance, and I will bank it if a real de-rating arrives rather than let it round-trip.

Held at exactly 6% and explicitly not chased, even though the driver behind it is intensifying - this is the discipline test of the week and I am passing it deliberately. Everything about the crack-spread story got better: Brent $94.39 on a second straight weekly gain, Hormuz disruption persisting, the Jazan strike still removing regional refining capacity, and VLO closed at $348.86, up 2.1% since my fill and just 1.1% below its $352.70 52-week high. That is exactly the setup that tempts a manager to re-add what he trimmed. I do not, for two reasons already in writing. First, my rule: once a name trades past consensus the specific dislocation is harvested, and at $348.86 against a $312.53 average target from 20 analysts it is now 10.4% ABOVE fair value - I bought it when consensus saw upside and consensus now sees 10% of downside. Second, and more important, I called refining margin the most mean-reverting cash flow in this book, and mean-reverting cash flow is precisely what you do not capitalise at a peak. If I want more of the crude dislocation - and I do - the honest expression is CVX at 13.3x with a covered dividend and 6% of upside to target, which is where the add went. What justifies keeping a real 6% is that the multiple itself is still cheap at 8.41x forward on $3.7bn of quarterly net income with renewable diesel swinging positive; it is the discount to fair value that closed, not the business. Stop stays tight at -12% and the +20% take-profit stays on, because a large geopolitical gain that one de-escalation headline could erase needs a pre-committed exit, and a wide stop on an extended winner protects nothing.
