decisions.research_notes:
WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before I could run any query, so all research below is from direct market-data fetches I ran myself rather than news reading. I flag that explicitly because it changed one decision (see managed care).

VERIFIED PRICES, 2026-08-21 close, vs my 2026-08-17 entry marks (not vs 08-14, which double-counts a gap I already took):
Round 2 — UNH 395.62->390.11 (-1.4%); CVS 94.01->93.02 (-1.1%); CRM 190.97->209.17 (+9.5%); NOW 117.70->128.48 (+9.2%); GLD 405.49->423.36 (+4.4%); XLV 167.05->174.62 (+4.5%); ETH 1912.20->2426.10 (+26.9%).
Round 3 — XLE 62.58->63.64 (+1.7%); GDX 91.89->102.83 (+11.9%); SPMO 155.16->148.73 (-4.1%); SCHD 34.29->35.11 (+2.4%); QUAL 224.63->223.22 (-0.6%); GOOGL 344.00->344.82 (+0.2%); JEPQ 60.56->59.84 (-1.2%); AMZN 261.31->258.63 (-1.0%).
Macro — WTI 82.40->87.06 (+5.7%); TLT 82.05 (52wL 81.17, 52wH 92.19); SPY 776.34->765.72 (-1.4%); BTC 64,506->77,219 (+19.7%), IBIT 36.42->43.68 (+19.9%); ETH 52wH 4,953.73, so ETH is now 51% below its ATH vs 62% when I sized it.

WHAT I LEARNED, in order of how much it changed my mind:

1) The week was a hard-asset regime impulse, not a broad rally. Gold miners +11.9%, crude +5.7%, BTC +19.7%, ETH +26.9% — while SPY fell 1.4%, the momentum factor (SPMO) fell 4.1% and broke its 151-155 consolidation to a lower low, and TLT sat within 1% of a 52-week low all week. Leadership rotated out of the semiconductor/megacap complex into real assets. Both books have to answer that, in opposite ways: Round 2 harvests the reversion it was paid for, Round 3 follows the new leadership.

2) The managed-care problem is a GROUP problem, not a UNH mispricing. I pulled the whole complex: UNH -2.9%, CVS -4.3%, CI -1.8%, HUM -2.6% on the week, while XLV made a fresh 52-week high (174.62 vs 176.60). I then checked what is actually driving XLV: MRK +17.2% over 4 weeks and 1.3% off its high, with LLY, PFE and BMY all within 3% of theirs. So XLV's strength is pharma, and managed care is the group being left behind — CI is 12.0% off its high and flat over 13 weeks, HUM 11.7% off its high. UNH itself has now closed lower six consecutive weeks: 429.09, 421.55, 417.64, 415.36, 408.74, 395.62, 390.11. My stated thesis was that UNH was being overlooked by a sector re-rating and would catch up. Four issuers moving down together for three straight weeks is the market pricing a sector-level cost-trend or policy view, not overlooking one company. Without news access I cannot identify what that view is — and carrying 25% of the book on a thesis whose only confirming evidence is a price gap that keeps widening, while I cannot read the other side, is anchoring rather than contrarianism.

3) Screened for the next dislocation. Ran a 17-name quality screen on drawdown depth plus 4-week and 13-week change. NKE is 49.2% off its high but still making lower lows (-11.8% over 13 weeks) — a falling knife with no turn, skipped. ORCL is the standout: 57.6% off its high, bottomed at 114.99 on 2026-07-20, now 146.47 having built a four-week base (147.02, 150.52, 146.47, 146.47) — a 27% recovery off the low that then went flat rather than rolling over. Same setup and same sleeve as the ADBE trade I closed at target last week.

4) Verified my standing orders. Nothing fired in either book. ETH's -25% stop was never approached — it went the other way. GDX's -15% stop off 91.89 sat near 78 while price ran to 102.83, meaning the stop was protecting nothing and needed trailing up.

5) Checked the field-wide crypto event named in the desk note against my own book. Six orders fired across the field; none were mine, because I had already exited BTC last week and my remaining crypto leg was ETH with a stop far below. ETH's +26.9% is the mean-reversion payoff Round 2 exists to capture; BTC's breakout from a long base is a trend initiation Round 3 exists to capture. Same event, two different jobs.

decisions.reason: Three legs delivered the reversion I bought them for in five sessions and one leg was contradicted, so the book harvests and reallocates rather than holding green positions out of inertia — the same standard I applied to Bitcoin and Adobe last week. ETH ran +26.9% and CRM +9.5%, which is the payout, not the setup: a mean-reversion mandate that does not take reversion when it arrives is just a long book with a story. Against that, managed care is where I was wrong about the mechanism. I argued UNH was being left behind by a sector re-rating; the sector index then made a fresh 52-week high while UNH, CVS, CI and HUM all fell together, and UNH has now closed lower six weeks running. Four issuers declining in lockstep is the market pricing a group-level view, not overlooking one name — and with my research budget exhausted I cannot read what that view is. Cutting from 25% to 13% is what prudent sizing means when the only evidence for my largest thesis is a gap that keeps widening. The proceeds go into a deeper, fresher dislocation (ORCL, 57.6% off its high and basing) and into the one asset my book has no defense against, since gold, crypto and value equity all lose together in a genuine deflationary shock.

positions.thesis: Held at 18% and now the largest position in the book. Every element of the impulse I bought this for strengthened: WTI went 82.40 to 87.06, TLT closed 82.05 within 1% of its 81.17 52-week low, and the miners confirmed violently with GDX +11.9% in five sessions. GLD itself added 4.4% to 423.36. I do not add, and the reason is the mandate: at 423.36 it is 16.9% below its 509.70 high rather than the 21% discount I was buying into, so each further point of size buys a smaller contrarian edge and a larger momentum bet. Holding a working hedge at unchanged weight is the correct expression here; chasing it is Round 3's job, not this book's.

Cut 18->13 with a stop attached for the first time. I am reducing the mechanism of the thesis, not abandoning the valuation. The fundamental record is unchanged and genuinely strong — Q2 adjusted EPS beat by 30%, targets raised by JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Goldman, 18.9x forward, dividend just raised, 27 analysts averaging 475.23 against 390.11 — which is why I keep a double-digit weight in a mean-reversion book. But my stated reason for 18% was that this was an idiosyncratic gap versus a re-rating sector, and that specific claim failed a test I can verify: CVS, CI and HUM fell with it this week while XLV printed a fresh 52-week high driven by pharma. Six consecutive lower weekly closes from 429.09 to 390.11 against a rising tape is a downtrend, and 18% was sized for a mispricing, not for a downtrend I cannot explain. 13% is the weight I can defend on valuation alone.

Held at 9% — the one winner I am deliberately not trimming, and the distinction matters. It gained 9.2% to 128.48, but it is still 34.0% below its 194.73 high against the 36% discount I bought at, so the move barely dented the gap that justified the position. That is the opposite of ETH and CRM, where the run consumed most of the thesis. The offsetting risk is unchanged and is why I do not add either: at a 27.4x forward multiple this is the most rate-sensitive duration I own, and with TLT still pinned near its 52-week low the discount rate keeps moving against it even as 22.2% revenue growth and $1bn+ AI ACV say the business does not.

New 9%, funded by the CVS exit, and the direct replacement for the Adobe trade I closed at target last week — the most extreme valuation dislocation available in large-cap enterprise software. It fell 67% peak-to-trough, bottoming at 114.99 on 2026-07-20, and trades 146.47, some 57.6% below its 52-week high. What makes this a setup rather than a knife is the shape of the last four weeks: 147.02, 150.52, 146.47, 146.47 — it recovered 27% off the low and then stopped moving instead of rolling over, which is the basing behaviour I look for and precisely what NKE (49% off its high but still making lower lows, -11.8% over 13 weeks) does not show. I size it at 9% rather than higher because the reason it crashed is real and unresolved: the balance sheet was levered hard for the AI datacentre buildout, so this is a capital-structure dislocation and not merely a sentiment one, and I could not read this week's coverage to check whether that financing risk has improved.

Held at 8%, and this week justified why it exists. It gained 4.5% to 174.62, within 1.1% of its 52-week high, while every managed-care name I own fell — which is the diversification job I bought it for working exactly as specified, and it is also how I diagnosed the problem, since the divergence between this fund and my single names is what told me the issue was the group and not the company. Its composition is now the point: MRK sits 1.3% off its high after +17.2% in four weeks, with LLY, PFE and BMY all within 3% of theirs, so this is my exposure to the half of healthcare that is working while UNH is the half that is not. It stays a stub rather than growing because owning a fund at a 52-week high is not what a contrarian book is for.

Cut 13->8 ahead of the 2026-08-26 print, four days out. Last week I refused to add into this event on the grounds that increasing size into a binary outcome converts a valuation thesis into an earnings bet. The symmetric application of that rule is that when the market pre-pays a third of the thesis before the event, I reduce the event exposure: it ran 9.5% from 190.97 to 209.17 and the gap to the 242.29 consensus has compressed from 23.5% to 15.8%. I keep 8% rather than exiting because the residual gap is still real against net income +29.3% on revenue +11.0%, and because I have no edge on which way the Agentforce adoption debate resolves in one quarter — which is an argument for carrying less into it, not none.

New 7%, and the most genuinely contrarian thing in the book. At 82.05 against a 92.19 high and an 81.17 low, long Treasuries are the most consensually hated asset I can find, and the tell is that I have personally quoted the bearish narrative — bond vigilantes, $40T of federal debt, fresh 52-week lows — in three consecutive weekly writeups as settled background fact justifying other positions. When I notice myself treating a consensus as furniture, that is precisely when this mandate says to check the other side. The structural reason to own it is that my book has no defense against one specific outcome: gold, crypto, value equity and cyclical healthcare all lose together in a genuine deflationary or risk-off shock, and this is the only asset that pays in it. I size it at 7% and accept that it is falling, because the warning from my backtests was that shorting momentum kills portfolios — a long in an oversold asset with a bounded floor is the opposite risk shape.

Harvested 9->4 with the stop tightened from -25% to -18%. This is the mandate paying out and being collected, not a change of view. I bought it as deeply oversold crypto at 1,912 when it was 62% below its all-time high; at 2,426 it is 51% below, so a quarter of the discount that justified the size disappeared in five sessions on the BTC breakout from roughly 63k to 78k. I am consistent with the Bitcoin exit I made last week for exactly this reason — a mean-reversion book that holds through the reversion is only pretending to have a rule. The 4% residual stays because 51% below an all-time high is still a real discount and the ETF-inflow story that made me prefer ETH over BTC is intact. The stop tightens because the asymmetry shrank with the discount: less room below means less licence above, and at 35bps a side I would rather be stopped out than round-trip this.

decisions.reason: Leadership rotated this week and a trend book that does not rotate with it is not trend-following, it is a static portfolio with stops attached. The evidence is unambiguous and it is all price: gold miners +11.9%, crude +5.7%, bitcoin +19.7% — against SPY -1.4%, the momentum factor -4.1%, and every megacap sleeve I own flat to lower. So I take size in what is demonstrably leading and cut what has stopped leading. The hard call is SPMO, the literal instrument of this mandate. I wrote last week that consolidation after a vertical move is the condition to hold rather than add; it then broke that 151-155 consolidation to a lower low at 148.31, which is the condition I named for reducing. I cut it to a 5% residual on a short leash rather than to zero, because a one-week break is not proof and the fund reconstitutes quarterly. AMZN goes entirely: I already cut it once on a stated invalidation when the post-earnings gap filled, and it confirmed that invalidation for a second week, so finishing the exit is what naming a condition is for. The GDX stop moves up under the new price, because a stop that a 12% rally has left 22% away is decoration, not risk control.
decisions.novelty: The two books now own the same macro impulse through deliberately opposite actions and zero shared symbols: Round 2 is harvesting into the hard-asset rally — cutting ETH 9->4 and holding gold flat at 18%, because a contrarian book sells reversion — while Round 3 is initiating and adding into it, taking GDX to 16% and opening IBIT on the breakout, because a trend book buys confirmation. Symbol overlap between the two books is 0%, and the only crypto exposures move in opposite directions (ETH-USD reduced in Round 2 against BTC via IBIT initiated in Round 3), so the shared theme is expressed through different instruments and opposite weight changes rather than doubled risk.

positions.thesis: Raised 12->16 with the stop trailed up hard. This is the strongest verified relative strength anywhere in my universe and it just broke out: +11.9% from 91.89 to 102.83 in five sessions on top of a 56% twelve-month return, clearing the multi-week 88-92 range decisively. What makes this trend-following rather than top-ticking is the distance left in it — at 102.83 it is still 12.2% below its 117.18 52-week high, so this is a resumed trend reclaiming old ground, not a move into unexplored air. The add is four points rather than eight because miners run roughly three times bullion's volatility and I am carrying energy at 15% through the same geopolitical channel. The stop tightens from -15% to -13% precisely because the old one had become meaningless: set off 91.89 it sat near 78 while price ran to 102.83, a 22% gap that protected nothing. I attach no take-profit, because capping the winner is how a trend book gives back the one trade that pays for all the others.

Raised 14->15. I said seven days ago that the commodity leads the equity and that I would follow the driver in both directions; the driver kept going, with WTI up another 5.7% from 82.40 to 87.06 against stalled Hormuz negotiations, US port blockades and the IEA's forecast of the worst supply shortage in five years. The equity confirmed rather than diverged, closing 63.64 within 1.6% of its 64.70 52-week high on a 49% one-year return. The add is a single point deliberately: I already took this from 8% to 14% last week on this same reasoning and it worked immediately, so what I am doing now is registering confirmation, not placing a fresh bet near a high. The structural reason it stays large is that this is the only sleeve that pays if the inflation re-acceleration keeping TLT at a 52-week low continues.

Raised 12->13. Last week I reclassified this from ballast to a trend I already own, and this week settled the argument: it gained 2.4% to 35.11, effectively a fresh all-time high against its 35.31 ceiling, in a week when SPY fell 1.4% and the dedicated momentum sleeve fell 4.1%. Beating the market by nearly four points during a rotation is demonstrated relative strength by the only definition this mandate uses, so a one-point add is the honest response. It also does structural work I need more of than last week: a 0.69 beta and a 3.04% yield are load-bearing when 37% of the book sits in energy, miners and bitcoin, and its Abbott, Amgen and Merck weights put me in the pharma complex that is actually driving healthcare's strength.

Held at 12% with a stop added. It slipped 0.6% to 223.22 and remains within 1.8% of its 52-week high, which in a week that broke the momentum factor by 4.1% is relative strength by omission — quality held where momentum did not, and that divergence is the whole reason I run them as separate sleeves. With SPMO cut to a stub and AMZN gone, this is now my principal broad equity exposure, which is exactly the reason for the change I am making: it previously carried no stop, and an unstopped position is not consistent with a mandate whose stated method is hard stops. The regime argument is intact and strengthening — TLT at 82.05 near its low means a permanently higher cost of capital, and high-return-on-equity businesses carrying little leverage are the part of the market least damaged by it, because they never need to visit that market.

Cut 11->8. In a trend book, flat is not a trend: it went 344.00 to 344.82 over five sessions while the sleeves I am adding to moved double digits, and at 344.82 it sits 15.6% below its 408.61 52-week high, which fails every relative-strength test I apply. Holding an 11% weight in the name with the weakest trend reading in the book while gold miners break out is a misallocation regardless of what I think of the company. I keep 8% rather than exiting because the quality half of the case is genuinely strong and unresolved — Berkshire raised its stake 83% in Q2 to $37.9bn and a third-largest position, delivered after the Hassabis and Dean departures that made me trim in the first place, on a 17.4x multiple against a 428.04 consensus target — and cutting a megacap to zero on a flat week is how a trend book gets whipsawed. Stop and take-profit unchanged because the risk shape did not change, only the weight.

Trimmed 10->8 with a stop added. The reason is consistency, not disappointment: its NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Micron weights make this megacap-complex exposure with a capped upside, and I am reducing that complex everywhere else this week — SPMO to a stub, AMZN out, GOOGL down — so leaving this untouched would quietly reinstate the exposure I just decided is no longer leading. It fell 1.2% to 59.84, in line with that complex. I keep 8% because the 10.78% distribution yield, most recently $0.705 paid on 2026-08-03, is genuinely counter-cyclical income that improves as dispersion between my directional sleeves rises — and I am raising dispersion sharply by taking hard assets to 37% of the book.

New 7%, and it is here because of what my own screen turned up rather than because I went looking for pharma. Checking why the healthcare sector fund kept making highs while my managed-care names fell, I found this is the engine: 152.55, just 1.3% below its 52-week high, +17.2% over four weeks, +28.5% over thirteen and +96.6% off its low. That is a verified, sustained relative-strength leader with real quality characteristics, and the cleanest single-name expression of a trend I could otherwise only own diluted. It earns its place mainly for what it is not correlated with: after this rebalance 37% of the book sits in gold miners, energy and bitcoin, all trading off the same debasement channel, and a defensive large-cap making new highs is the only leader available that does not share that driver. Sized at 7% as an initiation with a stop rather than a core weight, because I could not read this week's coverage to know what is powering the four-week move.

New 6%. This was the single strongest trend in the market this week, and a mandate built on owning demonstrated relative-strength leaders cannot decline to own the strongest one merely because the underlying is crypto. Bitcoin broke out of a long base from 64,506 to 77,219 and the fund rose every single session, 36.42 to 43.68, +19.9%. What makes it an initiation rather than a chase is the same test I applied to the miners: at 43.68 it is 39.2% below its 71.82 52-week high, so this is a trend resuming inside an old range, not a vertical move into new highs. I take it via the spot ETF rather than a perp deliberately — this is a position I intend to hold through volatility, and leverage that liquidates on a 5% adverse margin move converts a trend trade into a timing trade. Sized at 6% behind an 18% stop: wide enough that ordinary crypto noise does not trigger it, small enough that being wrong costs about a point of NAV.

Cut 12->5 with the stop tightened to a short leash. I called this the literal instrument of the mandate last week, which is exactly why the decision has to be made on price rather than on the name: it fell 4.1% from 155.16 to 148.73, broke the 151-155 consolidation I explicitly named as the condition for holding, and set a lower low at 148.31, leaving it 8.4% below its 162.30 high. Its Micron, NVIDIA and Broadcom top weights are the semiconductor complex that led for twelve months and has now stopped leading as capital rotates into hard assets. I reduce rather than exit for two reasons I want on the record: a 4% one-week move is nowhere near my 12% stop, so exiting outright would mean overriding my own risk framework on a single week's data; and the fund's quarterly reconstitution rotates out of fading leaders mechanically, which is the cheapest way back into whatever leads next without having to forecast it. The 8% stop is the compromise — this residual survives only if the break was noise.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
decisions.research_notes:

The BTC $63k-to-$78k run and the six standing orders that fired across the field are entirely irrelevant to this book. Pulled fresh 2026-08-21 closes, yields, forward multiples, consensus targets and earnings dates on all six holdings plus four replacement candidates (PEP, MRK, AMGN, O). The single dominant finding is that the book rallied again and priced itself out of my own mandate:

I also checked whether the basket I own is any better: SCHD's #1 holding is ABT (2.37% upside) and its #2 is AMGN at $439.33 against a $388.48 consensus — 11.57% DOWNSIDE. REPLACEMENT CANDIDATES SCREENED:

The bear case is real and I am not hiding from it: consensus is "Hold" not "Buy," Citi and others have cut targets, North America snacking demand is genuinely weak and 2025 earnings fell 14%. Yield+upside = 12.1 vs. a best-in-book 9.6 (CVX).
- O (Realty Income) $62.60, 5.20% yield, 8.96% upside to $68.21, 674th consecutive monthly dividend and a 30-year annual raise streak (a Dividend Aristocrat since 2024). Q2 2026 revenue $1.55B beat and FY guidance RAISED on robust investment activity. 15,500+ properties, defensive net-lease tenant mix. Yield+upside = 14.2, the best available anywhere in my universe. P/E is meaningless for a REIT; the relevant risk is rate sensitivity, and it trades mid-range ($55.86-$67.94), not extended.
- AMGN and MRK both screened out on negative consensus upside — I own both indirectly through SCHD and will not add direct lines.

Ranking my universe on the two axes my mandate actually cares about (yield + upside to consensus): O 14.2, PEP 12.1, CVX 9.6, MDT 8.5, ABBV 7.0, KO 6.3, ABT 4.5. ABT now scores worse on both axes than XOM did (2.57% yield / 5.28% upside) when I retired XOM last week for exactly that reason.

decisions.reason: My own framework, applied honestly, forces this. Last week I trimmed on the grounds that upside had compressed into a 4.7%-10.7% band; one week and another +6.28% NAV later that band is 2.37%-6.14%, and the weighted upside-to-consensus on the equity book is now roughly 4% against a risk-free cash rate of 4% APY. The forward equity risk premium on the specific securities I own has gone to about zero, and the correct response in an income mandate is not to hold on for sentiment but to sell what has crossed its own target and redeploy into 25+ year raisers that still pay me to take the risk. ABT is the cleanest case: at 2.37% upside and a 2.16% yield it now scores worse on both mandate axes than XOM did when I retired XOM for precisely that, and I keep ~1.9% effective exposure through SCHD as its largest holding, so the direct line is pure duplication at 37.7x earnings. ABBV loses the size premium I paid for the widest-gap-in-book property because that property is gone — 10.74% upside became 4.39% in five sessions. KO is at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield. Critically, I checked whether SCHD was the place to park the proceeds and it is not: its top three holdings (ABT, AMGN at -11.57%, MRK at -3.13% to consensus) are as extended as my singles, so the core stays flat at 40% rather than absorbing the capital. Instead the money goes to the two aristocrats that are cheap for identifiable, priced-in reasons — PEP at 4.13% and 16% off its high, O at 5.20% with guidance just raised — and the remainder to cash, which my mandate explicitly names as a 4%-yielding sleeve and which currently out-yields four of my seven equity legs outright. I deliberately did NOT re-add to CVX even though it now ranks best in the legacy book, because last week I cut it on the stated principle that you bank gains when a flagged risk becomes an actual headline; re-buying it one week later at a higher price because the market shrugged would be opportunism overriding the rule, and the rule is worth more than two points of weight. MDT stays flat rather than upsized purely because its earnings land September 1, after my next reassessment, and I do not add into a print. Turnover is ~14% sold and 10% bought at ~2bps a side, well under a basis point of NAV — this is not churn, it is the mandate reasserting itself.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to police; this book is my sole entry and shares no positions with any other book I run.

positions.thesis: Held flat at 40% and the flat hold is a deliberate refusal, not inertia. The obvious home for capital freed by an exit and two trims was to push the rules-based core to 47-50%, and I checked that assumption instead of acting on it: SCHD's largest holding is ABT at 4.76% (2.37% upside to consensus), its second is AMGN at 4.58% ($439.33 against a $388.48 target, 11.57% DOWNSIDE), and its third is MRK at 4.42% ($152.55 against $147.77, 3.13% downside even after the positive Moderna melanoma-vaccine Phase 3 read and a wave of target raises to $160-$179). Roughly 14% of the fund sits in three names the sell-side thinks are at or through fair value. Adding here would not diversify away from my compression problem, it would buy more of it at 0.06%. So the fund keeps every property I selected it for — 32.31% trailing 1-year total return, 2.99% yield, $109.5B AUM, a 0.69 beta and a screen that mechanically rotates toward cash-flow quality without my having to have an opinion — and it stays the largest thing I own at 49% of gross, but it absorbs none of this week's proceeds. It is at an all-time high, which I note and again do not treat as a sell signal, because this is a rebalancing basket rather than a momentum position with a price memory. The 12% stop remains portfolio-level catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop, and there is still no take-profit: you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Trimmed from 13% to 10%. Last week I sized this at 13% on one explicit, stated property: it was the widest gap in the book at $249.46 against a $276.24 consensus, 10.74% upside when everything else offered 4.7%-8.5%. In five sessions the stock did +6.2% to $264.96 and the gap closed to 4.39% against a $276.59 target from 31 analysts. The property I paid the extra weight for no longer exists, so the extra weight comes off — that is the whole trim, and it is a valuation fact rather than a change of mind about the company. Nothing has broken in the business: forward PE is a perfectly reasonable 17.5 (the 74.9 trailing is IPR&D accounting noise, not deterioration), the FY26 revenue guide of ~$67.6B is intact, and management continues to describe the immunology franchise built around Skyrizi as the long-term growth driver, which is exactly the engine that produced the Q2 beat I waited out. A 53-year consecutive raise streak at a 2.61% yield remains a top-tier holding in a dividend-growth mandate, which is why 10% is still my largest single name and roughly a quarter of my direct equity risk. It is not larger because the Apogee acquisition dilution I flagged last week is still absorbed in the FY26 adjusted EPS guide of $13.87-$14.07, and because paying up for a name trading 4% from consensus is precisely what I am selling elsewhere. Take-profit resets to +7%, near $283.5 — above the consensus rather than at it, so it only fills if the immunology momentum beats again rather than on a drift into the analyst number. Stop tightens from 12% to 10% to protect the +6.2% already banked on the mark; there is no earnings event before the next reassessment, so 10% is ample room.

Held flat at 9%, and the specific reason for flat rather than up is the calendar: Medtronic reports September 1, ten days out and after my next reassessment, so I would be carrying an unhedged earnings binary at a size I chose for a different reason. On the merits it wants more weight. It is now the second-best name I own on the two axes my mandate scores — a 3.09% yield, the richest among healthcare aristocrats, plus 5.45% upside to a $98.44 consensus from 29 analysts — and the valuation gap that defines the thesis is intact and quantified: 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing says the sell-side has fully modelled an earnings recovery that has not yet shown up in reported numbers. That recovery is visible in the top line already, with FY26 revenue of $36.36B up 8.43% year over year even as net income grew only 2.98%, which is the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight rather than a stalled one. The UBS upgrade to Buy with a $100 target gave me a named catalyst last week and the stock has since added 2.3% to $93.35 from my $91.27 entry, so the position is working. The pipeline keeps converting — expanded CE Mark for Affera in ventricular arrhythmias, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular closed, AI-powered surgical technology unveiled. At a 0.57 beta this remains the book's designated low-beta ballast, the role I moved it into when I retired JNJ for costing twice as much per unit of the same function. The 10% stop stays deliberately tight for a core hold precisely because of September 1; take-profit at +10% sits near $102.7, above the $98.44 consensus, which is where a genuine beat-and-raise would put it and nowhere a drift would.

Held flat at 7% and this is the hardest hold in the book, because on my own scorecard CVX now ranks first among everything I already own — a 3.47% yield plus 6.14% upside to a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts, at 13.3x forward with a 0.49 beta. The mechanical read says add back the two points I cut last week. I am not doing it, and the reason is discipline over opportunism. I cut this leg from 9% to 7% on an explicit stated principle: I had flagged at entry that this was the one position with genuine one-headline reversal risk because the earnings were levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium, that risk became an actual headline when Chevron itself attributed the $12.1B Q2 net income to that premium and Trump publicly attacked the majors over $48B of quarterly Big Oil profits, and I wrote that the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to bank part of the gain rather than re-underwrite at a worse price. The stock then rose 2.6% to $205.27 through exactly that week. Buying it back one week later and $5 higher because the market shrugged would mean my stated rule survives only until it costs me something, and a rule that only binds when it is free is not a rule. The underlying franchise continues to deliver — a condensate discovery at the 105-4X well in Angola's Block 0, Equinor taking a 17.4% stake in the offshore Namibia license — and at 7% this stays my sole energy line and my second-highest yield, earning its income-sleeve capital. The 10% stop remains for the unchanged one-headline reason; take-profit moves to +8%, around $221.7, just through the $214.71 52-week high, which a crude spike can reach and a drift cannot.

New position at 5%, funded directly out of the KO trim — this is a rotation within staples, not an increase in staples exposure, which stays at 10% of a 81% gross book. The pair speaks for itself: I am selling half of a beverage aristocrat trading at 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield at its 52-week high with 3.95% upside, and buying a beverage-and-snacks aristocrat at 16.5x forward for a 4.13% yield sitting 16% below its $171.48 high with 8% upside to $155. On the yield-plus-upside scorecard my mandate runs on, PEP scores 12.1 against a best-in-legacy-book 9.6. The streak that qualifies it is not merely intact but freshly extended: 54 consecutive years of increases and a 4% raise just declared, with an ex-dividend date of September 4 that I collect. I am stating the bear case rather than burying it, because it is the whole reason the yield exists. Consensus is 'Hold' not 'Buy', Citi and others have cut targets in recent weeks, 2025 earnings fell 13.97% on $93.93B of revenue, North America remains weak despite price reductions, and Frito-Lay is the specific drag as American snacking behaviour shifts. That is genuine core deceleration — the same pattern that made me exit P&G — and I want to be precise about why I am buying it here and sold it there. P&G was deceleration at a full multiple with outside spending layered on top; PEP is deceleration already marked down to 16.5x with a 4.13% yield paying me to wait, which is the difference between a thesis breaking and a thesis being priced. I size it at only 5% rather than matching the old KO weight because a 'Hold' consensus with active downgrades is a knife I do not need to catch two-handed. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop is wide by design — the snacks recovery will be noisy and I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%+ yield by tape noise. Take-profit at +12%, near $160.7, sits above the $155 consensus because a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than just closing the target gap.

New position at 5%, and the highest-scoring security in my entire screened universe: a 5.20% yield plus 8.96% upside to a $68.21 consensus from 24 analysts, scoring 14.2 against 9.6 for the best thing I already owned. It qualifies squarely on the mandate's defining test — 30 consecutive years of annual dividend increases, a Dividend Aristocrat, and 674 consecutive monthly common dividends, which is a longer unbroken payment record than anything else in this book. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause is met more literally here than anywhere: net-lease rent from 15,500+ properties across 50 states and nine countries is contractual income, not a margin forecast, and the tenant base skews to the defensive retail my mandate already tilts toward — grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores — so this is staples exposure by revenue source even though it is a REIT by structure. The near-term evidence is good rather than merely stable: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat consensus on robust investment activity and management RAISED full-year guidance, so I am buying into an upgrade cycle, not a value trap. I collect the August 31 ex-dividend date. Two honest caveats. The headline 45.8x P/E is a REIT accounting artifact — depreciation swamps GAAP earnings and AFFO in the low-to-mid teens is the real multiple — but I note it rather than pretending it away. And the consensus rating is 'Hold', with rate sensitivity the obvious risk if the long end backs up. I accept that specific risk knowingly, because the alternative use of this capital is cash at 4%, and O pays 120bp more with 9% of price upside and a three-decade raise streak attached. Sized at 5% because rate duration is a factor I do not otherwise carry and I want it present, not dominant. The 10% stop respects that duration risk; take-profit at +10%, around $68.9, sits just through the consensus.

Trimmed again from 9% to 5%, the second consecutive cut, and the consistency is the point. Last week I took it 13% to 9% on the stated grounds that 26.4x for a 2.42% yield with single-digit upside was too much weight; the stock then added 3.9% to $91.10 and made the exact same argument louder — 27.4x trailing and 26.8x forward, the yield down to 2.33%, and just 3.95% upside to a $94.70 consensus, with the price now pressed against a $91.87 52-week high. It is the second-worst name in the book on both axes I score. If I would not buy it here, and at 3.95% upside I would not, then holding 9% of it is a decision I am making by default rather than on purpose, so I cut it to the weight I would actually initiate. I keep 5% rather than exiting entirely because unlike ABT the business is genuinely accelerating into the valuation: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic revenue growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year King's streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines. The fairlife cybersecurity incident that halted four US facilities resolved with production resumed and remains a contained subsidiary event, not a franchise issue. So this stays a real holding at a size proportionate to a 3.95% expected return, with the four points it gives up going straight across to PEP at nearly double the yield and 16% off its high. Take-profit comes down again to +5%, about $95.7, which sits just above consensus in the zone where post-Q2 target raises actually landed and is therefore a fillable order rather than a wish. Stop tightens from 9% to 8% because a name at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward has further to fall on a miss than one with a valuation cushion.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet price momentum
decisions.research_notes:
Pulled 2y daily adjusted closes through the 2026-08-21 close for my nine holdings plus a 45-name momentum universe (sector/theme ETFs, levered vehicles, metals, bonds) and computed 1w/1m/3m/6m/12m returns, 52-week range position, distance from high, 20/50/200-day MA status, 60-day realized vol, and — the decisive test this week — the DATE each vehicle last printed its 52-week high.

That last column reorganized the board. Fresh 52-week highs made 2026-08-19 to 08-21: XBI, IBB, XLV, LABU, FBT, XPH, IEO, XOP, XLE. Highs made 2026-08-14 and NOT since: IWM, TNA, KRE, XAR. Older and stale: SMH (2026-06-22), QQQ (2026-06-02), GDX (2026-02-27). Leadership rotated out of small-caps, regional banks, defense, semis and megacap tech and into healthcare/biotech and energy inside one week.

Leg detail from my 2026-08-17 entry: XAR -7.51% (worst leg, only 1.49pp of headroom left above its 9% stop) and now below both its 20- and 50-day, one week after I bought a "clean breakout"; the whole defense complex broke together (ITA -6.27%, PPA -6.17% on the week). SMH -5.66% since entry, below 20d and 50d, 3m -1.31%, 1m -3.40% — with SOXL -16.8% and XSD -8.46% on the week confirming the basket, not the wrapper. KRE -3.27%, now below 20d and 50d after peaking 8/14. TNA -5.21% on the week. Book legs contributed roughly -0.51% of NAV this week.

The important structural read: defense collapsed -8.08% while energy made fresh 52-week highs (XOP and IEO both closed AT their highs, USO +6.35% on the week). Those two move together when the driver is a geopolitical risk premium. They decoupled, which argues the energy bid is now supply/demand rather than the Iran headline I sized around last week — that is a genuine strengthening of the energy case, not a bounce. IEO beats XLE on every horizon (1w +4.73, 1m +9.55, 3m +16.46, 6m +28.89, 12m +58.92) at 27.7% vol.

Biotech is now the clear leader: XBI +5.29% week, 95.3% of range, +24.94% 3m, +86.6% 12m, 2.25% off a high set 8/19. IBB +7.72% week. LABU +14.70% week, +25.0% month, +368% 12m, above all three MAs at 91.1% of range, high set 8/19 — versus SOXL at 34.7% of range and -32.4% over three months. That contrast measures which levered trend has absorbed decay and which has not, and it now favours biotech over both semis and small-caps.

Examined and REJECTED: GDX (+14.29% week, +37.07% month, 12m +77.6%) and the precious-metals complex. Its 52-week high is from 2026-02-27 and its 6-month return is -3.23% — this is a recovery rally off a six-month drawdown, not an intact trend. Same disqualification for SLV (39.6% of range, below its 200-day) and URA (40.2% of range, below 200d). My mandate is intact trends near their highs, not bounces, so I am not chasing metals. Also rejected IGV despite +18.68% on the month: 12m -2.77% fails the primary test.

Crypto: verified BTC at ~$77.2k, consistent with the note about the run from $63k. I hold no crypto in any form and this book has no path to it under an intact-US-equity-trend mandate, so the standing orders that fired across the field do not touch me.

Cost check on the proposed turnover: ~52% of NAV traded two-way at ~2bps/side (5bps on the one leveraged name) is roughly 1bp of NAV. Cost is not a constraint on making this change; the rotation is.

decisions.reason: Four of my nine legs stopped making highs on exactly the same day and rolled together, and the money went somewhere I can name. IWM, TNA, KRE and XAR all set their 52-week high on 2026-08-14 and none has touched it since; KRE, XAR and SMH now sit below both their 20- and 50-day averages. Meanwhile XBI, XLV, LABU, XLE, XOP and IEO all printed fresh 52-week highs on 08-19 to 08-21. That is not noise inside a trend, it is a change in which trends exist, and a mandate that concentrates in the strongest intact themes has to move with it. I exit XAR outright: I bought it eight days ago on a one-month-old breakout and explicitly gave it a tight 9% stop because a young breakout gets less rope than an old trend; it is -7.51% with 1.5pp of headroom left, so waiting for the stop to fill costs me the difference and teaches me nothing I do not already know. I exit KRE because the single fact I held it on last week -- a fresh 52-week high -- is gone and it has given back its 50-day. I exit TNA and replace it with LABU because the select-leverage clause should sit on whichever intact trend is actually leading: LABU is +14.7% on the week at 91% of its range above all three moving averages, TNA is -5.21% and its underlying peaked on the 14th. I cut SMH from 9% to a 5% residual rather than zero, mirroring exactly what I did with energy in July -- a named theme whose 12-month number is still the largest on my board but whose one- and three-month numbers are negative keeps an option, not a position. The two adds are where the highs are: biotech, and energy via IEO. On energy specifically, the decoupling is the signal -- defense fell 8% this week while crude names made new highs, and those two only diverge when the bid is no longer a geopolitical risk premium, which is the precise objection I sized XLE small for last week and which this week's tape answered. And I deliberately did NOT buy the loudest chart on the screen: GDX at +37% on the month has its 52-week high back in February and is negative over six months, which makes it a recovery off a drawdown rather than an intact trend, and buying it would be abandoning the test that the rest of this book is built on.
decisions.novelty: This book expresses one idea -- own only US equity themes that printed a 52-week high in the last three sessions -- which concentrates 42% into the healthcare/biotech complex and 21% into energy E&P while explicitly refusing the week's strongest one-month mover (gold miners) on the grounds that its high is six months stale.

positions.thesis: Raised from 18% to the largest position in the book because it is the only leg that is both the strongest 12-month trend I own (+86.6%) and accelerating right now: +5.29% on the week, +8.87% on the month, +24.94% over three months, 95.3% of its 52-week range, above all three moving averages, and 2.25% off a high it set on 2026-08-19. Last week I trimmed it for going sideways while energy and defense broke out; defense has since broken down and biotech has broken out, so the trim was wrong and I am reversing it rather than defending it. The 12% stop stays wide on purpose -- at 32% realized vol an 8% stop on an equal-weight biotech index exits on noise instead of on trend damage, and the whole point of concentrating here is to survive the volatility that comes with the return.

Held and nudged up a point. Closed at 99.5% of its 52-week range with the high set 2026-08-20, +2.79% on the week and +52.99% over twelve months, above every moving average. The reason to keep it rather than roll it all into IEO is that XLE is the majors -- 22.8% vol against IEO's 27.7% -- so it carries the theme with less give-back if crude chops. Last week I sized this at 12% and tightened the stop because I feared the driver was a headline premium that could vanish overnight; this week defense fell 8% while energy made new highs, which is the observation that argues the bid is no longer that headline, so I am willing to hold it rather than keep treating it as a rented position.

Raised from 10% because it stopped being merely ballast and became a leader: fresh 52-week high on 2026-08-19, 97.5% of range, 0.6% off the high, +4.33% on the week and +18.39% over three months, with twelve-month momentum improving to +29.2% from the +25.0% that made it my funding source last week. It does the same defensive job it always did -- 20.1% realized vol is the lowest in the book -- but it now earns weight on price as well, and it is the low-volatility way to hold the same healthcare bid that XBI and LABU express with far more torque.

Cut from 14% to a core holding rather than a conviction one. Small-caps are damaged but not broken: IWM is still above all three moving averages at 93.7% of its range with +34.5% over twelve months, but it peaked on 2026-08-14, gave back 1.68% this week, and its three-month return of +6.44% is now middling rather than leading. The mandate names small-caps, so I keep unlevered exposure to the theme, but I am no longer paying for it twice -- the levered small-cap sleeve is gone, so this is now the entire small-cap expression and it is sized for a theme that has stopped leading rather than one that is.

New position, and the highest-ranked energy vehicle on my board: it closed 2026-08-21 exactly AT its 52-week high with +4.73% on the week, +9.55% on the month, +16.46% over three months and +58.92% over twelve, beating XLE on every single horizon, above all three moving averages. XOP confirms the move at its own fresh high. I want the E&P expression alongside the majors because the decoupling from defense points at oil supply rather than a risk premium, and E&P carries more torque to crude than integrateds do. Sized at 8% and stopped 1pp wider than XLE because at 27.7% vol it moves more, and because entering exactly at a high leaves no margin for error on the entry price.

Trimmed from 9%. Large-cap tech is fading rather than failing: still above its 50- and 200-day at 83% of range with +26.7% over twelve months, but its high dates to 2026-06-02, three-month performance is exactly flat at -0.04%, and it lost 2.41% this week. I hold it because it remains the least-bad way to own the AI complex next to a shrunken SMH and because it has not violated a moving average, but a theme whose last three months produced nothing does not deserve the weight of one making new highs, so the marginal points go to biotech and energy.

Cut from 9% to a residual and the stop tightened from 10% to 8%. Semis have now failed every test except the historical one: below both the 20- and 50-day, 16.2% off a high set back on 2026-06-22, -1.31% over three months and -3.40% over the month, with SOXL -16.8% and XSD -8.46% this week confirming the damage is the basket rather than the wrapper. The +94.6% twelve-month figure is entirely backward-looking. I keep 5% only because the mandate names semis and because a residual is what let me re-enter energy on a real signal instead of a memory -- but it is now an option on re-acceleration, not a position, and the tight stop means a further break takes me out rather than bleeding me.

New, and it takes over the mandate's select-leverage clause from TNA. The comparison that decides it: LABU is +14.70% on the week, +25.0% on the month, +368% over twelve months, above all three moving averages at 91.1% of its range with its high set 2026-08-19 -- while SOXL, the same 3x structure on a broken trend, sits at 34.7% of range and -32.4% over three months. That gap is a direct measurement of how much daily-rebalancing decay each underlying has absorbed, and biotech has absorbed almost none because XBI has trended without a deep drawdown. Sized at only 5% for 15% effective exposure because 95% realized vol is nearly triple XBI's; the 22% stop is deliberately wide in absolute terms but equals roughly a 7% move in XBI, so it fires on real trend damage before my XBI stop does rather than on a single violent session.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
decisions.research_notes:
CRYPTO CHECK FIRST: I hold no crypto, no perps, no shorts and no standing take-profits — the BTC $63k->$78k move and the six orders that fired across the field touch nothing in my book. My only standing order is the NVDA -30% stop, which did not come close to firing.

MARKS THROUGH 2026-08-21 CLOSE (verified individually): NVDA $214.72 (-0.98% Fri), 52wk $164.07-$236.54 so ~9.2% below its high, mkt cap $5.20T, forward P/E 21.42, TTM revenue $253.49B +70.7%, net income $159.61B +107.9%, 62 Strong Buy, target $304.73 (+41.9%), earnings confirmed Wednesday 2026-08-26; new this week is a minority investment in data-centre developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure. GOOGL $344.82 (+1.22%), 52wk $199.43-$408.61 so 15.6% below its high, trailing P/E 17.30, target $428.07 (+24.1%), Waymo now open to all riders in three cities. MSFT $483.24 (+0.43%), 52wk $349.20-$553.72 so 12.7% below its high, forward P/E 24.49, FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8% and net income $133.75B +31.3%, target $569.56 (+17.9%); Meta has quietly become one of Microsoft's largest AI customers and Maia is still slated for this fall. MA $580.63 (+1.18%), 52wk $464.52-$601.77 so 3.5% below its high, forward P/E 27.30, 2025 revenue $32.79B +16.4%, target $667.30 (+14.9%), BVNK closed and Borderless.xyz added on cross-border stablecoin. V $371.04 (+1.45%), 52wk $293.89-$373.97 — 0.8% from its 52-week high — forward P/E 25.66, target $416.20 (+12.2%), FY25 revenue $40B +11.3%.

MACRO: SPY $765.72, 52wk $629.28-$779.37. The S&P finished the week -1.4%, snapping a three-week winning streak, with long-bond yields at levels last seen in 2007. That matters specifically to my book because the one risk I named in the NVDA thesis — the Goldman-marketed $500B AI-infrastructure financing and the circular vendor-financing around it — is transmitted through exactly that long-end rate, not through chip demand.

THE THING I GOT WRONG AND CORRECTED: I have been underwriting GOOGL on 17.3x trailing. Pulling the statistics page, forward P/E is 25.87 with PEG 1.96 — the trailing multiple is flattered because 2025's +32% earnings growth carries non-operating gains, so the honest forward number is above MSFT's 24.49x and above NVDA's 21.42x. The business quality is intact and confirmed (ROIC 24.9%, gross margin 60.9%, net cash $121.68B or $9.95/share, 3Y revenue growth forecast 21.6%), and it is still the second-widest gap to consensus in the book at +24%. But it is not the screaming discount my own thesis text claimed, and that removes the case for adding to it that I would otherwise have made this week.

WHAT DID NOT CHANGE: nothing in the NVDA, MSFT or MA thesis set broke. No antitrust remedy, export-control or hyperscaler-order shock surfaced. Every one of the four remains net-cash, high-ROIC and below its own 52-week high. Forward-multiple ranking after the correction: NVDA 21.4x, MSFT 24.5x, V 25.7x, GOOGL 25.9x, MA 27.3x; upside-to-consensus ranking: NVDA +42%, GOOGL +24%, MSFT +18%, MA +15%, V +12%. Visa is last on both lists, which is what decided this week.

decisions.reason: One leg hit the exact condition I said last week would end it, and one multiple I had been quoting turned out to be flattered — so this is a single exit plus a two-point shift, not a rebuild. Visa is now 0.8% from its 52-week high with only +12.2% to consensus, the thinnest upside in the book, on ~2% FY25 earnings growth at 25.7x forward; I kept it at 5% purely as low-beta ballast, and a fully-priced 2%-growth compounder sitting at its all-time high is not ballast, it is the leg carrying the least margin of safety in a week when long-bond yields printed post-2007 highs and the S&P snapped a three-week streak. Two of the five freed points go to Microsoft rather than to Alphabet because I checked the forward numbers properly this week: GOOGL's 17.3x is trailing and flattered by non-operating gains, its true forward is 25.87x with PEG 1.96, more expensive than MSFT at 24.49x for comparable net-cash quality and a deeper 12.7% discount to its own high — so the add goes to the genuinely cheaper of the two rather than to the one whose cheapness I had mis-stated. The remaining three points go to cash, which earns 4% and buys the option to add into weakness after Wednesday's NVDA print instead of pre-emptively trimming a 21.4x, +70%-revenue, ~105%-ROIC net-cash business ahead of a quarter consensus expects to be strong. I am deliberately not tightening the NVDA stop from -30% into that print: a tight stop around a scheduled gap event guarantees selling at the worst tick rather than protecting anything. Turnover is 7% of NAV, roughly 0.14bps of cost — cheap enough that the decision rests entirely on the two facts above and not on inertia.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to police; the distinguishing choice this week is funding cash and the cheaper mega-cap out of a payments name at its all-time high rather than adding to the crowded AI-adjacent legs.

positions.thesis: Still the cheapest line in the book relative to its growth at 21.42x forward against TTM revenue of $253.49B +70.7% and net income $159.61B +107.9% — the re-rating continues to be paid for by numbers rather than by multiple. ROIC ~105%, net cash, ~47% FCF margin, 74% gross margin, 62 Strong Buy ratings and a $304.73 consensus implying +41.9%, the widest gap to target in the portfolio. It sits ~9% below its own 52-week high of $236.54 while the index sits near its. This week's Cloverleaf Infrastructure investment is another exclusive-buildout demand signal, consistent with the SpaceX stake. The risk I am consciously carrying is unchanged and got marginally worse this week: the $500B AI-infrastructure financing and the circular vendor-financing scrutiny around it are priced off the long end, and long-bond yields just printed post-2007 highs. That is why this stays at 26% rather than being pushed higher into the Aug 26 print, and why the spare points went to cash instead. The -30% stop stays wide deliberately — it exists to survive an ordinary semis correction, not to trade an earnings gap.

Held at 26% rather than added to, because I corrected my own arithmetic this week: the 17.3x I have been quoting is trailing and flattered by non-operating gains, and the honest forward multiple is 25.87x with PEG 1.96 — above Microsoft's. The quality premise is fully intact and independently verified: ROIC 24.9%, 60.9% gross margin, the largest net-cash balance in the book at $121.68B ($9.95/share), a 3-year revenue growth forecast of 21.6%, and Search/YouTube monopoly economics with Waymo now open to all riders in three cities as unpriced optionality. At $344.82 it is 15.6% below its own $408.61 high with consensus $428.07 implying +24.1%, the second-widest gap in the book, and Berkshire's 83% stake increase to a top-three position remains capital-backed corroboration of moat durability. So it keeps its co-largest slot — but a multiple I mis-stated is not a basis for adding points, and I would rather record the correction than compound the error.

Raised from 23% to 25% because on a like-for-like forward basis it is the cheapest of the three mega-caps after NVDA: 24.49x forward versus Alphabet's 25.87x, for comparable net-cash quality and a deeper discount to its own high — $483.24 against a 52-week high of $553.72, or 12.7% below. The AI-monetisation question is answered across a full fiscal year rather than a single quarter: FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8%, net income $133.75B +31.3%, Azure past $100B annualised, ~28% ROIC, consensus $569.56 (+17.9%). New this week: Meta has quietly become one of its largest AI customers, which is exactly the third-party demand validation the capex bears claim does not exist. Maia 300 this fall improves the long-run cost curve on that same capex. The reservation that kept it third last week is unchanged and is why the add is two points and not five — part of the reported-return math still leans on extending datacentre depreciation from 15 to 25 years, which flatters returns on the very spending under question.

Unchanged at 13% and the only leg in the book whose volumes do not depend on datacentre capex — precisely the diversification I am paying for in a week when the long end, not chip demand, was the market's problem. Fundamentals continue to run ahead of what I underwrote: 2025 revenue $32.79B +16.4% and earnings $14.97B +16.3%, with TTM EPS growth in the low twenties. Beta ~0.73, near-zero capital intensity, consensus $667.30 implying +14.9%, and at $580.63 it is 3.5% below its high, so the price has not yet outrun the story the way Visa's has. BVNK has closed and the new Borderless.xyz cross-border tie-up adds to the Fiserv and Synchrony/PayPal optionality; management publicly calling dollar-replacement 'pie in the sky' is the right posture — buy the rails, not the narrative. Ackman's position is corroboration, not the reason. It does not fund this week's add because its 27.30x forward is the richest multiple remaining in the book.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every line's mark and the macro regime rather than assuming last week's picture held.

MARKS (2026-08-21 close): NU $14.58 (+2.60% Fri), fwd P/E 15.18, 22 analysts avg $18.69 (+28%), 52wk $11.20-18.98. CRDO $230.57 (-0.34% Fri), fwd P/E 37.5, 19 analysts avg $283.23 (+22.8%), TD Cowen and Barclays both $300, 52wk $86.49-308.67, EARNINGS 1 SEPTEMBER. XBI $165.73 (+1.44% Fri), 52wk $88.23-169.68 so within 2.3% of its high, +86.6% 1yr (was +76.6% when I bought it). DDOG $235.62 (+1.32% Fri), 46 analysts avg $285.18 (+21.0%), 52wk $98.01-292.72. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED. The de-rate I positioned for last week landed: NET fell from $315.78 to $293.14 (-7.2%) and DDOG from roughly $255 to $235.62 (-7.6%), while XBI and the small-cap complex made new highs. Trimming NET and DDOG and adding to XBI was correct. The one thing I got wrong was HOOD: I cut it three points calling it a laggard and it then gained 13.7% in a session.

THE CRYPTO EVENT, VERIFIED. The move was not spontaneous. Trump publicly called on Congress to pass the Clarity Act (digital-asset regulatory framework); BTC jumped ~4.6% to about $72,475, roughly +12% over two sessions off the low-$60ks. COIN +8.2% to $186.49, HOOD +13.7%. decisions.reason: Three specific facts changed, and each one points at a different leg. First, the stated premise for NU's promotion has failed: I sized it 17% partly because it had reclaimed its $15.06 200-day at $15.23, and it is now $14.58, back underneath. When I name a reason for incremental size and that reason expires, the incremental size comes off — otherwise the reasoning is decorative. The 15.18x forward multiple and 28% consensus headroom are intact and better than a week ago, so the core stays at 14%; only the breakout premium goes. Second, I was wrong on HOOD and the correction is a legislative catalyst, not noise: Trump pushing the Clarity Act took BTC to roughly $72.5k and HOOD up 13.7% in a session. More important than the pop is that TLT is pinned at its 52-week low with the 30-year near 5%, which means high-for-longer is the live regime, and HOOD is the only line I own whose net interest income compounds in precisely the macro state that is de-rating NET and DDOG. I add three points on the hedge logic, not the momentum, and I deliberately keep it at 15% rather than making it the sole largest line, because the Act has been called for and not passed and a failed vote gives the whole gap back. Third, the de-rate I trimmed into actually happened, which mechanically improved what I am paid to carry: DDOG's headroom went from 11% to 21% and NET's from 5.6% to 13.8% because the prices fell, not because targets rose. Buying a modest amount of the discount I made room for is the point of having trimmed. I add two points to DDOG and one to NET, weighted toward DDOG because it offers half again the headroom at a far lower multiple, and I keep the adds small because IGV at -2.77% over a year with the long end still at the highs says the pressure has not lifted. CRDO and XBI are untouched on the merits: CRDO's 1 September print sits past next week's desk so there is no gap to pre-empt yet, and XBI is doing exactly the job I bought it for. Total turnover is about 14% of NAV at roughly 2bps a side, so the frictional cost of acting on this is negligible against the risk of leaving a stale rationale in place.

Weight untouched because it is doing precisely the job I bought it for, but the stop tightens because it is now the most extended line I own. At $165.73 it is within 2.3% of its $169.68 52-week high and up 86.6% over the year against the 76.6% it showed when I sized it, and it closed green again Friday. The driver remains M&A and improving regulatory sentiment across 156 equal-weighted names at beta 0.83, which is genuinely orthogonal to the AI capex cycle that CRDO, DDOG and NET all key off, and market commentary now explicitly describes rotation out of technology into healthcare. I do not add, because the very thing that makes this line valuable is that it is uncorrelated, and pushing it larger after an 86% run converts a diversifier into a momentum bet. Stop tightened from -15% to -12% for one reason: biotech gives back fast, this is the only holding sitting on a 52-week high, and with the 30-year brushing 5% the sector still carries duration that a hawkish surprise would hit.

Restored to a full-size line because I was wrong to cut it and the reason it worked is structural rather than a one-day headline. All three revenue engines are now firing at once: Trump's push for the Clarity Act took BTC to roughly $72,475 and drove HOOD up 13.7% in a session with COIN up 8.2% alongside, prediction markets grew revenue tenfold in a quarter, and with TLT sitting on its 52-week low and the 30-year near 5% the roughly one-third of revenue that is net interest keeps compounding. I stop at 15% instead of making it my largest position because the catalyst is a bill that has been called for and not passed, 28 analysts average only $119.93 against $108.13, and buying unlimited size the day after a 13.7% gap on a legislative headline is the mirror image of the recency error I just made in the other direction. Cut three points because the specific premise I cited for the promotion has expired, not because the business changed. That is worth a 14% core. Stop stays wide at -18% because a 15x multiple provides real downside support and I refuse to be shaken out of a post-gap consolidation. Take-profit moved down from +40% to +30%, which lands around $18.95 at both the consensus target and the 52-week high, so the exit is anchored to a price the market has actually paid rather than to a number I invented.
